Our project focuses on the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, a vast collection of formally verified mathematics, to explore its complexity and analyze the underlying methods, such as proof styles, used to encode these concepts. Based on the findings, we offer guidelines for authors on structuring their work, employing common methods, and organizing their output. Additionally, we share our tools, which include a set of automated commands to generate statistics and visualizations, to help further develop the archive. Furthermore, we propose ways to enhance the quality and consistency of new contributions, including the introduction of a formal guideline document. Our initiative aims to facilitate the development of the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, ultimately aiming to make the majority of its content maintainable by a single person. The associated project resources, including our tools and the generated statistics, can be found at https://framework-in-theorem-verification.github.io/ and on GitHub at https://github.com/framework-in-theorem-verification. A related idea is the Coq MIND tool to help maintain the Coq Competition archive, which can be accessed at https://mind-in-theorem-verification.github.io/. The framework represents recall as a linguistic queryable facility for retrieving stored knowledge and leverages it to address the challenges of semantic parsing, a task requiring nuanced understanding of natural language. We outline the framework's underlying principles and illustrate its operationality through a simplified example utilizing Prolog. For practical applications, we discuss possible enhancements to the framework's representability and delineate its theoretical and practical distinctions from analogous concepts like database schema and schema-based web services. Furthermore, this research provides a foundation for declaring and executing informal procedural tasks using a declarative memory recall mechanism, thus bridging the gap between machine learning and symbolic rule-based knowledge representation. As a result, applications like information extraction and semantic parsing become feasible and the declarative memory recall can be utilized as either data pre-processing or post-processing. The framework's primary advantage lies in its ability to merge structured and non-structured data, effectively incorporating human-centric and artificial entities respectively. Additionally, this research highlights the importance of establishing a unified understanding of the two types of data and presents a novel approach to integrate them seamlessly. The framework's current implementation is available for public use. Lastly, future research directions are proposed. Precise nuclear mass measurements are essential for understanding various astrophysical phenomena, including the nucleosynthesis processes that occur during the rapid neutron capture process in rare astronomical events such as supernovae and explosive events like the pressurized shock from a collapsing star's core. A significant amount of data is needed to fully investigate these phenomena, which often conflict with the limited resources available for mass measurements. However, recent advancements in computing allow for the incorporation of new information sources, particularly machine learning algorithms. This research aims to measure the masses of hard-to-reach isotopes, including neutron-rich nuclei, by combining data from existing laboratory measurements and theoretical models using a machine learning approach. By extending a previously trained Gaussian Process to previously unmeasured isotopes, including 268082, 268084, 310112, and several other nuclei, our results show that the masses of these isotopes can be accurately determined, with errors predicted to be less than 100 keV, a level of precision necessary for the investigation of $r$-process events. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of machine learning in measuring nuclear masses, enabling us to account for uncertainties in the masses of newly discovered, previously uncharacterized isotopes. A significant consideration of our approach involves selecting the appropriate training and implementation methods for the machine learning model, which may ultimately influence the model's performance and reliability. Similar to measurements obtained through nuclear reactions, our results can also be validated by comparing the calculated masses to future experimental data. Our results indicate that the masses of newly measured isotopes can be consistently determined in experiments, with calculated masses showing a 1-to-1 correlation with errors of less than 0.5 keV. These predicted mass values, ranging from -6 to 12 MeV, are consistent with the hypothetical masses of unmeasured isotopes within the predicted uncertainty limits. When incorporating these newly measured masses into the calculation of trans-Fe isotones, our findings demonstrate that the total binding energy levels of these isotones closely follow the expected pattern of the nuclear mass surface as determined by Gaussian Processes. By investigating specific examples of isotopes within the actinide series, our research reveals that the model effectively captures the complex relationships between these isotopes and neighboring nuclei, including the predicted existence of a magic number of 106 particles. Our team has developed a technique for measuring the dielectric loss of microsapphire components with precision beyond 1 billion parts per billion. This is accomplished by using the'split-line' method, which relies on the analysis of two distinct transmission lines within a chain of high-Q LC circuits. The interaction between these linear elements and adjustable DC currents enables us to determine the dielectric loss through observations of the spectrum's spacing between sidebands, as this loss directly affects the Rabi frequency. Our device, which includes two separate microsapphire resonators and operates at a 4.5 GHz frequency, has allowed us to achieve an exceptional level of sensitivity, thereby facilitating the measurement of incredibly low dielectric attenuation rates. Specifically, we have measured the dielectric loss with an accuracy of 170 million parts per billion, which marks the smallest such measurement ever recorded. Our study of the dielectric loss serves as a comprehensive review of the phenomenon, encompassing both intrinsic and extrinsic dielectric losses, as well as their respective temperature and magnetic field dependencies. This research not only supplies the dielectric loss rates but also provides a solid theoretical foundation for the description of dielectric losses in terms of quantum mechanics. Our experimental findings demonstrate that dielectric losses in microsapphire components, which are commonly utilized in superconducting quantum processors, are predominantly extrinsic in nature. This discovery holds significant implications for the enhancement of the performance of such systems, where dielectric losses regularly serve as a major constraint. Our work highlights the potential of the'split-line' method to identify and measure the dielectric loss with unparalleled precision, thereby aiding the optimization of the components and conditions required for quantum computing hardware. This optimization could theoretically result in the enhancement of the maximum two-qubit gate speed limit to as much as 100 MHz, thereby transcending the limitations imposed by dielectric losses. Our research also serves as a model for measuring dielectric losses in various fields, which may find applications in the assessment of superconducting quantum systems, nanomechanics, and other quantum technologies. This study demonstrates the value of utilizing'split-line' spectroscopy in the precise measurement of the dielectric loss and has the potential to contribute to the development of future quantum technologies. Finally, we've initiated a discussion on the feasibility of using the optical pull effect to develop a high-resolution temperature sensor. We develop a novel modeling technique for robust optimization problems encompassing discrete uncertainty with continuous outcomes, utilizing a modified probability simplex cone. By constraining decision variables to form an exact probability basis, this model accurately captures probability transformation functions with binary dependencies. To address computational inefficiencies, we apply an iterative algorithm based on the Lagrangian dual method, which produces certificates of optimality and can be combined with other algorithms, such as Benders' decomposition, to enhance solution quality in two-stage robust optimization problems. We test the effectiveness of this approach through experiments on networks with uncertain capacities and a machine learning application involving multi-category prediction. For real-world problems involving mixed-integer decisions, we use an iterative Benders decomposition algorithm with the modified Lagrangian dual method in its inner problem. Numerical results demonstrate that the algorithm yields superior solutions to standard robust optimization problems. Due to its combinatorial nature, the modified probability simplex cone enables the generation of tight lower bounds and precise solution outcomes. Furthermore, the algorithm provides certificates of optimality for outer relaxation solutions and can be applied as a pre-processing step to filter candidate support sets in two-stage robust optimization problems. Our proposed algorithm is shown to outperform other methods, such as the greedy algorithm for reduced complexity solutions, as well as standard methods for large-scale problems without certification. We provide an open-source implementation of this algorithm at the following GitHub repository, which can be used for high-performance computing applications. Ultimately, the algorithm offers a novel way to enhance the computational efficiency and solution quality of robust optimization problems with discrete uncertainty and continuous outcomes. We anticipate its generalization to more complex problems as an area of future research. Neural network architectures that process graph data leverage node and edge relationships using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In contrast to traditional deep networks' focus on image or sound features, GNNs focus on exploiting graph structures to predict outcomes. The effectiveness of GNNs depends on selecting suitable layers, networks, and training methods. Graph representation learning is an emerging field that has gained momentum in various applications like node classification, link prediction, and graph representation learning. Research into GNNs has been conducted in an isolated setting, neglecting factors such as sharing knowledge across tasks, which is a common practice in deep learning. Our goal is to conduct a comprehensive analysis of GNN architectures' performance on multiple tasks, including semantic information transfer, by drawing insights from a survey of 96 published works on transfer learning. Our study evaluates how six popular GNN models and linear models perform on five dataset configurations, using six different training and testing task combinations, and optimising for both accuracy and transfer on the validation set, resulting in significant transfers of up to 48.9% with the average being 19.1%. Our code and experiments are available for reproduction on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/ GavinKy/Graph-NAS. Our experiment also indicated that models with latent representation transfer better than those with one-hot encoding, and the performance of GNN models depends on the choice of layer, with graph convolution being the strongest layer, and the degree layer having the weakest performance. Additionally, the performance of GNN models also depends on the choice of final layer, and the deep architectures perform better than shallow ones. Our study also indicated that the performance of GNN models can be improved by improving the performance of edge aggregation methods, and the performance of learning methods that adapt to node properties. Finally, the experiment indicated that future studies should conduct a thorough analysis of the impact of various design choices on the performance of GNN models in a more systematic way. The outcome of this study is the development of a platform for evaluating the performance of GNN models, and the platform can be used by researchers in the field of graph deep learning. The platform conducts a comprehensive analysis of the impact of various design choices on the performance of GNN models, and the platform enables researchers to share knowledge across tasks by retraining the models on the Facebook 042 datasets platform. As the internet grows, the information overload problem continues to hinder user experience across various platforms, including websites, social networks, and news feeds. A significant challenge is the information's relevance to users, compounded by the speed at which online content is generated and published. Various systems have been developed to address this issue, notably recommendation systems that provide personalized content suggestions to users, reducing their information overload. However, a significant shortcoming of existing systems is that they primarily aim to maximize user satisfaction in providing the most relevant content at the right time. Since users' preferences often shift over time, this strategy can ultimately lead to a suboptimal outcome. A more effective approach is to adapt a content stream in real-time by dynamically modifying the stream's characteristics, including the relevance and interest levels of individual items. By doing so, the system can ensure a continuous stream of relevant content, even as users' preferences evolve. A particular challenge in this context is that the optimal stream may not have a clear, interpretable structure, making it difficult to decide which items to include in the stream and how to configure the resulting content blocks. To address this issue, we introduce the Dual Feature Allocation Model, a Bayesian nonparametric model that enables online content streaming with seamless transitions between relevant items. Moreover, the model's flexible structure allows for easy customization through two adjustable parameters, determining the size of the resulting content blocks and the type of items within them. A key contribution of our work is that these parameters can be efficiently learned in a real-world setting with minimal supervision and human intervention. By applying the proposed model to the problem of news suggestion, we develop an innovative news suggestion system for readers to easily discover new articles. A user study involving 30 participants demonstrates that the proposed system successfully provides relevant content over extended periods, aligning with users' diverse interests and varying levels of engagement. Additionally, the results show that the system's performance can be further improved with the guidance of human preferences, even with minimal adjustment of the model's parameters. We develop a multi-diffraction method for molding electronic properties of quantum devices at the atomic level. Our approach begins with optimizing the momentum of an electron beam emitted from a source material through a series of angled nanostructures. These structures, spaced closely enough that the electron beam remains coherent, allow the electron wavevector to split and reflect multiple times off internal surfaces, allowing the electron to home in on specific atoms within devices. We propose the use of this method for scanning single-atom transmission electron microscopy (SAMT-EM), enhancing its selectivity by potentially increasing the yield of atoms imaged per second. By designing SAMT-EM with the ability to surround the electron source with materials of variable composition, the technique becomes auto-calibrating and resistant to variations in microscope focus. For the sake of efficiency, we also investigate the use of pre-prepared atomic patterns to guide the electron beam to specific locations within devices, a strategy that could aid in building complex quantum materials from the atomic level up. The design process for these patterns, based on the concept of coherent beam spread, is a key component of this investigation. Our findings open the door for the use of EM microscopy with previously unachievable resolutions and operate at the intersection of electron microscopy, materials science, and quantum engineering. Our work suggests new avenues for developing ultra-sensitive EM instruments capable of revealing the quantum nature of matter in various applications, including the characterization of quantum materials and the integration of quantum dots. Furthermore, the techniques developed can also be applied to illuminating atomic structures within nanoscale waveguides and to detecting the atomic-scale confinement of light. Ultimately, the use of multi-diffraction techniques to design electron trajectories holds the potential for significantly advancing the performance of quantum devices and EM instruments. A two-dimensional system with a specific band structure and exposed to a magnetic field is investigated for transport properties. This system is studied using a semi-classical approximation applicable to systems with little disorder. The Hall conductance is calculated based on the Landauer-Büttiker formalism and initial findings suggest that interaction effects are negligible in conductance despite disorder. However, as correlation parameters are considered, interaction effects can significantly impact conductance, leading to a non-linear Hall response. Furthermore, analyzing the system under ferromagnetic correlations and disorder shows that interactions and disorder compete in their effects, leading to a unique form of Hall conductance. Notably, a strong, nonlinear Hall response emerges when correlations are considered, and this effect is related to the system's Chern number. The latter is equivalent to the topological invariant obtained from a free fermion system and represents the total charge flowing along the edge of the system. Moreover, a nonlinear response model is formulated and a method to extract the full Chern number is developed through the linear and nonlinear conductance. This is achieved by extending the Landauer-Büttiker formalism to include non-linear terms and applying a formalism that relates the conductance to Chern numbers even in the presence of interactions and disorder. Finally, a second-order non-linear Hall conductance is calculated and its relationship with the Chern number is established. Additionally, the study demonstrates that interactions and disorder induce a cross-Jarzinski effect, allowing for the full Chern number to be extracted from a two-terminal setup by applying a parallel magnetic field, and this effect is relevant for 1D systems as well. Moreover, a method to achieve quantized Hall conductance even in the presence of interactions and disorder is developed by considering a specific form of correlations. The study shows that interactions and disorder induce a transverse current when a parallel magnetic field is applied, and this effect is equivalent to the Hall conductance of a free fermion system. By extending the Hilbert-Chantal effective Hamiltonian to a general form, the study demonstrates that interactions and disorder can be used to achieve a quantized Hall conductance even in the presence of interactions and disorder. The results are relevant for quantum simulations with cold atoms and systems of spinless fermions, as well as for materials with a non-interacting fermions, such as quantum anomalous Hall insulators. Atherosclerosis, a condition where the buildup of plaque may restrict blood flow, poses a substantial threat to patients' health. In an effort to increase oxygen levels in the brain, surgeons often turn to bypass grafts as a last resort. When two patients undergo simultaneous surgery, researchers have discovered a way to increase breathing synchronization odds through dynamic assistance. This paper involves modeling patient breathing patterns. By applying data-driven methods to a specific observational study, we aim to develop a model that accurately predicts oxygen levels in the brain based on several key variables including blood vessel complexity, respiratory rates, and oxygen intake. This model will serve as a foundation for creating a real-time algorithm that adjusts respiratory therapy for optimal results, with the ultimate goal of maximizing patient outcomes and quality of life. Using a direct transcription approach, we have developed a nonlinear model that incorporates multiple factors. This model highlights the value of data-driven approaches in medical settings and serves as a foundation for creating real-time algorithms with the potential to significantly improve patient results. Focusing on respiratory therapy, our model shows the significant impact it can have on the most critical aspects of patient care and quality of life, and how similar models can be created for other translational biomedical applications in the future. The bicritical nature of $f$ and its corresponding invariant line allow for a geometric interpretation of $R_{f} \cap Aut_{\mathbb{P}^1}(f)}$. Furthermore, $Aut_{\mathbb{P}^1}(f)$ can be further broken down into the following components: elements within the group consisting of elements $z \mapsto \frac{1}{c} \cdot z$ and elements $z \mapsto a \cdot z$ where $a$ is a location on the complex number unit circle, denoted $A_{\mathbb{P}^1}(f)$. The bicriticality of $f$ and its corresponding invariant line also enable the determination of the order in which certain components of $Aut_{\mathbb{P}^1}(f)$ operate, specifically those within $A_{\mathbb{P}^1}(f)$ and the elements not within this group. Two-layer sheets of transition-metal dichalcogenides, such as MoSe2 and WS2, have been studied to explore how their work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity vary with thickness. By modeling and computing, researchers found that the work function of these materials decreases in three-way, burried, and hybrid configurations compared to a single two-atom layer, with energies of 4.64, 4.71, and 4.67 eV, respectively. Similarly, their ionization potentials decrease with thickness, with computed values of 5.36, 5.21, and 5.44 eV for two-atom, three-atom, and hybrid configurations, respectively. However, the electron affinity of these materials exhibits an increase in three-atom configurations but shows no variation or a decrease in two-atom, hybrid, and burried configurations. The researchers attributed these findings to the impact of macroscopic thickness on the materials' environmental interaction, such as varying charge transfer like in the case of the buried configuration of MoSe2-WSe2, in comparison to their hybrid and single two-atom counterparts. Furthermore, the study reveals that the three-atom layer MoSe2 has the lowest fundamental gap, with a 1.18 eV gap in the hybrid and burried MoSe2-WSe2 configurations being significantly larger, with a 2.05 and 1.65 eV gap, respectively. The study also finds that the hybrid MoSe2-WSe2 exhibits a 2.05 eV fundamental gap, with a 1.64 eV gap for the burried configuration. These computed band gaps were found using the GW method, known for its great accuracy among DFT approximations and predictions. The study suggests that the work function of these materials could serve as an indicator to track their thickness variations. The band gaps calculated in this study were found to be in agreement with the findings of other high-accuracy calculations and experiments. The study offers a comprehensive understanding of the thickness variations of the work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity of two-layer sheets of transition-metal dichalcogenides. The rationale and explanations behind these findings, the impact of these thickness-driven changes on the materials' density of states, and the computational methods employed are thoroughly presented in this study. The study provides valuable insights to technologists working with these materials, with a particular focus on their thickness-driven changes. Change transmission, the process by which a signal modifies a system in real-time, is an emerging paradigm with far-reaching implications for artificial intelligence systems that can adapt to new information.  This paper introduces a mathematical representation of change transmission, referred to as delta lenses, and uses this framework to create universal supervised learning algorithms for neural networks.  These algorithms are based on the principle of equilibrium, allowing a system to incorporate new knowledge by balancing its current state and a projected future state, and can be applied across different neural network architectures, regardless of the system's original state.  This ability to adapt and respond to changing information is then applied to the domain of artificial neural systems and biological networks.  Additionally, the paper demonstrates the mathematical equivalence of change transmission with delta lenses and the balanced gradient system, providing a unified understanding of these concepts in the context of artificial intelligence and biological systems.  This research provides a foundation for a new generation of AI systems that can seamlessly incorporate new information and adapt to complex, high-dimensional data sets, as well as insights into the underlying mechanisms of change transmission in biological systems.  Furthermore, the paper highlights a key difference between the balanced and standard models of change transmission, revealing that most biological systems tend to converge towards equilibrium rather than optimal outcomes, as seen in the case of the well-known Lotka-Volterra model.  This important consideration underscores the potential dangers of AI systems that prioritize optimal outcomes over convergence, as seen in the case of self-reinforcing feedback loops.  Finally, the paper applies the principles of change transmission to the biological domain of artificial neural systems and suggests that future advancements in neuroscience and biotechnology could lead to the development of compact, atavistic systems capable of uploading and sharing knowledge across various artificial and biological domains.  This potential development could, in turn, accelerate the rate of progress in artificial intelligence and the related fields of bioinformation and change transmission.  As such, the paper provides an important foundation for a new generation of AI systems and biological technologies that can harness the power of change transmission to drive innovation and change the world. As an alternative, iterative techniques such as the linearization method are employed, involving iterative updates toward a solution under a dynamically evolving equilibrium state. However, large iterations leading to reasonable solutions necessitate computationally costly processes with CPU times ranging from hours to days. Notably, the collision operator's small local values, which ensure gas flow continuity while minimizing CPU time for simulations, also tend to result in small velocity changes during iterations, further extending computational time.

By exploiting the local maxima of the collision operator, this modified approach generates more substantial velocity changes during iterations, potentially reducing the required number of iterations and, in tandem, CPU time. Pencil-like solutions, which incorporate molecular exchange at the microscopic level, serve as the foundation for this modified method. Our work focuses on the p-divisibility of the Fourier components within the theta measures associated with primitive integral Siegel modular forms of degree (n+1), where n is at least 1. We provide a specific criterion in terms of the properties of the modular form's Fourier series and its relationship with the representation of its weight by quadratic forms. This criterion serves as a generalized version of a proven statement for n equals 0, which is equivalent to the Ramanujan delta function. Consequently, leveraging our established criterion, we are able to conclude that the p-divisibility of the Fourier components is consistently achievable. This achievement is particularly noteworthy in the context of Siegel modular forms that are known to have large weights or a specific type of Fourier expansion, as evidenced by examples in the work of Kitaoka-Akatsuka. Moreover, an additional consequence of our findings is the establishment of a specific upper bound for a standardized measure in the context of genus one elliptic curves, where the standardization is based on the type (an+b) of the modular form. The primary goal of this paper is to establish a precise understanding of sequences derived from sequences of fibrations with a fixed rigidity. A comprehensive universe with a hierarchy of types is employed for this purpose. The paper begins by introducing and exploring properties of the concept of rigidity. It then defines and studies precise sequences of fibrations, which are themselves a novel category, and establishes a correspondence between such sequences and isomorphisms between modules with a fixed degree of purity. By demonstrating an inductive relationship between the levels of purity and the categories of fibrations, the paper achieves a significant advancement in the theory of fibrations with a rigorous and comprehensive framework. This framework resolves long-standing open questions in the field, which have been discussed in a series of papers since 2005. Researchers exploring data-driven projects often encounter a major hurdle when trying to work with data that is stored in the Transit Feed Specification (TFS) format. Despite its growing popularity, which has led to numerous datasets being made publicly available, working with TFS is a laborious and error-prone process. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution in the form of an open-source neural network-based tool, which can generate TFS-compatible GTFS.zip files directly from the common tabular data structures like Pandas DataFrames. This tool is designed to simplify data processing and management, reducing the likelihood of mistakes that often plague manual TFS conversions. Our method's core consists of a set of carefully engineered algorithms, which are complemented by a practical demonstration showing its effectiveness in processing real-world datasets to 3D geometric data structures for an intelligent bike-sharing station predictor. By providing accessible code, pre-trained models, and suggesting possible extensions, this project aims to establish a new standard for TFS data processing and pave the way for future developments. Our approach's core algorithms and the entire project are available for use under the MIT license at https://github.com/hiinstamp/GTFS_fromDataFrame. Additionally, the pre-trained model can be directly deployed at https://haila-i.informatik.uni-frankfurt.de/bfm-geo-bike. An interactive demonstration of the method can be accessed at https://hiinstamp.github.io/GFST_fromDataFrame/. A related scientific video illustrating our work and its potential applications in urban settings can be found at https://youtu.be/wz_9D2y7gms. Future space-based observatories such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are expected to generate vast amounts of light data, including supernovae, galactic astronomy, and cosmology data. Classical statistical methods used for classification in these areas often fail to take into account the complex patterns in the data. In contrast, deep neural networks show promise in this field, but face challenges due to their inherently non-random nature, making it difficult to assess uncertainty and obtain accurate probability predictions. In supervised learning, Bayesian Neural Networks offer a potential solution by enabling the estimation of uncertainty at an image level. Our work involves the implementation of two BNN models using a real supernovae dataset from the Legacy Survey of Space and Time, including standard neural network components and a method to replace dropout layers. Our analysis includes uncertainty and classification metrics for these BNN models, in addition to a comparison with corresponding standard oversampling methods. Our findings indicate that BNNs outperform conventional CNNs in total classification accuracy, as well as in objective log-likelihood and precision-recall curves. Moreover, by using a label smoothing technique, a measure of model confidence can be obtained, mirroring the Rubin Observatory's 4 billion pixel charge-coupled device 'Luci' image format. We developed two novel local search methods tailored for the Budgeted Maximum Coverage problem, which shares similarities with this challenge. Our algorithms prioritize search strategies that minimize unnecessary computations and combine simple hyper-neighbourhood methods to ensure thorough exploration. We modified standard Max Conflict-free Maximal Matching algorithms, integrating conflict indicators to boost search efficiency and item selection fairness. Our product-based search strategies involve simultaneously adjusting items from multiple solutions, following a first-come-first-served approach. We also introduced a prioritized max matching procedure to optimize the selected items' potential for new solutions' creation. In the realm of online gaming and betting, customer retention is a top priority. 
A key issue is attrition, namely, the phenomenon where loyal customers stop
interacting with the service over a specified period. Predicting when and why
customers may cease engaging with the service or switch to rivals is a critical
challenge for businesses in this industry. This study presents an innovative
application of machine learning models designed to forecast when and why
customers may cancel their accounts. We successfully adapted established models 
like the Mixed Poisson Regression and the Capture-Retain-Attrite (CRA) model, 
initially created to model account status transitions over a set period, to 
forecast account cancellation within a specified timeframe. Our research also 
evaluates the performance of deep learning models as an alternative. To inform 
these models, we develop new features, combining real-time streaming signals 
with comprehensive user attributes, including past transaction records and 
account history. For example, we create a "at-risk" variable, indicating how 
much customers are at risk of cancellation based on their spending patterns, 
and distinguish between churning and non-churning customers during the final 
Cancellation Risk Period. In addition to quantitative models, our solution 
involves a Bayesian-enhanced Markov chain to provide a 95% confidence interval 
of the predicted cancellation probability. This allows online betting businesses 
to personalize their communication with customers, including timely 
communications-channels, to persuade account holders from cancelling their 
accounts or prevent them from switching to rivals. Our experiments with the data 
from an online betting firm demonstrate that these models achieve impressive 
accuracy, with a 85% to 90% hit rate in forecasting account cancellation within 
a specified timeframe. This study offers the first practical solution to cancel 
forecasting and cancellation prevention in the online betting and other service 
industries. Our study also extends the applications of the CRA model, originally

The growing popularity of cycling as a mode of transportation poses challenges to safe coexistence with automated vehicles. To address these challenges, our research focuses on developing predictive models of cyclist motions that automated vehicles can use to mitigate collisions. Prior studies have suggested that incorporating context and considering variability in pedestrian and cyclist movements is crucial for effective collision avoidance systems. In response to these findings, our team designed a risk assessment tool that takes into account the relative position, path, and speeds of cyclists and vehicles. By utilizing a comprehensive dataset of expert cyclists under various conditions, we trained this model to mimic expert riders' decision-making and observed that it performs equally well as human cyclists when simulating real-world scenarios. When tested on a challenging scenario, our model successfully identified and predicted most of a cyclist's visible pre-collision maneuvers, including braking, turning, and continuing straight. Notably, the model performed particularly well at predicting straight-line movements, with an accuracy of over 90%. By leveraging context and modeling video-based inputs, our system achieves state-of-the-art performance in simulating diverse cyclist behaviors, which has implications for automated vehicle safety. As a result, this model has the potential to contribute significantly to automated vehicle safety and is suitable for integration into collision avoidance systems. Moreover, this system can serve as a benchmark for evaluating the realism of automated vehicle risk descriptors for cyclists. This study proposes an advanced approach to robotic motion planning that prioritizes safety and adaptability to unpredictable environments. By dividing the challenge into two tasks - reaching the target and avoiding obstacles - and using control barrier functions, we develop a flexible and efficient planning framework with low computational requirements. The framework consists of an open-loop planner that calculates a initial trajectory and a closed-loop controller that ensures the robot stays on track and responds to sudden disruptions in real-time. Analogously, in the realm of ring theory, the bounding numbers of rings capture essential properties of rings. Specifically, for any infinite ring R, a Ramsey type number called the bounding number of R is defined. Unique to ring theory is the large family of subring-determining sets in R. Any set A with this property, when combined with its symmetric difference with another set B, yields the same subrings in R. If a large family of such sets have a finite cover, it implies the bounding number of R is finite. If no such finite cover exists, it implies the bounding number of R is large. We explore the properties of the bounding numbers of rings, including the relationship between the density of graphs G and the bounding numbers of rings R, if G is embedded in R. We also introduce an infinite family of rings where the bounding number of each ring is infinite. In the realm of gas dynamics, particular interest is afforded to kinetic and macroscopic models of fluid dynamics. The latter typically comprises conservation laws accompanied by a constitutive entropy, whose maximum principle ensures global entropy increase and the suppression of shocks. However, in regimes far from equilibrium, conventional entropy admissibility conditions become ineffective, necessitating a different theoretical framework. This absence of analytical tools has prompted the development of numerical methods aimed at approximating solutions to these equations. This paper explores the entropic consistency of numerical schemes in the nonlocal framework. Specifically, we examine a class of nonlocal models characterized by functions with arbitrary dependence, rather than the traditional von Neumann-Botella model with a specific shell-structure. Our approach involves analyzing the model's singular limit case, followed by the entropic consistency of a corresponding finite difference scheme, and finally verifying the scheme's rate of convergence. The method employed is reminiscent of the entropy dissipation linearization technique (EDL), originally developed for the analysis of discrete kinetic models. Nevertheless, due to nonlocal models' lack of a Fokker-Planck structure, we have introduced a new, more fundamental framework for the entropy dissipation linearization method. This framework, grounded in the dual approach of Leinhardt and Gordon, is applicable to a wide array of nonlocal models characterized by complex functions with arbitrary dependence. As an additional consequence of this framework's generalizability, we have been able to demonstrate the convergence of nonlocal models to the corresponding partial differential equations under specific approximation limits. Furthermore, our analysis has led to the derivation of precise rates of convergence for solutions to these models. These findings are of independent value, while also extending and refining previous research in the field. The method employed in this study is equally applicable to a wide array of nonlocal models, including those related to the widely recognized Frankl problem and its generalized versions in the context of the shell-structure model. As an illustration of the model's versatility, we have also explored the application of the method to a version of the Frankl problem with a rate of convergence. Due to space constraints, the detailed derivation of our main results is presented in the accompanying thesis, which has been filed with the local authorities. Further research is required to expand the method to a version of the Frankl problem with a rate of convergence, as well as to explore the possibility of deriving more precise rates of convergence for nonlocal models with complex functions with arbitrary dependence. We define an intersection index called the horizon saddle index for surfaces in a particular mathematical structure, and expand on existing definitions from previous studies. This new index, along with a type of intersection transcription, enables the generalization of notions from previous studies to any surface in a 2-dimensional sphere environment, without the need for additional assumptions about these surfaces' properties. Next, we establish a relationship between dilation surfaces and surfaces in a 2-dimensional sphere environment, enabling the application of our newly developed concepts to these surfaces. Since dilation surfaces are preliminary examples of recently discovered "ideal trinions", which have no geometric counterparts, this link represents a significant finding. Finally, we apply our analysis methods to a category of generalized hyperelliptic surfaces, characterized by minimal elliptic characteristics, and determine the configuration of their intersection points in relation to the fiber topology. This study provides a complete classification of these intersection points' behavior and confirms previous studies' findings on the structure of these intersection points, while also extending our analysis to various cases. Notably, we identify novel types of intersection points and demonstrate that all generalized hyperelliptic surfaces exhibit a particular cycle of change when viewed as part of a general category of surfaces. This cycle of change serves as a key factor in the identification of a 4-dimensional cycle of change for curves of constant curvature, which in turn helps to explain a link discovered by Dubrobin et al. between the structure of intersection points and system dynamics. As an additional finding, we demonstrate that all ideal trinions may possess a 4-dimensional cycle of change, connecting them to a type of cyclic behavior observed in dynamical systems. This finding represents a link of potential significance for researchers in the study of surface geometry and system dynamics. Systematic methods for the analysis of surface intersection points could facilitate the discovery of new ideal trinions, which in turn may reveal novel patterns and relationships in these fields of study. Notably, these methods could also be applied to a type of surface called compact deformation, which in turn may enable the analysis of intersection points on these surfaces. Notwithstanding our focus on these surfaces, the primary finding of this study - the generalized intersection index - remains a broad and versatile concept that can be applied to a wide range of surfaces beyond those discussed here. Notably, these surfaces may also be used as a key factor in the analysis of curve properties and system dynamics at a fundamental level. Notwithstanding these connections, the most basic level of system analysis - the study of system cycles - remains an open area of study. Notably

The human mind's functional connectome is a representation of neural relationships among distinct regions in the brain. Traditional approaches to study the functional connectome have been restricted due to a lack of sufficient and accurate brain data. However, large-scale brain imaging has become feasible through advanced techniques like resting-state fMRI, enabling the exploration of the functional connectome. Despite numerous analyses using correlation as a link measure between brain regions, this method has its limitations, as correlations can sometimes fail to represent causal relationships and is sensitive to noise. To address these limitations, we introduce the concept of Total Association, which quantifies the functional link between two brain regions using mutual information, correlation, and non-parametric density estimates. We demonstrate the efficacy of Total Association in studying the functional connectome and utilize it to identify seeds in graph algorithms. We also apply deep learning techniques to study the graph structure, and use the analysis to explain various aspects of brain functions such as resting state brain networks, local memory circuits, and the language attention mechanism of transformers. Our analysis reveals that the functional connectome contains prominent clubs, communities, and nodes of high importance, which have been linked to specific human traits and diseases. We also demonstrate the feasibility of local memory circuits using Total Association and reveal the causal relationships between aricular cartilage degeneration and knee rubbing. Our analysis also demonstrates the efficiency of Total Association in identifying the language attention mechanism of transformers. Finally, we employ Total Association to study the brain dynamics across species and demonstrate the feasibility of cross species analysis. We also demonstrate the efficiency of Total Association in identifying causal relationships between smoking and lung cancer. We conclude that Total Association is a versatile tool for studying brain dynamics and can be utilized for a variety of other biological and medical applications. Total Association is available as a open source Python library that can be utilized for a variety of applications in systems biology and medicine. The analysis utilizes large scale brain data available through public sources, as well as medical imaging data. The code is available at https://github.com/indianinstituteofscience/Total-Association. The transformer-based models are available at https://api.inci.io/totassoc/transformer. The code and data for the cross species analysis is available at https://github.com/indianinstituteofscience/Total-Association/tree/main/cross-species.

The classical Segal-Bargmann theory reveals that a unitary transformation from the complex Hilbert space of polynomial functions on $\mathbb{C}^d$ equipped with the norm $L^2(\xi_i)$ to the Fock space of $\mathbb{C}^d$ is represented by the Segal-Bargmann map.  In this study, a similar Clifford-algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann map is formulated and demonstrated to be isomorphic to the Taylor transformation.  The latter transforms Clifford-algebra-valued polynomial functions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ to Clifford-algebra-valued homogeneous elements in the Clifford algebra of the Fock space of $\mathbb{R}^d$.  A key step in establishing this isomorphism was the discovery of a new monomial representation of the Clifford algebra in terms of elements of the Fock space of $\mathbb{R}^d$.  This new representation of the Clifford algebra is denoted the $\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}$-representation.  The $\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}$-representation extends the conventional Fock representation of the Clifford algebra and facilitates the extension of Clifford-algebra-valued functions from the classical domain to a larger domain.  The relationship between these representations of the Clifford algebra and points on a paraboloid in $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ in a coordinate-independent (sheaf-theoretic) way is also investigated.  This relationship is denoted the paraboloid sheaf $\mathcal{P}$.  The Clifford-algebra-valued functions on the paraboloid are related to elements in a specific quotient of the Clifford algebra.  These functions form a space isomorphic to a specific unitary representation of the Lorentz group on a subspace of a Clifford algebra element space.  This unitary representation extends a previously published Lorentz group representation in physics literature.  The Segal-Bargmann map and Taylor isomorphism are revealed to be special instances of a Clifford-algebra-valued Clifford group element transformation from the classical $\mathbb{R}^d$ domain to its $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ extension.  This transformation transforms Clifford-algebra-valued functions on the Clifford group to elements in a specific quotient of the Clifford algebra.  The transformation forms a unitary representation of the extended Clifford group with extended domain and image.  The transformation also defines a sheaf

The notion of pathwise conditioning of a Gaussian field $G$ given another Gaussian field $F$ originates from the real-line case where the Gaussian distribution $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ can be expressed as a conditioning operation for another Gaussian distribution $N(\mu',\sigma'^2)$. This results in the conditional distribution $N(\mu,\sigma^2)|F=\mu'+\sigma'\zeta)$ being standard normal for any real $\zeta$. In the context of Gaussian fields, the conditioning of a Gaussian process by a Gaussian field based on the underlying space of $G$ is explored. This is framed within the context of the existing theory of irregular operator ideals, specifically with regard to the ideal of transversal operators, known as $[\perp]$. For Gaussian fields $G$ with specific properties related to sample mean square integrability and separability, the existence of pathwise conditionings by other Gaussian fields $F$ is demonstrated, including cases where the underlying space of $G$ is a Banach or Hilbert space. This work also provides conditions under which unique pathwise conditioning by Gaussian fields is ensured and investigates the question of whether pathwise conditioning by a Gaussian field is a unique feature among Gaussian field conditions. Additionally, the field of $G$ being a Banach space is used as a case study to demonstrate these conclusions. Finally, the method of operator ideals is used to establish a connection between pathwise conditioning and the concept of irreducibility, specifically with regard to the properties of $(\alpha,\beta)$-cocoherent operators. This is in addition to the investigation of conditions under the sole influence of mean square integrability, without requiring separability. Moreover, the underlying space of $G$ can be any locally convex space, thus broadening the scope of these findings. Following this, an examination is made of the significant differences between the sample integrability requirements for conditioning on the real line versus the underlying space of a Gaussian field, highlighting a notable gap in the literature. This work is split into two self-contained parts, the first focusing on the scope of sample integrability in the underlying space of $G$ and making significant contributions to the literature, specifically [CS91], [CS95], and [Sz00]. A 52-node test ground-and-sky distributed sensor network employing wireless radios was established on the top of the Santa Cruz Mountains' mountain crest, capturing temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, sky temperature, and solar radiation data for an 8-hour period at 10-minute intervals. The radio sensors were positioned at 40 intervals on the ground and 12 above the ground at roof-level, and data from both ground-level and roof-level sensors was transmitted to a central node equipped with a 2MB wireless USB adapter. The collection of this multi-modal data lasted 5 months during both summer and winter seasons, and the implementation showed that wireless connectivity is a suitable and reliable option for distributed sensor networks. The evaluation also involved determining the optimal antenna placement for future deployments and the most effective data transmission strategy to minimize interference from other devices. The outcome of this evaluation confirmed that wireless connectivity is a viable and trustworthy method for synchronizing a distributed sensor network. The theoretical underpinning of wireless communication, specifically the Rayleigh signal scattering model and Rician fading in wireless sky-to-ground and ground-to-ground connections, was also explored as compared to the actual measured signal strength through comparison. The study further observed that wireless ground-to-ground connections exhibited more consistency with the theoretical model than ground-to-space connections. Consequently, it is implied that wireless ground-to-ground links could be utilized for creating a ground-to-ground shadow radio network that can aid in maintaining ground-to-space connections. The concept involves utilizing a central node as a retransmission hub for sensitive or intermittent sky temperature and atmospheric pressure data. The outcome of this implementation demonstrated that wireless connectivity is a viable and trustworthy method for synchronizing a distributed sensor network. The collection of this information can potentially be exploited to model key environmental characteristics, such as atmospheric pressure distribution across the sky and ground levels and temperature profiles. The study highlights that there exist significant discrepancies between ground- and sky-level atmospheric pressure, suggesting a ground-based model may effectively predict atmospheric pressure across the sky. Similarly, it is found that there exists only a slight variation between ground- and sky temperatures, suggesting a ground-based model may effectively predict sky temperatures. The outcome of this implementation demonstrates that wireless connectivity is a valuable tool for advancing our understanding of atmospheric phenomena. Eventually, the study shows that wireless connectivity is a valuable asset for ground-based meteorological research and could be a crucial element in future meteorological research. Additionally, it is hoped that this information will also have practical applications in areas such as agriculture, specifically precision agriculture techniques. We examine the validity of a widely used assumption in top tagging techniques, specifically the limitation that a hadronic decay product must not exceed the mass of a top quark. To test its robustness, we conduct a systematic evaluation of light jet combinations in top substructures. Our application of enhanced top tagging involves reclassifying particles to primary and secondary tops using a modified tagging procedure. By calculating Shapley values for all particles, we show that a significant portion of top substructure configurations yields more profit with the refined tagging procedure. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the success of the original top tagging technique in light jet scenarios with large mass limitations largely results from neglecting possible contributions of secondary tops. By strategically including these secondary tops as primary tops, we achieve substantial improvements in signal acceptance for 1-3 jet topologies in both t-t and t-h scenarios. We anticipate these findings to be generally applicable to any top tagging algorithm. After performing a detailed sensitivity analysis, we estimate that the assumed threshold of a 1 TeV mass limit incurs a loss of 20-40% in discovery significance for 1 jet, 5-15% for 2 jet, and 1-5% for 3 jet cases. By implementing the refined tagging procedure, we achieve increased sensitivity, amounting to 30-60% improvement in discovery significance for 1 jet, 10-35% for 2 jet, and 5-20% for 3 jet cases. Using Shapley values, we demonstrate that the secondary top contribution to top tagging algorithms is substantial in such scenarios, accounting for a value of at least $\sim$$0.15 in scenarios with large mass limitations. Furthermore, the interpretation of such values in scenarios involving mock benchmark models shows that the assumption of a hadronic decay mass limitation of a top quark mass is valid for regions of parameter space where the coupling to the Higgs particle is weak and the mass of the lightest supersymmetric particle is greater than the mass of a top quark. On the other hand, the assumption of a hadronic decay mass limit of a top quark mass does not hold for regions of parameter space where the coupling to the Higgs particle is strong or the mass of the lightest supersymmetric particle is less than the mass of a top quark. In such regions, the contribution of secondary tops to discovery significance may be substantial. This research centers on translating Voice of the customer (VoC) meanings into a formal framework and evaluating the efficacy of each VoC in a given context, as well as merging related VoCs into broader categories. We've successfully implemented these concepts in a formal setting using a context-free grammar and relational algebra, and their applications are showcased through a concrete example. By leveraging formal methods, our approach enables VoC meanings to be adaptable to diverse scenarios, allowing VoCs to be tailored to specific use cases without compromising their inherent meaning. Furthermore, this methodology serves as a starting point for developing sophisticated natural language processing (NLP) systems capable of voicing and categorizing customer sentiments in a structured format. Building on this foundation, we're exploring the utilization of formal concepts and techniques to enhance NLP systems and identify implicit relationships within customer feedback. In our upcoming work, we plan to utilize these discoveries to create a unified framework integrating existing NLP technologies, and also investigate methods for extracting voicing information from customer feedback even when phrases are ambiguous or have multiple possible meanings. This project aims to ultimately benefit industries by transforming textual data into standardized, structured inputs that can be leveraged more efficiently. In particular, we envision our work enabling voicing and categorization capabilities to be integrated into various systems, providing a deeper understanding of customer sentiments and behavior patterns in a measurable format that can be utilized in system design and development. Furthermore, such analysis capabilities could also inform the generation of automated customer responses (e.g., in chatbots) based on the patterns and themes present in customer feedback. We also intend to analyze customer sentiment patterns over time and recognize explicit or implicit requests for product improvements based on repeated customer queries and desires for product enhancements. By achieving these goals, we're confident that our approach can yield significant, data-driven insights for both businesses and their customers, ultimately leading to a more informed, customer-centered approach. We're currently working on the second aspect of our research, which involves the automatic extraction of voicing information from customer feedback even when the language used is informal or ambiguous. This requires the integration of multiple NLP technologies, including part-of-speech analysis and various machine learning models, in order to prioritize the relevance and efficiency of the voicing information with minimal manual oversight required. In our research, we're employing the concept of entity relation graphs (ERG) to standardize and structure voicing information in a standardized format. ERG allows the creation of node and edge labels in a graph based on specific rules and guidelines, effectively providing a structured interface for voicing

In order to speed up the training process of reinforcement learning agents, researchers have introduced the concept of experience replay. This strategy involves storing past interactions and replaying them as part of the agent's training. The standard method of priority experience replay is designed to improve the efficacy of replay by prioritizing episodes or transitions with higher rewards and their inversely related importance weights. The current research presents a new approach, variance decrease based experience replay, that efficiently use information from high reward containing episodes and transitions without the need for calculating an importance weight. The proposed method is validated through its application in the Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm, resulting in successful outcomes on multiple benchmark problems. The experiments show that variance decrease based experience replay achieves training performance comparable to priority experience replay with a significantly reduced computational overhead. Furthermore, the research demonstrates the theoretical basis for our approach, showcasing its general applicability to off-policy algorithms, including their theoretical connections to policy enhancement. The findings indicate that utilizing a second optimization process can lead to a direct relationship between the optimization process and the estimated action-value function, resulting in the formulation of policy enhancement. The theoretical work highlights the relationship between policy enhancement and natural gradient descent and demonstrates how natural gradient descent can lead to the minimization of the KL divergence between the old and new policies. The research also introduces a new metric, transient entropy, that may serve as a stabilization criterion during the policy optimization process. The experiments show that minimizing transient entropy leads to stabilization and improves the overall training performance of the agent. The complete implementation of variance decrease based experience replay is available at the repository located in the reference at the bottom. The repository includes the source code and the data that was used in the generation of the results presented in the paper. The results indicate that variance decrease based experience replay achieves reliable training performance even when exposed to noisy data. This property makes it suitable for applications requiring robust systems, as demonstrated by our results on an application of a robotic system subject to external forces beyond the modeled distribution. The research presents the results of the experiment and demonstrates the property of robustness in the learned agent. The results show that variance decrease based experience replay achieves generalization to out-of-distribution data, as evidenced by the results of the experiment where the agent is trained using a variety of data and achieves superior performance on an unseen environment not seen during the training process. The research also introduces a new method for generating results presented in the paper, specifically an application of a task automaton to automate the results generation process. The results show that task automata can be utilized as a tool

Recent advances in machine learning and data enrichment methods have improved single-image forecasting significantly, yet the capability to accurately predict detailed motion is still limited in image-based spatiotemporal forecasting. In this study, we introduce Multi-view Differential Representation MoDeRNN, a novel approach that uses multi-view representation and differential operator alignment to generate a novel data framework. This novel framework can efficiently capture high-level motion details and is compatible with recurrent neural networks, such as those used in CNN-RNN hybrids. Our results confirm that MD-RNN achieves superior performance in both 2D and 2D+1 forecasting, outperforming alternative methods like integrating optical flow and hierarchical hidden state learning. In particular, MD-RNN is effective in 2D forecasting, surpassing state-of-the-art methods in both single-image and video forecasting on datasets like DrivingData, FluidData, and TreePendulum. Notably, our approach also facilitates new optical flow prediction methods, where the extracted motion details from a target frame are utilized along with initial optical flow. This combination of motion details and optical flow enables the model to generalize better and accurately predicts detailed motion. When applied to $n$-qubit quantum circuits with $m$ gates, it uses $O(m)$ memory. This method is an improvement over previous studies on quantum verification, which had either higher time complexities or increased memory usage. Our study introduces a new understanding of quantum verification, utilizing a flow-based verification approach, leading to a breakthrough in time efficiency and verification complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that verifying closed quantum circuits is more complex, requiring $O(m^2)$ memory. Additionally, we propose specific applications where this method facilitates faster verification, resulting in improved runtime. Our study also explores the difficulties in verifying quantum circuits with specific properties (unitarity, trace preservation) in closed circuits. Notably, for open quantum circuits, we demonstrate the possibility of validating trace preservation in $O(m)$ time with $O(dm)$ memory usage. While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning by leveraging permutations of factorization order and, due to its autoregressive formulation, avoids the limitations faced by BERT. Moreover, XLNet incorporates key aspects from the advanced autoregressive model, Transformer-XL, thereby achieving notable advancements. According to comprehensive benchmark testing under similar settings, XLNet consistently outperforms BERT across 20 tasks, including several benchmark assessments, by substantial margins. Furthermore, XLNet sets new standards for state-of-the-art performance on key tasks such as SQuAD 1.1, SQuAD 2.0, and RBer, while exhibiting superior efficiency than Transformer-XL. Experimental analysis reveals that the primary advantage of XLNet lies in its ability to effectively model the contextual dependency between any two pieces of text, regardless of their positional relationship in the input sequence. This capability is distinct from BERT's ability to model positional contextual information. Moreover, XLNet's performance is notably improved by handling the pretraining process at a factorization order permutation level rather than individual tokens. The corresponding code and pre-trained models for XLNet have been made publicly available at the website https://github.com/yeray Santana/XLNet.

Research into the locomotion patterns of Arthropoda, particularly centipedes, has revealed similarities between their gait mechanics and principles of naval propulsion. Whereas naval propulsion relies on hydrodynamic forces, centipedes' movement on water surfaces utilizes buoyancy forces, as evidenced by the gecko-like single-film walking technique they employ. Our study delves into the dynamics of centipedes' water surface locomotion, as exemplified by the lightweight centipede, Eupolybothrus, through a combination of field observations, laboratory analysis, and computational modeling. Our investigation, grounded in measurements and experiments, identifies the primary factors governing their gait dynamics and establishes a theoretical framework based on these findings. The unique gait dynamics of these Arthropoda, characterized by the interplay of resistive forces and the absence of propulsion forces, presents an intriguing case. Our research not only offers new insights into the mechanics of centipedes' water surface locomotion but also explores the broader applications of their gait dynamics to the design of soft robotic systems and drag reduction strategies. Moreover, our work highlights the adaptive capabilities of Arthropoda's water surface locomotion, a phenomenon distinct from their terrestrial locomotion, as exemplified by the anatomical adaptations of their leg structures. To our knowledge, this research marks the first documentation of Arthropoda's water surface locomotion dynamics, supplementing the existing knowledge on their terrestrial gait dynamics. Our study, characterized by the integration of experimental and computational approaches, sheds new light on the fundamental principles governing the dynamics of water surface locomotion, as well as the adaptations of the subject's anatomy and physiology. Our approach subsumes the probabilistic $\pi$-calculus and CSP with probabilistic annotations and unspecified receiving variables, thus providing a more comprehensive basis for understanding quantitative aspects within concurrent software systems and communication protocols. Specifically, we formalize the concept of entropy, define its equivalence relative to a subject's observation capability, and establish a compositionality principle for abstract concealed Markov models within the CSP dialect. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of our framework through a real-world example illustrating the application of compositionality in the context of a confidential chat room. Furthermore, we provide a semantic interpretation of our construct within the applied $\pi$-calculus, thus highlighting the connection between our work and existing Markov models. However, our treatment in the applied $\pi$-calculus setting does not follow a denotational semantics but rather a nominal one based on a distributive bi-modal semantics with an embedded modal operator describing the actor's perspective in a given process. This study has been presented in a paper at the 32nd Workshop on the Semantic Framework for Applied Modal Logics, hosted by CFIL. The associated presentation can be found at slideshare.net. Furthermore, a related thesis containing the initial version of this content was published in a dissertation by the first author. Our work focuses on a, to date, underrepresented area within process algebra research, which investigates the parameterised composition of probabilistic Markovian processes under partial observability and without full abstracion. CompEArT is a comprehensive software system designed for computing scattering phenomena in particle physics model extensions. It can utilize a variety of effective theory models, including dimension-$6$ effective operators, and compute observable cross-sections, scattering matrices, and partial widths essential for defining photon-pair production operators in the context of $\text{EFT}$~\cite{deBl\'ajanque:2021ovs}. Furthermore, the system facilitates the definition of specific "behavioral" models to simulate how particular "behavioral" particles, e.g. Z', behave during scattering processes. These "behavioral" models can be used in conjunction with observable measurements or CMB data to set limits on the production of such "behavioral" particles. Currently, the system is capable of computing $\gamma \gamma \to W^+ W^-$ and $4 \gamma$ scattering, as well as the matrix elements necessary for defining the "behavioral" models mentioned. It accepts a range of parameters, including masses and couplings for "behavioral" models, and is able to generate "behavioral" matrix elements and widths for simple decays. Future updates will include the integration of "behavioral" models for $3 \gamma$ and Higgs decay into $\gamma \gamma$, and the ability to define "behavioral" models for fermion pair production, e.g. $\gamma \gamma \to f \bar{f}$. This document provides an overview of the system and generates "behavioral" matrix elements and widths for use in simulating the production of such "behavioral" particles, e.g. Z' during scattering processes. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the electromagnetic interactions between a blackbody and two parallel dielectric plates, positioned to reflect the incoming radiation from the blackbody. Similar to the Casimir effect, the energy exchange between the blackbody and the mirrors affects the blackbody's thermodynamics, leading to altered radiation spectra. To model this interaction, the classical electromagnetic field formalism is combined with Maxwell's address function, incorporating reflection coefficients for different electromagnetic modes. By modifying the traditional blackbody radiation formulas using product integrals of these reflection coefficients, the effects of mirror radiation on the blackbody are calculated. These calculations yield new spectra with enhanced energy densities and altered frequency distributions. The total energy density of the modified system is demonstrated to be thermodynamically stable, yet dynamically unstable. Furthermore, the altered radiation mechanisms lead to novel energy patterns and flow directions, even in equilibrium states. These findings may have significant implications for future space missions, particularly in scenarios where the Casimir effect could potentially alter thermodynamic equilibrium. The study also explores generalizations of these concepts in the context of relativistic invariants and discusses methods for calculating reflection coefficients. Additionally, the equilibrium thermodynamics of the system are examined in detail, including demonstrations that entropy and energy inversely depend on the spectral density distribution, and that the radiation energy density is proportional to the temperature. These findings align with traditional blackbody thermodynamics, while the energy exchange is zero. The study culminates with discussion of the system's electromagnetic fine structure and possible applications to the polarization anomaly in Magellanic Cloud globular stars. The investigation reveals the possibility of resolving this anomaly using a variant of the Lamb shift theory, as well as the coexistence of zero-point energy and thermal energy, and a potential connection between zero-point energy and thermal radiation in the far-infrared and submillimeter spectral ranges. The study may also shed light on the mechanism behind highly polarizationized optical radiation from red supergiant stars. The work includes various supplementary materials. A popular method for 3D point cloud localization utilizes point cloud-based depth sensors to determine a device's position within a constructed 3D environment. Conventional methods, such as 3D descriptors and PC-Localizations, employ global descriptors like Global Point Cloud Descriptors, to align reference and query point clouds, but suffer from inaccuracies due to alignment issues and limited contextual understanding. Alternative methods focus on 2D feature learning within the point cloud, but are susceptible to errors and lack contextual knowledge. Our research introduces the Normal Distribution Transform Depiction (NDD), based on the principle that a point cloud's local geometry adheres to certain statistical patterns. We combine this with a novel Transformer architecture, the NDT-Transformer, which captures the 3D point cloud's contextual information by focusing on the probability density of the local normal distribution. Our approach leverages this information to provide more precise geometric insights and improve localization accuracy. We conducted extensive experiments on the IFM PC-Localisation Dataset and the Real-world 3D point cloud dataset, outperforming existing point cloud-based PC-Localizations methods. Our research makes the NDD-Transformer code publicly available for the benefit of the Machine Learning and Geolocation communities. A secondary demonstration can be found at the accompanying YouTube video. Furthermore, affiliated authors have published relevant work at the workshops of the ICML, IJCAI and CVPR conferences.  The IFM-PC-Localisation dataset was presented at the workshops of the ICML, IJCAI and CVPR conferences.  The Real-world 3D point cloud dataset was published separately by the dataset's original authors.  The YouTube video mentioned in the acknowledgement statement can be accessed via the provided link. Furthermore, affiliated authors have published related work at the workshops of the ICML, IJCAI and CVPR conferences. Recent advancements in word embedding have greatly improved performance for code-mixed language models. Although positional encoding has been crucial in enhancing model achievements, its uniform application across sentences has been suboptimal. This paper introduces a novel approach called PESTO, which incorporates a transition point positional encoding (TPPE) scheme for code-mixed texts. The proposed method considers the inherent properties of code-mixed sentences by dividing them into English and non-English parts, incorporating transition points between language switches, and leveraging time-related positional information. Experimental results in code-mixed English-Portuguese and English-Spanish text classification datasets have shown TPPE to outperform traditional positional encoding methods. Furthermore, combining single-linguage monolithic approaches with the TPPE scheme achieved comparable or superior outcomes compared to existing code-mixed language models, including neural machine translation techniques. The proposed framework also led to significant time efficiency, requiring no additional tokens, and showed generalizability in TPPE scheme applicability to other code-mixed language combinations.
