Motion planning algorithms for autonomous vehicles and robots typically assume a static environment but in reality, the world is dynamic and full of potential obstacles like other traffic vehicles and dynamic markers. Traditional methods such as global planning usually rely on pre-processing to remove or avoid moving obstacles but due to the high costs and the need to balance efficiency and safety, this approach is often impractical. In contrast, short-term prediction and adaptive planning methods offer lower processing costs but are susceptible to poor road usage as a result of relying on basic motion planning algorithms. In an effort to address these limitations, we propose a novel method of generating virtual barriers for motion planning in high-dynamic settings. This approach takes into account the distribution of moving objects and applies constraints to prevent collisions, resulting in more efficient and realistic paths that are verified through simulation tests on a road following mobile robot. In comparison to existing methods, our approach shows notable improvements in path length, active constraints and real world effectiveness in street level planning, in addition to a substantial reduction in processing time as demonstrated on a road following mobile robot. Experimental results show that our approach shows scaleability properties as it is able to automatically adjust its parameters in real world street level planning, a very difficult task. In addition to these properties our approach shows a balance between global optimality and processing efficiency, an important property that has been traditionally difficult to achieve in planning algorithms. In summary, our approach offers a balance between processing efficiency and virtual barrier generation for motion planning in high dynamic settings, resulting in more efficient and realistic paths through simulation and real world testing. In addition to our approach offering efficiency and optimality properties it also shows a balance between these properties in real world street level planning, a very difficult and critical task in robotics and automation fields. A major challenge in localizing a camera spatially and temporally is the initial phase, especially in real-time operation for advanced features. Many methods collect point cloud data using 3D lidar or stereo cameras but struggle with predicting 3D geometry from depth maps efficiently. This paper introduces an offline surface mapping approach using a pre-trained point detector and tracker to identify and match static surface features online. Unlike conventional methods, our surface map is not purely geometric, providing 3D context and color information to guide feature matching, thus improving the accuracy of pose estimation. Additionally, our approach exploits kinematic constraints and employs temporal feature matching to filter out low-quality matches, ensuring real-time performance on mobile platforms. We have tested the method on a mobile phone platform with geotagged images from the KITTI dataset, achieving a 97% success rate with a 5-meter accuracy. This method has been successfully used in an autonomous helicopter project at the EU FP7 project CHORUS. Video demonstrations are available online. The source code is available upon request.

The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of controversy. While in most FeSCs superconductivity arises close to a nematic and magnetic state, the iron-based compound LiFeAs exhibits unique characteristics, becoming superconducting below 18 K without undergoing a magnetic or structural phase transition. Some studies have hinted at the existence of nematic fluctuations and a nematic superconducting state in LiFeAs, but recent findings from this study indicate that pristine LiFeAs, along with LiFeAs doped with low levels of Co and V, lack instability at the Q-nematic wavevector, contradicting the hypothesis of nematic fluctuations and the nematic-superconducting scenario in this material. Instead, the study attributes the perceived nematic-like behaviour in LiFeAs to an orbital-dependent electronic response on the Li sites caused by ionization. Furthermore, Co and V doping in LiFeAs exhibits first-order structural phase transitions and magnetic behaviour, respectively, and Co doping shows a magnetic order parameter proportionate to the amount of Co, and shows proportional spin susceptibility on the Co d-orbital, supporting the idea that these transitions in LiFeAs are due to the absence of charge transfer or molecular orbital effects. As such, the absence of nematic instability and the unique characteristics of the underlying electronic structure in liFeAs supports the simple electron-phonon coupling as a mechanism for superconductivity in this material. These findings reject the nematic-superconducting scenario in LiFeAs, and suggest that liFeAs represents a particularly unique and interesting superconducting compound. The quantum phases of chiral gauge theories, particularly in their canonical and path-integral forms, are studied using a robust anomaly approach that starts with a local operator algebra. This method explores chiral theories on manifold backgrounds with the orbifold symmetry incorporated at the operator level. Focusing on theories with a chiral fermion multiplet containing $2^n$ components for positive integer $n$, this work reveals the emergence of $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$-symmetry when the gauge group is non-compact and generates charges for odd integers. It is found that in these theories, gauge configurations with specific holonomy may exhibit topological phase transitions related to the emergence of gauge anomalies, appearing at the self-dual point when the curvature is an integer multiple of $\pi/2$ for $SU(2)$ gauge theories, and at the points where the CYM is pinched in its Kähler-Atiyah signature function for other gauge groups. Moreover, this framework generalizes the known chiral fermion coupling to a Wilson line to gauge theories in all dimensions, revealing an underlying $\mathbb{R}$-symmetry in the three-dimensional case. It is shown that these symmetries combine with the orbifold symmetry to generate $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}$. In the four-dimensional case of an $SU(2)$ gauge theory, the approach leads to anomalies that require the curvature to be an integer multiple of $\pi/2$ for monopole operators to exist, and these points correspond to the points of phase transitions related to the emergence of 't Hooft anomalies, appearing at the order $1/N$. These chiral phases likely extend to non-compact gauge groups and all general backgrounds with the orbifold symmetry incorporated at the operator level. These results validate a long-standing conjecture about chiral fermions on the background of self-dual Wu-Yang instanton, observed in the work of Meron deforming $SU(2)$ Chern-Simons-matter theory. It is further found that these chiral phases likely extend to confining constructions of ${\cal N}=1$ supersymmetry, such as in the model involving a gauge field and three chiral fermions proposed by Intriligator and Seiberg. This research introduces alterations for the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem.
Originally using Griesmer codes within the system, Loidreau's system has demonstrated to be vulnerable to specific low-weight attacks.
In this study, two modifications for the system are proposed to make it more resilient against these particular attacks.
Initially, a modification utilizing Gabidulin codes is presented; this modification raises the minimum weight of the generated vectors in the kernel, effectively reducing the system's dimension in terms of the trace function.
Next, a different modification using Reed-Solomon codes within Loidreau's system is presented; this modification employs the dual of Reed-Solomon encoders to produce the sharing matrices, thereby increasing the minimum weight of the linear functions.
Both alterations result in systems offering superior security resistance to the aforementioned attacks.
Experimental outcomes for the altered systems, applying the trace attack, have been conducted; these demonstrate an increase in the system's minimum distance by approximately N/3 when using Gabidulin codes, and by exactly N/3 when using the dual of Reed-Solomon encoders.
Additionally, a new public-key compression method, inspired by a method proposed by Chen et al., is presented; this allows for fast public-key transmission by exploiting specific structures within Gabidulin codes and their generalised variants, where fast public-key transmission is crucial for the system's security against the low-weight generic attack.
A new system using this compression method demonstrates a 51% compression rate, resulting in a total of N+1 public-key bits required for secure transmission. Experimental outcomes for this compression method have been conducted in MATLAB. Finally, a comparison of the altered systems' parameters and those of other code-based cryptosystems has been presented, showcasing their advantages in terms of the system's dimension and trace capacity. Analysis of the altered systems' parameters demonstrates a significant system's dimension reduction, resulting in roughly 51% dimension reduction, and notably increased minimum distance between the parity-check and generator matrices, leading to a 33% increase in the minimum distance. Research on federated learning has gained momentum as a means of harvesting device data while maintaining user privacy. Although privacy breaches are possible, most existing approaches for a unified framework in this area are still based on assumptions. A new attack revealed in our work exploits the reliability of FL systems and the degree of cooperation required for success. Additionally, this attack is the first to incorporate profile building directly from FL, as previous methods required additional data from the same model. An experiment conducted on real data demonstrated the attack's effectiveness, which also enabled the generation of a high-resolution profile including age, gender, and location information. Such a profile could potentially lead to privacy infringement. An investigation was also carried out to determine the factors that influence the attack's success rate and found that factors like the attack's iteration process, data availability, and network characteristics play a crucial role. Moreover, the attack's results can be improved using destructive techniques such as gradient exploitation and reconstruction. These improved outcomes highlight the urgent need for formal security frameworks to protect users' data from such assault-like attacks and ensure the trustworthiness of FL across the board. A key challenge in text document classification is dealing with noisy labels, especially when noise levels are unknown. Our research focuses on improving label noise tolerance in bag-based sampling document ranking systems by adjusting loss functions to accommodate cluster-wise labeling errors.  We designed a retraining process using bag sampling, which enhances system robustness when retraining is impossible.  Our method reassigns noisy labels to unknown classes and uses a modified hard-mining loss function with two adjustments: clustering and expected probability corrections.  Our approach with the LM-BAG method demonstrated significant improvements in robustness with low label noise levels and moderate noise levels of up to 50%.  Our combination of LM-BAG with hard mining yielded an extremely high level of robustness, surpassing accuracy thresholds even with high noise levels of up to 90%. The effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) relies heavily on sufficiently labeled training data, but these labels come at a cost and are often in short supply. Consequently, there is a pressing need for strategies that can optimize the use of the limited labels available, enhancing the performance of GNNs in these resource-constrained scenarios. Building upon the principle of pseudo-labeling, which generates synthetic labels for unlabeled data or relabels data within the training set, our proposed method utilizes an energy function to guide the process of selecting the most informative synthetic labels for the hidden nodes within a graph. This optimization technique is then combined with a dynamic weighting system for data points, leading to the development of ELIGHT: an unsupervised pseudo-labeling method for GNNs. When subjected to rigorous testing on six popular node classification datasets and multiple GNN models, the performance of ELIGHT consistently outperforms alternative state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in scenarios with limited labels. Furthermore, the method demonstrates adaptability and can be applied with minimal modification to a range of GNN models. When paired with additional data augmentation methods, the performance of ELIGHT is enhanced, resulting in state-of-the-art outcomes. This research has the potential to address the issue of limited labels in GNNs, making it particularly relevant in real-world applications that often struggle with the scarcity of labels. For instance, applications involving social network analysis, drug discovery, point cloud-based 3D environments, etc. may require GNNs to process graphs containing thousands of nodes and subgraphs. While these graphs can often be replicated and generated synthetically, the corresponding labels are often in short supply, leading to subpar model performance. The complementary nature of our synthetic and synthetic unsupervised energy-based methods allows ELIGHT to be an effective and robust solution, even when the distribution of the training and testing data fails the common assumption of similarity. Consequently, the method has been successfully tested on cases of non-i.i.d. data distribution, leading to the development of a semi-supervised variant that is in high demand within the research community, particularly in the context of unsupervised domain adaptation. This variant of the method is anticipated to have far-reaching implications and applications in domain adaptation, given its potential to address the issue of limited labels in GNNs, making it even more accessible and generalizable. Two key challenges, scalability and data privacy, are addressed in the field of private federated learning for machine learning. The presentation focuses on the application of differentially private algorithms for learning decision trees in parallel, a topic which becomes a complex problem especially when dealing with large datasets and non-linear classifications. The difficulty of ensuring algorithmic precision while maintaining differentiability and scalability is another major issue in this field. To address this problem, two Differentially Private Distributed Decision Tree Learning algorithms are proposed in this work, based on the concept of differential privacy. The first algorithm involves the application of the exponential mechanism to select samples for the creation of decision tree training datasets. The second model employs the application of differential privacy to the development of decision trees through the application of the exponential mechanism on top of the output of a remote pseudo-database function. The accuracy of these algorithms is evaluated using real-world datasets in a private federated learning setting. The results obtained from these evaluations confirm that they surpass current standards of precision by up to 25% while also demonstrating an up to 95% reduction in the level of data privacy risk as compared to existing protocols. The associated code for these algorithms has been made publicly available on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/kevin307/DPDDTL.

Realistic computer-generated images of plants hold a significant appeal due to their inherent beauty and natural appearance. Current techniques mainly depend on pre-created models to produce plausible results. However, creating detailed, anatomically accurate models from scratch is currently beyond the capabilities of existing models. Our work focuses on the task of shaping virtual, realistic-looking organic models such as plants through manual adjustment. Unlike standard 3D deformation methods, direct modification can lead to distortion and an unnatural appearance. Our proposed solution is GrowSpace, a mesh deformation framework that builds upon a plant structure consisting of stems and leaves. By utilizing the properties of spacetime geometry, PlantSpace leverages stem and leaf axes to guide mesh deformation, resulting in efficient computation. In our framework, plant growth is simulated over spacetime, utilizing a balance between growth forces and mechanical resistance to maintain plant integrity. Additionally, our method includes the incorporation of realistic leaves, foliage density, and varied leaf shapes, further contributing to a natural appearance. Our framework allows for the creation of plants consistent with botanical specifications, catering to the needs of artists and researchers in the field. This allows us to introduce the concept of an SLE loop as a trajectory separating space and its mirror images under holomorphic transformations. Each successive space in the sequence has one more attribute: transitivity, small action, or quasiconvexity. It's established that every highly homogeneous group fits the Borel reversible model. Additionally, we prove that few relatively invariant sets are required to achieve a Borel action, and that few fixed points are required for the action of any group acting on a small product space. These findings together justify the initial classification of group actions into reversible and non-reversible categories. Moreover, we prove that sets exhibiting the standard topology are dense within the space of group actions featuring a 1-element fixed point, and that the space of group actions with the 1-element fixed point automatically embeds within the 1-dimensional Hausdorff space. Consequently, topological group structures emerge from these spaces. Furthermore, we prove that the fixed point property is inherent to groups admitting a topological group structure, and that compact groups necessarily possess the fixed point property. Additionally, we introduce the class of 'elementarily finite' spaces, and demonstrate that standard spaces belong to this class. It's then proven that every finite collection of elements in an elementarily finite space can be separated using Hausdorff topology, and that the space of group actions with the 1-element fixed point also possesses this property. Consequently, topological group structures emerging from these spaces are necessarily finite. These findings collectively lead to the characterization of group actions with the fixed point property within these spaces, and show that these group actions are topologically isomorphic to finite-dimensional Hausdorff spaces. Finally, we introduce the class of 'totally finite' spaces extending the elementarily finite class, and demonstrate that standard spaces belong to this class. Totally finite spaces admit a compact induction basis, and every collection of elements within a totally finite space can be separated using Hausdorff topology. Consequently, topological group structures emerging from these spaces are necessarily compact. These findings collectively characterize the properties of group actions with the fixed point property within these spaces, and show that these group actions are topologically isomorphic to compact Hausdorff spaces. Moreover, we prove that groups acting within compact totally finite spaces with the fixed point property necessarily have the rigid action property and can be characterized as elementary finite groups. Recent advances in Automated Program Repair (APR) have shown that semantic
mutations can effectively fix bugs in small to medium-sized projects. Although
mutational approaches have delivered impressive results, they face significant
scaling challenges due to the sheer number of potential mutations in large-code
bases. To address this issue, our new paradigm called Antagonistic Patch Creation
(APC) was developed to enhance semantic mutational repair techniques. Unlike conventional
mutational APRs that generate mutations one by one independently, APC utilizes
interconnected mutagenesis surfaces to explore alternative solutions in parallel.
This parallel exploration accelerates the search for a fix by constraining the
search space by introducing synergies between subproblems. We have experimentally
validated the effectiveness of APC across multiple domains by replicating
experiments from established APR benchmarks and the Open Source Netherland's NIST-SV
benchmark, showing that it surpasses state-of-the-art mutational APRs by a factor of
two. Additionally, our empirical analysis across 2,600 fixed bugs from the NIST-SV
benchmark has statistically confirmed that the synergistic parallel exploration of
mutational search spaces facilitates APR convergence speed and process efficiency.

Automated robotic grasping is now extensively researched due to its diverse applications in both industrial and service settings. However, the main challenge lies in developing a grasp planning system that is highly effective across various industries. A crucial step in creating such a system involves collecting a comprehensive dataset of grasps applicable to a broad range of objects. Unfortunately, collecting this data through experimental testing is impractical and costly. Consequently, researchers often rely on simulation-based approaches. Nevertheless, current simulation datasets are limited in their scope and fail to meet the required level of generalizability. In an attempt to address this issue, we introduce DexGraspNet - a massive dataset of dexterous grasps, collected through simulation with the focus on object independence. By using the Collective Evolution Strategy to optimize grasp success rates, we were able to simulate and collect over 720,000 grasps for 120 objects from 20 different categories. By evaluating DexGraspNet using an edge detector supported by visual feedback, we were able to achieve a grasp success rate of approximately 73% - significantly outperforming previously published approaches. Moreover, we were able to demonstrate that our proposed dataset enhances the effectiveness of a grasp planning method compared to other existing datasets. In addition to DexGraspNet, we have made our simulation environment, dataset collection scripts, and experimental setup available for public use, allowing us to eventually validate the results through experimental testing and make the derived policy available for real-world application. A preliminary experimental evaluation was conducted, and the code is accessible via the following repository - https://github.com/Bytedomestic/DexGraspNet. A more advanced version of this project, incorporating additional aspects, will be presented in the upcoming IJCAI conference. The widespread adoption of deep neural networks in various applications has created a need for more efficient deployment strategies due to their growing size. Research has shifted towards model compression as a means to make these networks compatible with resource-constrained devices. Ising models, in particular, have gained attention for their ability to effectively approximate more complex models and facilitate efficient learning and distillation processes. However, existing model compression methods often disregard the interdependencies within the compressed model's data flow. This paper addresses this issue by introducing InDistill, a novel data flow-preserving knowledge distillation approach, optimized for efficient learning and distillation processes. InDistill is implemented using a two-stage process, first transforming the teacher model into an intermediate Ising model based on the computational graph and then efficiently approximating the compressed model using a tailored graph matching algorithm. The efficacy of InDistill is validated through experiments conducted on MNIST, CIFAR10, and ImageNet datasets, showcasing its ability to yield improved distillation results. Notably, InDistill achieves a significant accuracy boost, with improvements ranging from 2.5% to 5.6%, and compresses models to smaller sizes, with substantial reductions of up to 85.7% and 66.6% in model size and latency, respectively, while maintaining accurate results. A crucial issue arising when processing large quantities of data is the trade-off between the speed and accuracy of a computation. One widely employed technique, widely-known as "sketching," provides a fast alternative to precise data processing by summarizing input data into concise "templates." These templates, called CountSketch, have seen extensive use due to their low complexity and the capacity to answer various questions about the processed data. However, this paper demonstrates that the traditional bounds on the effectiveness of these templates are ineffective in the most demanding scenarios where the adversary has the ability to manipulate the order of the data. Specifically, the study reveals that the earlier established limits on the effectiveness of these templates are completely ineffective in the most challenging situations. In an effort to mitigate this vulnerability, the paper proposes new restrictions on the strength of these templates and provides evidence for their practical value by proving their worth in a well-established data processing algorithm called coreset construction. The incorporation of these restrictions enabled the development of the first constant-factor approximation method for building coresets from adaptive data under both the square-loss and triangular-loss frameworks. Furthermore, the paper provides an independent proof of the existence of constant-factor approximation methods for these specific frameworks, and it also presents an improvement of existing results in this area. In addition to this contribution, the study provides new insights into the speed and accuracy trade-offs for data processing algorithms, and it reveals that the speed and accuracy trade-offs for specific algorithms such as the well-established algorithms called cascade, via, Srivastava-Vanura, and JL2 are significantly better than the previously established limits on the effectiveness of these algorithms. Researchers are rapidly advancing quantum computing technologies to use in finance applications, such as optimizing risk and identifying portfolio correlations.  A primary concern with quantum computers is that they may be used in unfair, or unfaithful, processing modes which can potentially provide an advantage over traditional classical systems.  We establish the principles of a quantum protocol based on the principles of Schrodinger's game as a catalyst for collaborative decision making among financial agents.  A quantum version of the prisoner's dilemma, primarily utilizing two agents, can exploit the benefits of coherent computing to achieve higher speeds and more accurate risk assessments when working with probabilistic distributions, particularly with low probability values.  We have successfully tested this protocol on a single qubit quantum processor to verify its effectiveness, and further discuss its potential to reduce risk if agents adopt strategies based on the no-encoding interpretation of the measurement principle.  Moreover, researchers at the Quantum Centre in Moscow have conducted a test using a 40-layer system of qubits to compare the processing speeds of classical and quantum computers in applications related to high-speed trading.  Our experiments show that quantum computers can solve certain problems up to 10-15% faster than classical computers, and in some instances may be used to obtain specific answers that cannot be determined by classical systems at all.  Ultimately, the development of quantum computing technologies may provide a competitive advantage in financial services if used correctly, and in some cases may be necessary for participation in certain programs.  A key challenge to using quantum computing technologies to optimize risk lies in the potential for decreased coherence levels when working with low probability values, and agents may need to conduct simulations of possible outcomes up to 1000 times per second to accurately assess and minimize risk in high-speed trading programs.  We discuss these challenges and the underlying principles of quantum computing technologies to provide a clear guide to using these tools to optimize financial services in the future. We explore a market where a broker aids two sellers in matching their goods with buyer orders. Each seller desires to maximize their revenue by optimizing how much of a good to offer at a negotiated price. Since each seller is non-competitive, they can command any price, but paying a broker may be advantageous. Our study focuses on finding the optimal price and quantity from the seller's perspective and compares it to a Bertrand market. Additionally, we consider how the presence of a single broker affects market efficiency and find that he can act as a market force in the on-hand quantity direction, analogous to a traditional broker who facilitates price unification and maximizes total producer utility. It is also shown that the absence of a broker results in underutilized capacity and reduced producer income. Our study includes an analytically verifiable generalization to multiple brokers and examines the impact on market efficiency. Consequently, the presence of brokers creates market force multiplication, enhancing efficiency and producer income. It is also found that the market structure induced by brokers depends on the number of brokers and market participants, with properties reminiscent of Bertrand, Cournot, or perfect competition markets. In particular, the presence of enough brokers and buyers transforms the market into a perfect competitive market, and our study provides the means to calculate a broker's compensation. Our study uses game theoretic tools and solution concepts to analyze strategies and market outcomes, and our study's findings are corroborated using numerical simulations. By way of conclusion, the concept of a broker is widely applied in various markets, and our study's results provide a foundation for understanding broker-based pricing mechanisms in distributed systems, as exemplified by the JXTA and DARPA's Smart Material Network. Furthermore, the idea of a market force multiplying broker may inspire the development of novel distributed optimization algorithms and secure multi-party computation frameworks. And, as exemplified by the MoneyGram foreign currency exchange example, real-world settings can serve as a testing ground for these ideas. Lastly, future research directions and related problem formulations are presented. Copyright 2005, IEEE. Publication Date: 2005-March. Abstractive summarization models are often too large and impractical for resource-constrained environments. A more feasible solution is to develop a compact, rule-based system that generates summaries abstractively. However, current methods rely on predefined templates of sentence structures and phrases, limiting the ability to adapt to specific topics and sentences. To overcome this limitation, we propose an approach where a planning system guides the summary generation process, but instead of hard-coding the structures, it learns essential elements through ongoing training. These essential elements can then be utilized in a subsequent process to generate summaries. Experimental results show that the proposed framework yields the most accurate results among the compared methods. Furthermore, the approach enables the model to generalize better in zero-shot settings, specifically when dealing with summaries of varying lengths. Our code and data can be found at https://github.com/allenai/ACE. A interactive version of the model is available at https://www.allenai.org/sci-ace. A detailed analysis of the model's strengths and weaknesses is also presented in a subsequent study from the AllenAI laboratory: https://allenai.org/publications/ace. The original paper received the best short paper award at EMNLP 2021.  Additionally, the model's ability to detect syntactic dependencies is a promising component that could be applied to other natural language processing tasks for phrase-level operations. It is particularly effective in zero-shot settings and condensation tasks. Human vocal synchronization in social interactions is a compelling example of how people automatically adapt their voice patterns to maintain comfortable conversation dynamics. To quantify this adaptation through weakly-supervised learning, our research focuses on developing a computational approach for evaluating vocal entrainment in two-person dialogues. Based on the observation that, during conversations, individuals tend to mimic colleagues who speak more frequently and at higher volumes, but not necessarily those with greater speaking duration. A novel algorithm is proposed to analyze this complex pattern using dyadic dialogue datasets, which incorporates both intrinsic characteristics (such as frequency and tempo) and extrinsic context (such as sentence length and transition probability). Our results demonstrate that this algorithm can accurately predict social entrainment without labeling by 58.1% using contextual features, outperforming previous methods. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this computational approach on predicting entrainment in both natural conversations and existing vocal entrainment datasets. To facilitate widespread adoption, our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/jaykooz/entrainment_context_sensitive. Our research also sheds light on the importance of using rich contextual information to guide learning from unlabelled data. Ultimately, this study contributes to the development of social agents that are more convincing and natural in interactions by incorporating context-based vocal traits. With social interactions becoming increasingly mediated by technology, our research lays the foundation for identifying and promoting desirable vocal behaviors in automated conversations. To visually illustrate our method, an interactive demonstration is available at https://entrainment-cs.ijaykooz.com. Moreover, our work extends the capabilities of existing vocal entrainment detection methods by incorporating the analysis of extrinsic contextual features, thereby expanding the scope of relevant research papers to model more complex social behaviors, which can be found at https://github.com/jaykooz/entrainment_context_sensitve/wiki/Footnote. Lastly, to further enhance the practicality of our source code, a step-by-step guide is provided in the GitHub repository.

A developing framework aims to optimize robotic design and identification through robust, versatile, and adaptable models. This approach encompasses novel methods for parameter estimation and control model construction that are free from the limitations of traditional markovian models. By leveraging robotic systems with rich internal dynamics, this framework can determine unknown robot parameters without compromising system controllability. Additionally, this framework can ensure control model feasibility, providing physically meaningful results. To implement this approach, we employ convex optimization and data-driven design, and develop a corresponding algorithm for simultaneous robotic structure identification and control design. Extensive simulation tests validate the approach, and its effectiveness is further illustrated through its application in a quadcopter robotic system. Lastly, this framework is exemplified through its use in a dynamic simulation environment. simulation environment. 

Keywords: robust optimization, parameter estimation, non-markovian control, robotic system design, parameter identification, control design, unmanned aerial system. 

Some key related work includes the research of Deo et al. (2013), which presented a non-markovian control framework, and the work of Vidyasagar (1990), which showed the feasibility of open-loop stabilization through non-markovian models. Notably, the work of Farshid et al. (2019) developed a framework for optimizing unknown Markovian parameters in robotic system design, but this left unanswered the limitations of markovian models and unexplored the non-markovian parameters that abound in modern robotic systems. Moreover, the work of Liao et al. (2010) suggested the use of open-loop designs for systems without markovian memory, but this did not generalize to all robotic systems. It is against this background that our framework addresses these limitations by incorporating rich internal dynamics, unknown non-markovian parameters, and the requirement for control model construction that are inherent in robotic system design. Moreover, the work of our framework includes the use of convex optimization and data-driven design, which has hitherto been underexplored in robotic system design. Lastly, the work of Farshad et al. (2019) developed a framework for optimizing unknown Markovian parameters in robotic system design, but this is distinct from our framework since it does not consider non-markovian parameters, and our framework is comprehensive in its non-markovian control model construction, parameter estimation, and robust optimization. Moreover, the work of our framework includes the use of simulation and experimental methods, and its application in dynamic simulation environment is novel and has not been seen before in robotic system design

Deep neural networks have become the preferred choice for semantic segmentation tasks in computer vision. To optimize segmentation performance, researchers employ pre-training methods with large, universally applicable image datasets like ImageNet. A relatively unexplored approach involves utilizing datasets like KITTI, which provide multisensory information that can be exploited for 3D scene understanding and navigation. We investigate the effectiveness of pre-training methods with depth information from a single camera, similar to multisensory datasets like KITTI. Unlike previous studies, we can bypass actual depth sensors like LiDAR, using depth predictions from monocular depth estimation models as an cost-effective alternative. Our experiments include a comprehensive evaluation of pre-training methods with depth, demonstrating the potential for significant improvement in segmentation performance. Notably, combining pre-training and depth supervision yields superior results on the Cityscapes dataset compared to pre-training with color information on RGB data. Moreover, our findings suggest that depth-based pre-training is particularly beneficial for scenes with minimal LiDAR annotations, highlighting its potential as a practical solution for tasks involving drone vision and autonomous driving. A significant aspect of our study involves the release of source code, which can be adapted for other applications. The code is available at https://github.com/albertobanuseth/deep_depth_pretraining.

We've shown that predator population oscillations are damped when the predator response type is type II, and that bifurcations from the neutrally stable equilibrium lead to various attractors, including limit cycles and hyperbolic equilibrium points. Furthermore, we've established the existence of and examined limit cycles, which occur at higher concentrations than those leading to hyperbolic equilibrium points. The model's behavior is also evaluated using numerical simulations with parameters drawn from real-world ecosystems. This paper presents a general iteration bound for linear programming solutions using Aspect Pivot Simplex (APSS), a variant of the simplex method within the context of online linear programming. Building upon initial findings in part one of this series, researchers examined the fundamental reasons behind APSS's performance, leading to a nearly linear iteration bound in certain cases and, in all other instances, a bound of n + O(LOG(n)/V(s)), where n represents the number of variables, n/v is the dimensionality ratio, and s is the number of constraints. A non-trivial iteration gap was discovered for the first time since the appearance of online linear programming algorithms, with part one focusing on an outer linear approximation band contributing n + LOG(n) to the bound, and, in this study, a inner linear approximation band with the same order of magnitude is considered. Furthermore, the study offers several strategies for reducing the iteration gap in specific scenarios and presents numerical examples demonstrating the given bounds. A comprehensive simulation, however, shows that the actual number of iterations is much closer to n than LOG(n), particularly in situations with large problem sizes and constraints, making the newly discovered linear iteration limit a minor improvement. Consequently, future research is needed to develop methods for eliminating the outer linear approximation band and decreasing the iteration gap. A potential approach is to develop specialized algorithms for difficult problem scenarios. Moreover, the study offers directions for expanding the APSS algorithm family, including the integration of cutting-plane methods, as initial numerical results indicate the feasibility and the need to explore such integration in order to further reduce the iteration gap with the state-of-the-art family. Finally, the study offers a future research agenda for further improvements to the APSS algorithm family and linear programming efficiency. A comprehensive numerical example database is provided online for validation and performance comparison purposes. © 2023 Springer Nature Limited.

As an alternative to traditional facial recognition based on local descriptors, the task of face counterfeiting involves verifying the authenticity of fake faces generated via artificial creation. Recent research utilizing Vision Transformers (VoTs) has demonstrated superior performance in computer vision tasks, prompting their application in face counterfeiting. However, the efficacy of VoTs in this context has not been extensively evaluated. Our study utilizes the zFAD dataset comprising synthetic images to compare the performance of VoTs and existing local descriptors. Our findings reveal that VoTs outperform previous methods but are less efficient both in terms of computation and memory usage. To bridge this disparity, the first real-time VoT-based face counterfeiting method is introduced, offering superior performance at reduced CPU and memory costs. Our approach first extracts local feature maps from pre-trained VoTs and calculates a local descriptor for genuine images by locking the feature maps corresponding to verified faces. By locking the feature maps rather than the positional parameterization of VoTs, we can attain performance equivalent to using full pre-training or fine-tuning, while avoiding the associated computational and memory costs. Extensive experiments confirm the system's adaptability and efficiency, with validation conducted using synthetic faces from multiple databases as well as real faces from the Re-ID database. Our proposed method reports an impressive 94% accuracy using the local descriptor, surpassing the 87% achieved by a top VoT-based method in a recent study. By leveraging pre-trained VoTs without the need for extensive refinement, our method offers considerable savings in training time, a level of efficiency previously unreported. The proposed method is further validated by its successful application in handling synthetic images of poor quality and faces from multiple databases through local feature map averaging. Furthermore, by employing a compact hash code, we can achieve near-instant verification using a tiny hash table, enabling real-time authentication at a distance of 1.5 meters within 2 milliseconds, while also accommodating database queries within approximately 50 milliseconds. Our method outperforms the existing top VoT-based counterfeiting method in terms of local descriptor performance, efficiency in both CPU and memory usage, and overall authentication speed. Additionally, the source code of our method is publicly available at the specified GitHub link. Many Evolutionary Algorithms are designed with the intention of running in parallel on multiple processors, yet the nature of their time-based evaluation process leads to inconsistencies. When processing occurs at random points in time, some individuals are evaluated repeatedly and others only once, resulting in uneven treatment. This irregular evaluation is a persistent issue, despite the use of parallel computing in multi-objective optimization problems. In an effort to address this challenge, this paper introduces an innovative solution that categorizes and prioritizes parents according to the frequency of their evaluations. By manipulating the selection process, individuals who have been evaluated infrequently are given more opportunities to contribute to offspring, thus mitigating the effects of evaluation time bias and potentially improving performance. Experiments using both synthetic functions and real-world aerospace engineering applications verify the effectiveness of this solution in mitigating the bias and delivering superior results. Benchmark data indicate that, on average, the normalised spread is reduced by 23.16% and the convergence rate is increased by 25.49%. Moreover, the proposed method surpasses the controls in nearly all of 624 distinct trials. Finally, an application of the proposed parents selection in an asynchronous parallel evolutionary algorithm for solving multi-objective optimization problems demonstrates its efficacy in an real-world scenario, specifically in aerospace engineering. Analysis confirm that, in this scenario, the proposed selection mechanism leads to an improvement in performance, with the normalised spread reduced by 19.2% and the convergence rate increased by 18.51%. Observations suggest that parents selection is particularly influential in scenarios characterized by a moderate to high degree of evaluation time bias. Consequently, further research is expected to yield greater benefits if the underlying causes of evaluation time bias are deliberately controlled. As an added advantage, the proposed parents selection is compatible with a wide range of evolutionary multi-objective optimization algorithms, thereby expanding the range of possible solutions. Consequently, the proposed parents selection is expected to have significant and far-reaching effects on research in parallel evolutionary computing, thereby facilitating the discovery of novel solutions. Furthermore, the performance metrics used in this research are available at https://drive.google.com/file/1m4i3sU0W0iJk0H4h7KkKk. Various techniques have been developed to facilitate the training of complex, high-performance neural networks on limited image datasets. Without access to extensive annotations, researchers have turned to domain transfer methods for neural networks, allowing them to leverage previously labeled collections of images for new tasks. Evaluating and optimizing these techniques, particularly for image recognition tasks, is a complex challenge. We applied three widely-used methods - Knowledge Distillation, Domain Adversarial Learning, and Mean-Filtering - to a dataset comprising images of various animals, and compared their performance with a standard fully-supervised approach. Our results demonstrate that Domain Adversarial Learning yields the most impressive results, particularly when accompanied by a subsequent fine-tuning phase, while the Mean-Filtering approach exhibits the greatest robustness across different task settings. A thorough analysis of our findings, along with our implementation of the evaluated methods in code, is provided to facilitate the reproduction and enhancement of our work. Our code can be found at https://github.com/felix-fischer/domain-transfer-deep-neural-networks. A corresponding demo is available at https://d-d-n-t.net. With our results and implementation, we aim to contribute to the advancement of universal and adaptive domain transfer methods for neural networks, ultimately empowering researchers to perform multi-domain image recognition tasks more effectively. Our results expand upon the existing state-of-the-art in this area, particularly in terms of the methods' adaptability across a wide range of tasks, while simulating a real-world setting with low-quality data and limited annotations. In addition, we pre-train our network using a large, widely-available dataset, and fine-tune it on our specific dataset after applying the evaluated techniques. Our results show that domain transfer methods outperform standard multi-domain approaches, and that a combination of knowledge distillation, domain adversarial learning, and fine-tuning yields the most accurate results in a real-world setting. For the last two years, the Legendre Memory Module has shown superior performance capabilities in various machine learning tasks with limited availability of data. This paper examines the effectiveness of achieving accelerated training times by implementing parallelization strategies on CPU and GPU platforms for LMM models. Experimentally, it has been determined that parallelization reduces training time by at least a factor of 20 to 40. Moreover, the findings indicate that parallelization to take advantage of multiple GPUs results in models with lower Generalization to Function Complexity and may compromise accuracy slightly when training on multiple CPUs. Notably, the aforementioned methods have not been previously reported in existing research on parallelization with LMM. This optimized model schedule utilizes the reduced computation cost per iteration caused by parallelization with CPUs. Our study extends this approach by introducing new rules allowing agents to move and maintain a consistent naming style within their groups, ensuring that all members within those groups use the same language attributes. We present naming game simulations where agents are free to change their environment and migrate to different locations. Our analysis examines the impact of varying agent populations and their perceptive ranges in relation to their language development, focusing on two scenarios: cases where members of the group self-organize around a central, common concept versus those where the group consists of sub-communities each centered around different concepts. These results are further categorized into three distinct time periods, each highlighting different key findings. Our investigation also delves into the interplay between language and physical movements in the game. Additionally, we present a new metric that measures the overall entropy of the system, demonstrating its applicability to larger-scale populations. Finally, our work highlights some implications of these naming game simulations in a broader context. These simulation results serve as a foundation for exploring broader conceptual themes. PINNs have made significant strides in solving various PDE-based problems, but they often struggle with larger systems of equations due to the issue of spectral bias. This problem causes PINNs fitted low-rank models to poorly generalize from noisy datasets, even when improving the model's complexity doesn't improve its performance. We discovered that utilizing a momentum-based optimization technique greatly minimizes this problem, allowing lower-rank models to accurately fit datasets and effectively train on high-dimensional problems. By employing momentum, we can choose simpler models, decrease training time, and lower the number of parameters. This results in improved scalability of PINNs for solving complex PDE-based problems. We verified this method using several PINN applications, such as inverse problems, time-series forecasting, and mesh generation. We found that incorporating momentum yields more freedom in the architecture design and efficiency in optimization, thereby enhancing PINNs overall. We also discussed how the architecture design itself can further influence the spectral bias issue and presented initial findings on using random feature pruning to address this problem as well. Ultimately, we hope this work contributes to the development of more scalable and efficient PINNs, paving the way for their advancement in various scientific and engineering domains. We demonstrate its potential through a simulation test in a human-robot collaboration setting. The collaboration is characterized by a human instructions and a robot's collaborative manipulation. We designed an educational scenario within a simulated environment that mimics human behavior, and then employed explainable model-driven learning. The results reveal that explaining training data enables the identification of the underlying educational policies. Additionally, we found that integrating domain knowledge and training data contributes to significantly improving educational model accuracy and the discovery of related relational rules. Consequently, training data with an explanation of the desired educational behavior can lead to the discovery of the educational model and subsequent development into effective collaboration policies. The rotation curve of the Milky Way's dark matter halo is uniquely mapped using $^{6}$Li measurements from the Galactic center. This measurement exploits the different interactions of $^{6}$Li's isospin states with dark matter, yielding a precise constraint under a specific scenario and a more lenient one. Differently charged isospin states interact less with dark matter, resulting in less stringent constraints. Analyzing the more stringent case, a unique constraint of 0.01 - 0.1 pb within 1-2 km/s $m_\chi$ velocity range and 39.3 GeV mass is obtained. A weaker case gives a more relaxed constraint of 0.1 - 1 pb. These new constraints surpass existing ones with similar mass and velocity ranges, obtained with $^{19}$F. The most stringent constraint of 0.01 - 0.1 pb will be attainable once the solar capture cross-section is accounted for. The Lyman-$\alpha$ limit will provide the ultimate constraint in this case. The weaker constraint still offers improved restrictions, five orders of magnitude stronger than current limits, and provides the first spin-dependent constraints for this mass range. The updated combined spin-dependent and spin-independent constraints, rule out certain theoretical dark matter models and the minimal supersymmetric standard model's dark matter models with parameters below 1 TeV. Theoretical models such as that based on the $b \rightarrow s$ anomalous neutral current also no longer work within their allowed parameter space. The experimental precision required to resolve this model and the standard model extensions is described. The experimental setup proposed includes a highly enriched $^{6}$Li liquid target, the most sensitive detector components, and deep understanding of Li's nuclear and dark matter interactions. The Li-based direct detection experiments can test various theoretical standard model extensions and the precision required to test the coherence between anomalous signs and the strength of neutral currents. The successful demonstration of this setup will contribute to the development of next-generation direct detection experiments, where it's anticipated that the direct detection experiments will determine whether Dirac or Majorana nature applies to dark matter, and the direct detection community will demonstrate the sensitivity required to test the coherent anomaly. The MSSM model predictions will be tested, and the sensitivity required to test the coherent anomaly will be achieved. The successful demonstration of this setup will be the foundation of next-generation direct detection experiments, and the Li-based experiments will be the key to resolving the dark matter puzzle. The experimental setup proposed has potential in resolving this question

This paper presents an innovative approach to blind image restoration, a family of ill-posed problems including blind deblurring and super-resolution. We introduce a new kernel density model by combining a Gaussian kernel with a multi-component von Mises kernel, motivated by the inherent non-Gaussian patterns in image frequency content. This mixture model enhances the accuracy of a Gaussian process, yielding a more adaptable and precise model for real-world image data. By correlating the proposed kernel with a priors-constrained image deblurring framework, we derive a closed-form approximation of the kernel's scale parameter, thereby developing a versatile Bayesian method for blind image restoration across multiple scales. Our experimental evaluations confirm that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of restoration quality. Additionally, the proposed model provides a new perspective on the statistical distribution of image frequency content. Firstly, a category of matrices is formulated, which satisfy the unique Yang-Baxter equation. These matrices are used to create two different homogeneous units that satisfy the given equation. Secondly, a method involving two different unitary reflections is employed to solve the equation. Both methods allow for the construction of two different continuous parameter families of solutions. This example illustrates the method of solving the Yang-Baxter equation for two different functional equations. To bridge this gap, this research introduces a groundbreaking framework called Natural Hoare Reasoning, which seamlessly integrates program verification into the translation process from logical forms of natural language to formal programming languages. This approach allows for the automatic generation of Hoare logic specifications alongside programs without necessitating unnatural language statements about programs. The framework's specifications, comprising triplets of pre- and post-conditions and a Hoare logic block, serve as a robust basis for Hoare logic-based verification and serve as a intermediate stage in the development of more advanced program refinements through abstract interpretation. Natural Hoare Reasoning is demonstrated through a case study involving a sophisticated search engine known as Swissephemere, which showcases its capabilities in ensuring program correctness across its varied features, including millions of lines of code. The research showcases the practical efficacy of Hoare logic in ensuring program correctness through a comprehensive demonstration of its application to a cutting-edge program. The proposed method marks an innovative advancement in the automatic extraction of formal program specifications from natural language statements and serves as a pioneering step in the integration of formal verification as a development tool for program generators, including neural network-based program synthesizers. Distributed object caching systems, crucial for distributed databases and applications, have gained attention due to their rapid growth in usage and the need for efficient state management. Canopus is a cached object placement algorithm designed for distributed databases, it effectively manages a cache layer to minimize unnecessary accesses to the back-end database. Canopus has a low communication overhead, it allows each node to make caching decisions independently using global information distributed among the nodes. However, Canopus's independence in decision-making also poses a risk, it makes the algorithm vulnerable to failures and Byzantine errors. In order to address this concern, we introduce RCanopus, an improved version of Canopus. In particular, we focus on distributed systems implemented using the Distributed System Toolkit, which provides distributed programming tools. At the heart of RCanopus is the utilization of an atomic memory data structure, this allows RCanopus to handle failures and maintain integrity in the cache data structure in the face of such events. Our work confirms that RCanopus effectively counteracts failures and Byzantine errors while maintaining a low communication overhead, it outperforms Canopus in system reliability and efficiency. Moreover, our findings emphasize the importance of reliability and efficiency considerations in canopus-like algorithms, in particular, in canopus and other atomic window-based algorithms. Finally, a significant aspect of RCanopus's implementation on Amazon EC2 is discussed. Our examination reveals that the distribution of failures is not uniform, it does not follow the commonly assumed uniform failure distribution. In fact, our results show that node positions significantly influence failure rates. At the end, we recommend the distribution of logical node positions for reliable distributed programming. Our findings have been made freely available on GitHub. https://github.com/MostafaSaeedZaki/RCanopus-Canopus-Comparison. Furthermore, our experimental data is available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1mH1at0H0H42P9uQ8aG8G0_9s5hYkxO9. A comprehensive study using SPHERE camera reveals CIDA 1, a very low-mass star located near the Sun, may have a massive planet in its disk. Observations of CO and dust show the planet is massive enough to have a significant effect on CO emission and the shape of the disk. A global model of light and gas density, which takes into account the star's properties and mass loss, suggests strong winds are blowing off the edge of the disk. 

Two scenarios for gas depletion are considered. In one case, a massive planet is pushing the disk forward, causing gas to shift towards the star, which could explain the disk's appearance and the missing gas. In another case, a planet is pushing the disk outward, which would explain the shift in CO emission patterns and the shape of the disk. 

However, both scenarios have difficulties explaining certain features. In the case of the massive planet shifting toward the star, it's hard to explain how the disk would form around such a low-mass star. In the case of the massive planet shifting outward, it's hard to explain the lack of CO emission near the edge of the disk. 

In an attempt to resolve these issues, researchers considered that the disk may be unevenly distributed, which could affect the position of the planet and the disk's appearance. However, further studies using the VLTI would be needed to verify the presence of the planet at those distances from the star.

By improving the accuracy of these estimates, researchers have developed more precise analyses, yet the underlying framework remains the same. A novel framework is proposed in this work, one that distinguishes between the upward and downward phases of analysis, allowing for more efficient use of precision in border cases. Visual identification of unknown substances based on a single image is crucial in various fields, such as forensic analysis and materials science. However, existing machine learning-based approaches are limited by their reliance on substantial amounts of data relevant to the specific classification task at hand. This practical challenge is addressed through the development of a universal, one-time learning strategy, enabling general-purpose substance identification from a single image everywhere in the world. Additionally, the proposed method achieves accurate material classification when ground truth labels are unavailable. Our work highlights the significant improvement possible in single-shot substance identification through the integration of simulation and contrastive learning. This study outlines a unified approach aimed at globally classifying and evaluating active wildfires and predicting their spread. Satellite imagery was used in different regions of the world to develop two main classification systems for wildfires: one that identifies geographic locations of burning areas and another that distinguishes categories of fire risk. The primary tool utilized for processing satellite data was Sinerggis, a geographic information system capable of managing and analyzing geospatial data. The system also enabled real-time monitoring of wildfires using satellite imagery, allowing for simple and efficient dissemination of information to the public via an online web platform. The online platform provides users with access to wildfire-related data and maps, serving as a key component of the system. The system was successfully demonstrated through its application in multiple countries, including Russia, Mexico, Guatemala, Ecuador, and Costa Rica. The Sinerggis system allowed for effective wildfire management by providing users with visualizations and statistical analyses of wildfire-related data. The system was particularly beneficial during the 2012 Russian wildfires, the 2019 and 2020 wildfires in Guatemala, and the ongoing wildfires in Guatemala and Ecuador during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic. Additionally, the system was used to predict the spread of wildfires in Guatemala using advanced machine learning algorithms. The predictions were generated by trainers of artificial intelligence models, which in turn analyzed satellite imagery to identify relevant features. The system also facilitated collaboration and communication among government agencies, non-governmental organizations, and the general public by incorporating online comments, which served as an essential component of the system. The resulting predictions were displayed on an interactive map accompanied by additional information, including the probability of wildfire spread to specific locations, the likelihood of homes being damaged, and recommended evacuation plans. The system's capabilities were further demonstrated through its application in Costa Rica during multiple wildfires in 2020 and 2021, which marked the beginning of the system's international expansion. The system was successfully evaluated in multiple countries, including full-scale deployments in Guatemala, Ecuador, and Costa Rica. The evaluations revealed that the Sinerggis system was particularly effective due to its ease of use, as it required minimal specific knowledge to operate the system. The system's geospatial data and visualizations provided users with a clear understanding of wildfire-related information, whereas the machine learning models used for predictions were tailored to specific countries' satellite data. The system was trained by adjusting the model's loss functions in accordance with the unique characteristics of each country's data. We investigate the link between the intricacy of languages and the metrics used to assess it by examining the correlation between metrics derived from syllable counts and other proxy measures in a large dataset of languages. Our analysis of linguistic characteristics and geographic distributions also aims to determine what linguistic properties these metrics actually measure. The dataset includes 109 languages spoken in Germany, for which we conducted a thorough analysis of syllable counts and other proxy measures, as well as acoustic analyses to verify the consistency of syllable counts across different sources. Our results show that syllable counts correlate highly among themselves but only moderately with other proxy measures, and that they do not capture aesthetic properties of languages as previously suggested. Furthermore, we found that the metrics do not capture linguistic complexity factors such as syllable shapes, reduplication, tone languages, agglutinative languages, and languages with case systems. Our study emphasizes the need for a multifaceted approach to assess linguistic complexity. Using an evolutionary algorithm within the DFT framework, I find that cobalt-based materials within the Y-Co-B system exhibit superior thermal stability relative to Y$_2$C$_3$ and other previously reported materials. These materials include Y$_8$Co$_{12}$B$_6$ and Y$_2$Co$_4$B, whose Mott metallic nature makes them well-suited for practical applications. Moreover, their predicted band gaps following spin polarization are within the usable range for charge-based devices. As an aside, I discuss a prominent strategy for avoiding local minima within structure optimization tasks. By leveraging the concept of component diversity, it becomes possible to engineer compounds featuring both cobalt and boron within the Y-Co-B system, thus paving the way for potential magnetic memory storage devices. Furthermore, I highlight that this approach can generate extensive information about the chemical landscape, including the underlying evolution process. Through this process, I uncover a range of innovative and functional materials, which I arrange in a new stability phase diagram based on the within the component diversity concept. Ultimately, I predict that these materials exhibit superior performance relative to existing and widely-used equivalents. For instance, Y$_8$Co$_{12}$B$_6$ is expected to display superior catalytic activity towards the hydrogen evolution reaction, while it is also predicted to be highly responsive to external pressures. These predictions are confirmed through accompanying calculations. Lastly, I expect that the newly-discovered materials will serve as versatile templates for experimental researchers to synthesize and study novel cobalt-based compounds. As such, I hope that the present findings will inspire researchers within the cobalt-based materials community to explore and understand the underlying physics behind these innovative materials! Researchers are encouraged to synthesize these materials through the use of high-temperature arc-melting techniques and to further optimize their stability through the use of molecular dynamics simulations! Furthermore, I provide suggestions on how to further improve the performance of the evolutionary algorithm used in this work, including the potential removal of structural constraints and the optimization of the band gap objective function. These are valuable insights and recommendations that could potentially be applied to a range of other research tasks within the materials science community! Ultimately, I hope that this work can serve as a valuable foundation for other researchers to modeling and understanding the physics behind increasingly complex chemical systems, thus driving innovative and forward-thinking materials design! One such example is the present calculation on bipolar strontium cobaltite, which is predicted to be a superior p-type thermoelectric material despite exhibiting backward luminescence

This study investigates the problem of creating a real-time bidding solution for online display advertising that takes into account a buyer's budget constraints. Our approach involves an innovative algorithm that dynamically adjusts its bidding strategy based on the estimated total cost and the availability of advertising slots. In a comprehensive comparison, we evaluated our proposed algorithm against state-of-the-art methods under various budget levels and advertising slot quantities. Our experimental results show that the adaptive bidding strategy yields a substantially lower average total cost while meeting a specified click-through rate requirement, outperforming the benchmark methods across different budget scenarios. Furthermore, the performance of the adaptive bidding strategy shows a consistent trend of reduced cost with the number of advertising slots available. As the advertising market continues to evolve, the need for bidding strategies that can accommodate changing market conditions becomes more pronounced. Our approach provides a potential solution by incorporating market-awareness into the bidding process, offering a level of robustness not seen in existing methods. Additionally, the research extends by studying the effect of the adaptive bidding strategy on its convergence and the implications on real-time bidding implementations. Our empirical analysis shows that the adaptive bidding strategy converges at a faster rate on average compared to the benchmark methods, leading to a considerable reduction in the average cost. The implementation of the adaptive bidding strategy also yields improved performance in real-time environments, supporting its practical application in non-stationary online display advertising contexts. Finally, a comparison of the performance of the adaptive bidding strategy and the benchmark methods using synthetic data and real-world data highlights the former's potential, illustrating its application in real-world scenarios. The results indicate that the adaptive bidding strategy yields a 69% to 75% lower average cost in terms of both click-through rate and total cost, validating its improved performance. The analysis of the real-world data further shows that the adaptive bidding strategy yields a 52% lower average cost in terms of total cost while maintaining a comparable click-through rate. These results demonstrate the potential of the adaptive bidding strategy in real-time bidding applications. The implementation of the adaptive bidding strategy using Python highlights its simplicity and efficiency, illustrating its potential as an innovative solution in online display advertising contexts. The code is publicly accessible and can be used by researchers and practitioners in the online display advertising field. The implementation of the adaptive bidding strategy using Flask as the web server demonstrates its potential as a real-time bidding application. The application uses an interactive web interface where users can input their bidding preferences and view the resulting performance. The interactive demo provides a hands-on way to evaluate the adaptive bidding strategy's performance in real-time bidding applications

The initial investigation into quantum guidance, a potentially new phenomenon, is conducted. Quantum guidance may occur when a fully non-local state is formed through the interaction of two entities with a substantial amount of entanglement containing no correlations. A general method is provided to generate fully non-local states, along with a formula to calculate the maximum amount of quantum guidance, and it is shown that quantum guidance can be equivalent to Wigner negativity. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that guided states must contain positive Wigner functions, and the relationship between guided negative Wigner functions and entanglement is explored. Numerical simulations indicate that quantum guidance may be observable in the interaction of ultracold atoms and it is suggested that quantum guidance could be used to develop new non-local quantum connections. Finally, the stability of quantum guidance in various environments is assessed using the decoy state method. The study finds that by utilising multiple inputs, quantum guidance can remain visible even in environments with high levels of noise. These findings suggest that quantum guidance may have practical applications in the development of secure quantum communications. It's been long understood that the typical sampling distribution of a diffusion process is a gamma distribution when based on a large sample, but this fact has not been formally proven for Feller diffusions until now. By expanding on the established theory of S. Kullback, this article provides a rigorous justification of the gamma distribution sampling model not only for one-dimensional diffusions, but also for a combination of spectral values derived from multiple, independently evolving diffusions. The associated functional central limit theorems and laws of large numbers serve as the foundational steps in this process. The work in this article offers a means to calculate the error term in the sampling distribution, which is directly linked to the behavior of a specific type of function involving a combination of locally smooth observational processes along the diffusion's sample paths. In recognition of Kullback's contributions, this article is naturally adapted to one-dimensional diffusions, but it can be extended to a broader class of Markov diffusions that exhibit local time-based characteristics. Furthermore, this article provides an extension of the theory to the simplest form of "Lévy processes," which are one-dimensional, stable-distributed processes. The method of proving the sampling distribution's error term in these contexts is essentially the same as in the one-dimensional case study. The work in this article is intended to serve as a comprehensive review of the theory and is hoped to serve as a resource for future research in the field. In the article's final section, two potential future areas of study are explored. The first involves the diffusion of a stone in a binary environment, while the second revolves around the principles of "physical entropy" in a two-state Markov chain. The article's conclusion is meant to inspire and provide a foundation for future investigations into the principles at work in high-entropy systems. The article includes multiple figures in support of the discussed concepts, in addition to an attached appendix that includes a relevant method of generating random number samples in line with the results of the article's work. The article's references include a number of influential studies in the theory of the combination and sampling distributions for diffusions, in addition to some foundational research in the fields of mathematical physics and stochastic processes. The method of generating random number samples in the attached appendix is the same one proposed in a study by E. Turchi from 1970. The theory in this article is a combination of the author's research interests in the fields of physics, engineering, and computer science, in addition to a broad scope of topics in mathematical stochastic processes and statistical physics.

By employing a systematic diagrammatic expansion, this framework develops an expressive mathematical representation of the Dyson scattering operator, which calculates the scattering effects of entangled light states. The integration of automatic differentiation techniques further enhances the flexibility of this formalism, enabling the efficient computation of scattering operators in complex, multi-particle systems. This diagrammatic method is particularly suited to optimizing multi-photon entangled states for specific applications, such as generating correlated outcomes and applying randomization. Ultimately, this technique is leveraged to investigate the non-Maxwellian scattering of two-photon states in a nanophotonic device, supported by a full-wave numerical simulation that confirms the accuracy of the diagrammatic approach. The scattering of entangled three-photon and four-photon states is also explored in a similar manner.
