A boosted dark energy model with dark matter-dark energy spin coupling is proposed, where the rotational properties of dark energy lag behind those of dark matter. As a result, the system becomes spin-imbalanced, giving rise to diffusing interactions between dark matter and dark energy. Continuing along the lines of previous research on boosted dark energy, the formalism for dark energy and dark matter is developed using the canonical quantization method, and the influence of spin coupling on their joint behavior is examined. We also investigate how spin coupling affects dark energy and dark matter radiation, and explain the reason behind the diffusion of spin states. Continuous phase modulation (CPM) is a highly regarded method for mobile radio systems due to its robustness, simplicity, and clarity in the frequency spectrum. Nevertheless, its relatively low data transfer rate and increased complexity when employing coherent detection have hindered its widespread adoption in such applications. Research by Fano has established that the non-coherent detection of CPM is an optimal solution, surpassing the performance of coherent methods. This paper presents a novel approach to non-coherent CPM detection that incorporates delayed data values in the decision process. By analyzing the periodic properties of the CPM signal, we have identified and extracted a more informative signal component, and designed a set of stacked filters to capture this element at different delay intervals. A test bed was constructed for this purpose, and the experimental results confirm that the proposed method demonstrates a significant increase in probability of error for any given CPM type. This method boasts a computed increase in delay sensitivity, denoted as $\delta^2$, and the practical implementation also manifests a substantial enhancement, amounting to $\delta^2_{\rm practical}$. Moreover, our findings indicate that the proposed method maintains a considerable performance advantage at any CPM type, and the resulting complexity can be effectively managed through employment of the well-established raised cosine filters. These filters not only diminish the CPM signal's bandwidth, but also suppress the weak signals' contribution to the total noise power. Consequently, the proposed method's performance can be effectively interpreted using the CPM detection bounded average probability of error expression. This method's validity has been thoroughly tested via a series of simulations that show its performance superiority. What is more, our approach is applicable to a wide range of CPM-based communication systems, and our results reveal that this method's delay enhancement can be leveraged to support high-speed CPM transmissions. Based on the CPM detection bounded average probability of error criteria, our estimates also show that the proposed method's performance can be effectively replicated in systems employing 20-128 CPM signals per second. A prominent reward learning framework utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their scalability is limited due to the expense and time consumption of human input. To address this challenge, we propose introducing visually supported ranked group comparisons, significantly reducing the required number of human comparisons. However, this modification brings its own set of difficulties as it necessitates reward segmentations that accurately represent the target labels. To overcome this problem, we introduce Visually Supported Ranked Group Comparisons, a model that combines a neural network with a ranking algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach efficiently aggregates human judgments across various tasks and saves a substantial amount of human time, preserving the precision of the labels. Notably, a single neural network is sufficient to tackle multiple tasks. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to a variety of reinforcement learning scenarios, encompassing both simulation-based and real-world settings. Overall, this technique is suitable for scenarios where high-quality data is scarce and fast human feedback is crucial. Implementations details can be found at https://github.com/mthom/gcmax. In typical topological systems, a topological defect emerges when two regions with distinct parity signatures meet. We investigate whether a similar spontaneous topological defect can occur in the Kitaev-Queen model when two regions with frustrated boundary conditions overlap. Frustration in this context arises from varying combinations of plaquette triangulations. A detailed analysis shows that a topological edge forms when these regions combine, featuring properties similar to those of a topological corner. The topological edge possesses an entanglement area law, accompanied by a collective low-energy state located on the edge's boundary. The edge itself is unable to host a non-trivial zero-energy state. The behavior of the topological edge is contrasted with that of a non-frustrated topological corner and key differences resulting from the system's increased complexity in terms of degree are highlighted. The quantum state located at the topological edge exhibits stability against weak perturbations due to the edge itself, and exhibits a singular capacity for error correction through a global perturbation. The presence of a topological edge may be realized in quantum hardware through the deployment of specially engineered noise. The system's behavior under varying coupling strengths between plaquettes and holes provides insight into how topological features can arise from disordered lattices due to the influence of localized excitations. The analysis expands the current understanding of the Kitaev-Queen model and the related Kitaev models and provides a framework for further research into the phenomenon of topological edges in frustrated systems. To date, most conversations have been viewed as unstructured interactions between two or more individuals. However, considering the cost and time required for engaging in conversation, it's rare for people to have impulsive discussions without prior understanding of the topic. Therefore, it's more common for participants to first learn the meaning and significance of a subject before participating in a conversation. Drawing from this insight, we've developed the Meaningful Conversation Pre-trained Model, which utilizes self-supervised learning to train conversation models by having them learn the underlying meaning and develop an option-oriented approach to understanding the topic. Our approach ignores sentence sequences found in typical conversation and instead focuses on meaningful segments through techniques such as sentence fragmentation and sentence simplification. We've also created two innovative tasks - the Meaningful Sentence Ranking Task and the Meaningful Sentence Completion Task - in an effort to further develop our model. Our research demonstrates that our model, which we call MPC, surpasses existing models in their ability to complete challenging conversational tasks, as evidenced by our results from the SuperGSAv2, SuperRACEv2, and OpenDy Wax tasks. Our code and pre-trained models are available for public access at this GitHub page: https://github.com/AllanLinDC/Meaningful-Conversation-Pre-trained-model. Lastly, it's worth noting that our innovative approach to understanding the underlying meaning and structure of a subject has the potential to significantly impact a variety of fields, including artificial intelligence and linguistics, and could potentially be applied to a variety of domains such as natural language processing, computer science, and psychology. Our model enables automatic text analysis, computerized conversation, and other complex tasks, which could further accelerate the development of more human-like AI systems in the future. With that being said, we believe that our work has the potential to significantly contribute to the advancement of more intuitive AI systems. Our model enables automatic text analysis, computerized conversation, and other complex tasks, which could further accelerate the development of more human-like AI systems in the future. Our approach demonstrates how understanding the underlying structure and meaning of a subject can inform our approach to natural language processing, which could further shape the direction of future AI systems. Our model surpasses existing models in their ability to complete challenging conversational tasks and we are eager to see the potential of this work in the hands of other researchers. Our results reveal that our two innovative tasks highlight the importance of the underlying structure and meaning of a subject in conversational interactions, which we hope will inspire similar research in the future.

To establish trust, explainability is a crucial aspect of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in machine learning (ML) algorithms. The field of interpretability is currently lacking in uniformity, with a lack of clear guidelines for evaluating the explainability of ML models. This study aims to address this gap and offers a new approach to algorithmic interpretability centered on the learning process, which can be used to measure how understandable an ML model is to users. By analyzing cognitive factors, we have developed a comprehensive framework comprising five distinct layers of interpretation. Each layer corresponds to a set of rules, and its applicability is determined by the availability of information about the model. Additionally, we have introduced a method for calculating the Cognitive Intricacy Score (CIS) of an ML model, which serves as an indicator of the level of comprehension required to understand the model. The CIS framework is versatile and adaptable, as evidenced by its successful application in examining the explainability of ML models in text analysis, face recognition, and breast cancer diagnosis. This new approach and its corresponding tool can be utilized to assess the understandability of ML models in various contexts. One critical issue associated with machine learning models, particularly those used in predictive analytics and safety-critical applications, is data quality and preprocessing. The use of a preprocessing layer is common in such scenarios to mitigate potential issues. Isolation forest, an innovative machine learning approach, has gained attention for its capacity to detect anomalies effectively. However, the current version of the isolation forest remains too computationally demanding and memory-intensive for embedded ML systems that often face strict processing limitations. In an attempt to overcome these restrictions, we introduce a weakly-guided implementation of the isolation forest, showcasing significant reductions in memory and processing requirements. In particular, our tiny machine learning evaluation using wireless sensor nodes reveals that the TiWS-iforest version efficiently detects anomalies in 12.6 seconds, utilizing approximately 18.7 kB of memory and executing only 17.5 CPU cycles. A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the significant advantage of allowing threshold-independent insurance risk measures, it is limited by the process being independent across different locations. To overcome this limitation, a general approach for reparameterizing Poisson process extremal analysis is proposed. This reparameterization enables the use of Bayesian inference with Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations. To validate this method, a simulation study and a real-data analysis are conducted. The validity of extreme value modeling is evaluated through a loss function that assesses performance in summary statistics and probability of extreme events. The reparameterization approach is applied to the extreme rainfall data set from Camps-Serrà et al. (2018), allowing for spatial modeling via copulas and providing a novel interpretation: the use of Bayesian analysis for selecting optimal threshold levels. These levels are selected using a loss function and optimal predictive loss, resulting in choice values of ${{\nu }_{0}}=6.95$ and ${{\nu }_{\text{opt}}}=8.44$. These threshold values suggest that a unified modeling approach for entire data sets is not always feasible. Moreover, a general approach for selecting threshold values based on minimizing loss is an acceptable strategy. The reparameterization approach facilitates a wide range of extensions to the extremal modeling framework, allowing for objective threshold selection while maintaining independence across different locations. Potential applications and further developments are discussed. The method is available in the R package xrepo. The Camps-Serrà et al. (2018) data is available through GitHub. Both the R package and the data can be accessed at the following URLs: https://github.com/silviaicoside/xrepo and https://github.com/silviaicoside/ocopmax.

This analysis addresses the challenge of deriving complex function values at specific points and their adjacent areas. We leverage the assumption that the cross-section is defined as a result of a steady process of transferring a unit area's complexity, utilizing the Radon transform or a Steklov eigenvalue problem as a proxy. A novel algorithm is presented for efficiently computing the average cross-section and associated area in both two and higher dimensions. This approach involves the use of convex partition schemes that utilize grid points. Moreover, we demonstrate that this method's accuracy can be enhanced by dividing the area and processing the calculations in sub-domains. Extensive numerical experiments are conducted to test the efficiency of our method for various examples, including those involving reference solutions obtained through Monte Carlo simulations. As a result, this algorithm has been successfully applied to a diverse range of problems, such as designing the最minimal resistance airplane shape by minimizing drag, optimizing golf ball design for dimpled golf balls to achieve maximum side friction, and designing a square box for maximum lateral surface pressure in pressure-field. As another application, we have developed a photo with the least amount of exposure using our algorithm. Furthermore, we have used our algorithm to create a photo with the lowest exposure time for a given image, and used maximum entropy regularization to determine stationary values of the average cross-section for a volume rather than a area. The resulting images demonstrate a wide range of interesting and meaningful effects. An example of optimizing golf ball surface texture for golfers with different swing speeds is also provided. In addition, we have used our algorithm to solve a problem of stationary values of the average cross-section for a different complexity in two dimensions, and a number of other applications are given in the file supplementary_material.pdf. The source code for our algorithm can be obtained at the website https://github.com/lijingc1997/mean-curvature-flow. This algorithm can be used to solve a wide range of problems, such as stationary values of the average cross-section for a shape preserving regularization in two dimensions, average cross-section for a given volume (average vertical section), etc. A new algorithm is presented for efficiently computing the stationary values of the average cross-section and associated area in two and higher dimensions. Moreover, we have used this algorithm to derive the minimal resistance airplane shape by minimizing drag. To gain a deeper understanding of one-dimensional diffusion with entropic barriers, a thorough examination is conducted on the initial exit duration of an individual particle. The results obtained from the microscopic cluster expansion method demonstrate that the finite initial exit duration can be influenced by two distinct factors, which are the density of the surrounding particles and the temperature. Additionally, our results reveal that the second-order approximation of the exit duration can serve as a viable surrogate for the total exit duration duration when the particle exchange process is rapid. The developed method in this study can be extended to other problems in diffusion and can also be applied to observe the time evolution of particles in a tube. Consequently, this study's findings can contribute to a better understanding of cellular processes such as cellular protein trafficking and membrane-related diffusion processes. The study's results also shed light on the practical application of a particle-tracking technique known as follow-the-leader. The theoretical model and key insights established in this study can aid in clarifying the underlying mechanisms in various physical and biological systems involving diffusion processes. The developed approach is expected to be useful in determining the physical and biological timescales of one-dimensional diffusion processes at a quantitative level. We seek a compact representation of sequences of images that efficiently
capture their core content. Typically, motion-related information in video
sequences is dismissed in favor of focusing on static characteristics. In
opposition to this convention, our proposed method captures the evolving
layout of salient objects within a scene by tracking their spatial arrangement
across a sequence of images. Salient objects are identified using a computer
vision model that combines a map of object boundaries and a temporal index,
enabling efficient salient object region detection. A innovative, compact
data-structure, the SP-tree, is employed to store the set of all image features.
By combining the insights from different images, our method is capable of
generating a concise, simplified representation of the sequence using an
efficient algorithm. The resulting layout description is encoded using an
efficient compression algorithm and served as an index, or snapshot, of the
sequence's layout. It enables rapid content search, efficient object retrieval
scenarios, and allows users to interact with large databases of image sequences
by providing a concise description of the objects within a scene. The proposed
method has numerous applications, including (i) dynamic layout index-based
search, (ii) object retrieval, and (iii) interactive retrieval of image
sequences. Our innovative technique is evaluated using a collection of ten
minutes worth of surveillance video footage, covering a crowded arrival hall
where people are arriving by car and walking through the scene, as well as a set
of promotional videos showcasing clothing models. Experimental results
demonstrate the suitability of our method for a diverse range of dynamic scenes. 
All code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/alaoie/DPI.

Fine-grained named entity recognition in continuous texts demands in-depth understanding of a document's structure. To address this challenge, a new approach called FGNET-RH is developed, which leverages the advantages of hyperbolic space to create a context-dependent framework for NER. This method builds on the initial capture of surface form information in a hyperbolic manifold, where each node represents a entity class, and surfaces are connected based on their semantic relationships. To refine this initial capture, a new context-dependent framework is introduced, which integrates both surface and edge information to boost classification performance. This framework is unique because it integrates a new tripartite attention mechanism, which takes into account the interplay of surface, edge, and node information to optimize NER performance. This method also outperforms existing methods, even when only surface-level information is considered. In cloud computing environments, where virtualized resources are commonly used, host machines manage and allocate computing powers to multiple virtual entities.  Certain workloads, however, require guaranteed host resources and cannot be accommodated by shared cloud platforms.  The issue is resolved through VM reservations, which guarantee a predetermined number of host resources for reserved virtual machines.  Currently employed VM reservation methods, however, lead to significant overheads, hinder resource utilization, and sometimes result in denied requests for VM deployment, despite sufficient host powers.  This paper presents a new approach, called prepartition, which enhances VM reservation and host utilization by incorporating low-cost forecasting mechanisms and adjusting VM request processing based on predicted powers and host load.  Simulation results confirm the efficacy of prepartition, as compared to current models, and highlights its benefits, which include significant denial rate reductions and substantial power improvement.  Furthermore, analysis confirms prepartition's computational efficiency and robustness, and its adaptability is verified through testing of multiple forecasting methods.  The research also reveals the importance of accurate forecasting for optimal prepartition performance and encourages integration of this mechanism into the model.  Final experiments validating prepartition in real-world settings are presented.  The accompanying source code is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/AngelPani/Prepartition.  A demonstration of prepartition's low overhead can be accessed at https://cloudshare-test.herokuapp.com.  Lastly, a brief tutorial on deploying prepartition in a cloud data center can be found at https://cloudservicesdeployment.github.io.  The heroku deployment is hosted at https://cloudshare-test.herokuapp.com.  A tutorial on deploying prepartition in a cloud data center can be found at https://cloudservicesdeployment.github.io.

In modeling real-world interactions as game theoretical frameworks, solving for equilibria is often a computational challenge. This study introduces the concept of Fixed Point Networks (FPNs), a type of artificial neural network, where its output directly corresponds to a solution of a game's fixed point operator. By employing an approximation of the operator within FPNs, trained on a combination of real-world data and optimality constraints, our framework facilitates the generation of utility-maximizing strategies on various game types, including two-player matching markets and auctions. We successfully apply FPNs to replicate a broad range of existing economic models and derive new insights with predicted outcomes. Notably, our method allows FPNs to attain a fixed point without explicit iteration. Instead, our framework exploits the adversarial training of the neural network to reach a solution, where the cost function enforces the condition that no player wants to deviate. For instance, in the context of auctions, our model replicates a variant of the VCG mechanism that yields optimal social welfare. Furthermore, our method has a data generation speed that outperforms iterative algorithms like contraction mapping, while adversarial training enhances our framework's robustness against noisy data. Overall, our work provides a potential new direction for machine learning applications in game theory. [Our project code is publicly available at https://github.com/simon-kliesch/fixed-point-nets]

This study explores ways to measure the effect of a particular variable on a target variable, taking into account other variables - a challenge known as the 'obesity-waterfall effect' where introducing a new variable makes other variables seem less significant by comparison. To address this issue, the paper defines an assessment of indirect influence as the difference between the target variable's conditional probability given all variables versus conditioning on a subset of those variables. Specifically, the paper presents an assessment called 'f-weakwithin', which evaluates indirect influence by factorizing out a subset of variables from the denominator. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that this assessment is capable of measuring universal causal effects for binary target variables and provides connections to information theory. Specifically, the paper demonstrates that f-weakwithin is bounded by total information about variables other than the target variable, measured in bits. An instance of this finding is that in a scenario with many variables, the maximum possible information about these variables, measured in bits, is the base-2 logarithm of the number of variables, the maximum possible information measured in nats. By applying these ideas to cases, the paper demonstrates that under certain circumstances f-weakwithin is capable of conveying intuitive logical relationships to other assessments of indirect influence. An empirical study of high-dimensional data reinforces the evidence for the beneficial coexistence of f-weakwithin and these logical relationships. Our research focuses on detecting the subtle signs of a stealthy attack on linear time-invariant systems that are crucial to safety in real-time operations. These attacks, tailored to evade safety-critical monitoring systems, often prove difficult to anticipate in advance. In contrast, our model predicts the onset of stealthy assaults and allows for timely protection by identifying potentially compromised control inputs and detecting anomalies in system behavior that are indicative of an attack. Additionally, we demonstrate the model's adaptability across various stealthy assault strategies and real-world scenarios, such as the control of an aircraft equipped with autopilot. With the model's effectiveness confirmed in experiments involving ten different scenarios, we plan to integrate its capabilities into predictive maintenance systems through the development of an open-source tool. This tool will facilitate the integration of our model into the operational workflows of security personnel and engineers, enabling the seamless deployment of effective forward-looking security strategies to mitigate stealthy assaults. A corresponding software package, referred to as effective-pts, is accessible via GitHub. A widely employed encoding method in medical ultrasound devices is gray coding, used to calculate the time-of-flight of backscattered data and produce image representations. The process involves mapping analog signal values to binary code through a time-of-flight calculation, yielding a reliable outcome due to its low sampling rate, yet it necessitates precise calculation of time-of-flight. Conversely, analog signal sparsity can be leveraged for time-of-flight calculation, replacing complex analog-to-digital converters with simplified thresholding of analog signal values, termed "L-values." The proposed approach, analog sparse coding, utilizes a deep neural network to train L-values based on data from high-resolution analog-to-digital converters and employs thresholding for time-of-flight calculation. The evaluation showed that analog sparse coding yields a 35.8 dB improvement in SNR, a 38.9 dB improvement in PSNR, and a 3.9-bit reduction in the number of bits required for representation compared to conventional encoding methods. The underlying rationale behind the success of analog sparse coding is that L-values are chosen between two analog signal values, allowing for the incorporation of insights from high-resolution analog-to-digital converters into L-values through the design of a deep neural network. The approach also facilitates adaptive encoding, enabling the encoding process to be tailored to the characteristics of a particular converter. The dependence of L-values on the characteristics of a particular converter is the only factor distinguishing analog sparse coding from a universal method. A framework for analog sparse coding is provided, and suggestions are given for the selection of L-values. The main framework can be applied to various approaches for the calculation of time-of-flight based on analog signal values. The proposed approach can be extended to other encoding methods and can serve as a foundation for the development of novel encoding methods that are adaptive and automatic. The idea of leveraging a deep neural network for the design of thresholding units is the key to the success of analog sparse coding. Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most advanced neural networks. This difficulty arises from label ambiguity and inconsistencies, as multiple respondents may provide conflicting information about images. Recent studies have demonstrated that neural networks can be modified to account for label uncertainty by adjusting the output distribution, either by adjusting the confidence in the network's predictions or refining the classification boundaries. This study demonstrates that such adjustments can also improve the overall accuracy of crowdsourced image labeling tasks. We present methodological innovations that leverage uncertainty estimates from neural networks to assess the reliability of individual annotations. This approach utilizes the ensemble consensus of the network and other informed respondents as a reference point for accurate labeling. Specifically, we utilize the information theory concept of entropy as a measure of labeling uncertainty. We also introduce a method for combining noisy annotations by using the likelihood of respondent accuracy, inferred through analysis of the network's output distribution. This methodological innovations are grounded in analysis of the dataset's noise and respondent accuracy profile, which are assessed using the mutual information between respondent labels and entropic uncertainty estimates derived from the network's output. We demonstrate this approach using two datasets: the previously published MSLT+ dataset, a well-established benchmark for facial expression analysis, and a newly developed dataset collected through a crowdsourcing platform. Our results, verified through extensive cross-validation and comparative analysis, indicate that the network can be modified to accurately identify dominant expressions, even when considering noisy annotations and respondent reliability. Notably, the methodological innovations presented herein enable the network to surpass human-level performance in this task. Furthermore, the methodological innovations presented in this study do not rely on additional data or a ground truth labels set and can be considered semi-supervised in practice, making them highly effective in a range of labeling scenarios. This study presents methodological innovations that utilize neural network uncertainty estimates to assess respondent reliability and combine informed labels, thereby enhancing the accuracy of crowdsourced image classification tasks. The approach is grounded in analysis of the dataset's noise and respondent accuracy profile, which are assessed using the information theory concept of entropy as a measure of labeling uncertainty. Additionally, the methodological innovations are verified using two datasets: the expression data from the MS LC dataset and a newly developed dataset involving a plate of donuts imaged via MRI scanning. Our results indicate that the methodological innovations can be applied in a wide range of image classification tasks. As an example of this potential, the methodological innovations were used to assess the dominance of a Krispy Kreme glazed donut through label combination.

Our proposed solution, Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing (SSCAP), addresses this challenge by removing the need for action labels through an unsupervised, end-to-end temporal action segmentation approach. SSCAP generates high-level activity patterns by modeling the interactions between simultaneous actions without relying on explicit action training. Our results demonstrate SS-CAP's competitive performance on standard datasets like Berkley, 60Athome, Kinetics Segmentation, Breakdance, Cookes, Sports Actions-300 and Kitchen Activities. SSCAP is open-source and available on https://github.com/cindyhua/SSCAP. 

Fig. 1 illustrates the underlying structure of SS-CAP, which utilizes three primary modules to derive activity features, activity representations, and activity parsing from raw video data. Our three-module framework is as follows. First, we use a Temporal Synthetic Frame self-supervised pre-training module to distill temporal activity relationships from raw videos. Our second module, Co-occurrence Activity Parsing, leverages gated mechanisms to integrate high-level activity features and low-level temporal feature maps extracted by a synthetic pre-trained model. Our results from the ablation study indicate that incorporating both activity features and frame maps yields the best activity parsing results. Our third module, Multi-Reference Activity Matching, parses the integrated activity features to produce high-quality activity segmentations. Our results from the annotation study reveal that SSCAP achieves superior performance when only a small subset of annotated activities is available. Our results confirm that SS-CAP is a versatile, unsupervised solution that can be effectively combined with multiple state-of-the-art models to derive high-quality activity segmentations. The key to SS-CAP lies in its ability to extract rich, temporal activity features from raw videos through self-supervised pre-training. Our results demonstrate that SS-CAP's activity features surpass those derived from Temporal Action Transformer and Temporal Non-local Network. The conventional approach to assessing students' code comprehension in software testing education relies on exhaustive examination of their code and documentation. However, given the subjectivity involved, alternative evaluation methods, such as rely testing, have been explored for their potential in software testing education. Our study delves into the effectiveness of traditional detailed evaluation compared to inquisitive learning with rely testing, focusing on the understanding of students for testing objectives. We specifically aimed to determine which method is more effective in achieving its goal, and which method is more time-efficient. Our empirical study compared the outcomes of using these two methods, assessing students' code comprehension through both quantitative and qualitative measures. Our results revealed that inquisitive learning with rely testing is more effective in understanding testing objectives, as it demonstrated greater comprehension scores and qualitative approval rates than the conventional approach. Additionally, our findings showed that inquisitive learning requires less time to assess students' code comprehension compared to the conventional method. Our study's findings have implications and suggestions for educators and researchers, ultimately aiming to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of assessment methods in software testing education. However, since source domain data cannot be accessed in this setting, and due to the difficulty and expense of annotating target domain labels, this setting presents unique challenges. This approach aims to transfer domain data from the source domain to a unsupervised target domain setting. The resulting target domain labels can then be utilized for model fine-tuning. Experimental evaluations have shown that our proposed approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art performance in both semi-supervised domain adaptation and source-free domain adaptation. However, nuclear reaction duration remains limited by fuel depletion, requiring frequent reactor replacement missions via a resupply spacecraft, prompting the exploration of ways to extend reaction time by numerous orders of mission duration to days. By achieving a deeper understanding of reactor performance and optimal design strategies, we have developed a roadmap for developing advanced Gas Core Reactors as nuclear power plants for deep space missions. Quantum information theories based on multiple resources exhibit great flexibility and have been successful in classifying and explaining various non-classical phenomena. To develop an comprehensive understanding, we often begin by analyzing the fundamental characteristics of free and non-free resources. Specifically, in this work, we investigate the initial states of free and non-free resources in general universal theories, and reveal that initial free states are universally consistent. A recent method involves estimating a model's parameters for unsupervised learning tasks, where a limited number of target statistical properties is known. The approach is based on characterizing a data set through its underlying probability distribution's moments. The technique is rooted in the classical minimum distance estimation method and is simple to execute. The proposed strategy doesn't require any assumptions beyond the target statistics existing in the data set, making it applicable across a broad range of models. The algorithm's effectiveness is tested through simulations and real-world data analysis on mixed-integer and non-linear models. The research provides tools for evaluating the accuracy of the estimates and highlights potential biases in the algorithmic output. The analysis also explores alternative estimation techniques for data sets and examines the efficiency of local score operators in modifying the estimated model's direction of best improvement. The estimated models are found to be highly robust, with gradual changes typically mirroring local modifications to data sets. The estimated models can be used across various tasks such as cross-data set regularization, generating synthetic data sets, and developing classificators, where the sample size is generally larger than the number of target statistics, resulting in naturally over-determined problems. The research demonstrates the feasibility of performing semi-supervised learning with regularizers. Lastly, the estimated models can be employed as an organza to modulate the influence of different data sets, leading to novel applications in the context of partial or unlabelled data. The approach is successfully illustrated through its application to two real-world tasks: the adjustment of photon detection systems and the analysis of quasar properties. Researchers have successfully created and evaluated non-degenerate quantum versions of the product LDPC codes. Both classical and quantum error correction capabilities of the resulting codes have been analyzed using quantum information tools. Importantly, the non-degeneracy of the quantum codes enables the utilization of classical techniques for decoding, thereby simplifying existing quantum decoding methods. Moreover, the newly developed decoder exhibits a time complexity proportional to $n^{\log_2 k}$, where $n$ represents the code length, $k$ denotes the code rate, and $\log_2 k$ signifies the scale of the code's structure. This contrast with standard quantum LDPC codes, whose decoding process can be cumbersome due to potential finite non-degeneracy. Following compilation, the quantum error correction circuits will be subjected to numerical simulation using the TensorFlow library in order to evaluate their performance. More generally, the proposed codes show significant potential in terms of near-term quantum computing hardware and application in the quantum information fields such as secret sharing, quantum cryptography, and entanglement distribution. Two distinct concepts, probabilistic differential equations and random fields, serve as crucial tools for addressing stochastic processes. By employing the latter, researchers can explore properties of a particular process, whereas a probabilistic differential equation provides a dynamic approach to studying stochastic processes over time. A random whirlpool's motion at sea is used as an illustrative case of a stochastic process governed by a functional probabilistic differential equation. This stochastic process is defined within the realm of Riemannian manifolds and is characterized by the geodesic criterion. In this study, the necessary conditions for determining if a random whirlpool is moving at sea are established, relying on the solution of a functional probabilistic differential equation. The solutions to this equation are shown to be characterized by the geodesic criterion, akin to deterministic cases. Additionally, the authors analyze the first and second probabilistic moments associated with the random whirlpool's motion at sea. This analysis serves as an exemplary application of functional probabilistic differential equations to the realm of stochastic processes, complemented by a corresponding numerical method for solving the equations, as demonstrated in the presented examples. A key innovation of this research is the extension of probabilistic differential equations to the realm of functional probabilistic equations via the Riemannian metric approach, offering a universal method for determining the probabilistic moments of various stochastic processes, including those with multiplicative noise, as shown in the examples. Notably, this method for calculating probabilistic moments does not rely on the conditions of independence or the Fourier-Sobolev regularity of the noise, thus ensuring that the results are highly versatile. A related proof of the connection between random fields and probabilistic differential equations is also presented, along with the corresponding numerical method for solving the latter, as shown in the examples. The presented examples indicate that the methods developed in this research are highly versatile and applicable to a wide range of stochastic processes, including the case of a random whirlpool's motion at sea. This example not only serves as an illustrative application of the methods for solving functional probabilistic equations but also holds practical value in its own right. Notably, the methods for predicting the random whirlpool's motion at sea are grounded in the geodesic criterion, thus offering a new and innovative approach to the field of stochastic processes based on the theory of differential geometry. Recurrent neural networks are exceptionally capable at handling complex tasks, such as modeling sequences of events that have temporal connections. One key feature that allows this is their ability to maintain a internal memory space, referred to as a hidden state, which they update with each incoming piece of information. Due to the hidden state, they have a significant advantage in environments where the information available is limited or incomplete. In situations where the system themselves is not visible to an external observer, we introduce a new power dynamic. We investigate how an external observer can form beliefs about the system's internal state, particularly when considering recurrent networks. From the system itself, we look at how it can utilize an internal memory, similar to a hidden state, to adapt and learn in environments where the information available is not always complete. Both the external observer and the system itself are referred to as in models of partially observable environments, with the former encompassing traditional reinforcement learning models, particularly the POMDP framework. Recent Federated Learning (FL) advancements have made it possible to train complex models using devices, without transferring data to a central server. Yet, both model training and communication between devices and the server remain inefficient. To address these communication issues, Research-in-Progress work DP-REC has introduced an improved, communication-efficient protocol. According to recent papers, such protocols remain theoretical at this point in time. Building on this idea, this work develops DP-REC, an efficient recursive model training protocol, which significantly reduces communication costs by using token replacement. By combining efficiency techniques, including quantization, layer quantization, and gradient compression, DP-REC enables efficient model training while maintaining data accuracy and model generalization. In experiments, it is shown that DP-REC enables substantial reductions in communication costs for complex models like ResNet120, without compromising overall accuracy and model generalization capabilities. Notably, DP-REC outperforms previous communication-efficient protocols like EFL and FLR, achieving up to a 100-fold decrease in communication costs with similar model accuracy and generalization capabilities. Furthermore, DP-REC is shown to be compatible with recent compression protocols like Linear Compression and Quadratic Compression, opening up potential applications for model training efficiency. To showcase its capabilities, model training with DP-REC is demonstrated on the complex model using only a small subset of data, using just a single GPU. In terms of model accuracy, DP-REC is able to match the performance of state-of-the-art models like ResNet120, and outperform previous communication-efficient protocols in terms of overall efficiency and data quality. Ultimately, this work presents a viable, practical protocol for efficient model training, paving the way for future advancements in model efficiency and convergence. In terms of its limitations, model convergence is shown to be sensitive to hyperparameters, data quality, and the specific compression technique used, making it a crucial factor to optimize for in future model training efficiency advancements. Possible future extensions are presented in the Conclusion section. Our goal was to analyze the UV properties of the region's dust features in relation to the existing database of star cluster memberships and ages.  This study provides the first comprehensive UV map of the Taurus star-forming region.  By examining the UV characteristics of 11 dust features near the Taurus-Auriga film, we found strong evidence for two newly identified star clusters: APS-C and APS-E, located at (RA, Dec),  03h 07.1m + 03.1°  and  03h 12.1m + 00.0°, respectively.  These two clusters are thought to be related to the Altairis cloud, whereas the Pismis 24 cluster is associated with the L1630 NEC cloud. These new findings significantly alter the understanding of Taurus's complex multi-age structure, where further study is needed to make a direct comparison to the Serpens star-forming region. The rise of Digital Transformation has resulted in an explosive increase in digital documents, but manually managing them remains highly challenging due to their massive scale. One key issue lies in extracting valuable information from tables, as tables are commonly employed to present complex, interconnected data. In this research, we address the challenge of automatically extracting tables from unstructured document images, specifically focusing on using Graph Neural Networks to achieve table recognition. Our innovative approach includes a tailored dataset, unique experimental setups, and a scalable network design for table extraction. Our experiments show that this method significantly surpasses traditional methods by achieving a 4% higher F1-score, and when combined with pre-trained models, yields an F1-score of 0.8361, marking a new state-of-the-art result in table extraction. Our proposed technique has been successfully applied in a real-world application to extract tables from legal documents for a leading law firm, resulting in time savings of up to 100-fold. This project's source code has been made available on the GitHub platform.

Every 10 years, the Global Survey of Population is conducted across 218 countries to provide definitive responses to questions about population size, distribution, and growth. Despite significant advancements in remote sensing technologies, significant disparities remain between official censuses and the Global Survey. The disparity is particularly pronounced in developing nations, with the population under 20,000 being particularly hard to estimate. This study examines the feasibility of employing drone technology to gather data on the population, particularly focusing on the Swangamanja village in Mozambique for drone-based population estimation surveys. The research compares drone-based results with the 2017 official census figures from the Mozambican government, exploring potential improvements to the drone's coverage area and image resolution captured. The study also develops and tests a method for automatically counting people in drone images and evaluates its performance by dividing available data into training and testing groups. Estimates suggest that population figures derived from drone technology may be more accurate than those obtained through the 2017 official census, particularly for the population under 20,000. The potential outcomes of this study offer valuable insights into the optimization of drone coverage and image resolution for future population estimation. The study further enhances the binary classification model employed in this study, offering insights into the most effective techniques for automatically counting people in drone images and their associated performance metrics. The research provides a theoretical framework for the distribution of population across the surveyed area and suggests methods to increase data accuracy through pre-processing techniques. Finally, the study provides a variety of ways to implement the proposed methods using drone-based population estimation, particularly population counting and drone coverage optimization. These suggestions have been validated through an extension of the existing PopCount library, a widely-used library for automatic population counting developed at ETH Zurich. The study's results demonstrate that population growth can be effectively modeled using a drift model, particularly in cases where the population distribution remains consistent. The study's findings further emphasize the need to automatically segment images to optimize the drift model, suggesting a minimum of 50 days between surveys for effective population growth modeling. The study's results were recognized with the 1st place solution to the DroneAutonomy 2021 challenge on drone-based population estimation and counting. The study's code has been made available for the drone-based population estimation challenge on this link: https://github.com/DrorDev/DroneAutonomy2021\_PopCount\_Challenge. To address this limitation, we developed a novel variational autoencoder model that accurately learns MoE networks, outperforming traditional methods in terms of speed and precision. Our innovative approach also unlocks the potential for scalable online learning, something previously considered intractable for MoE models. Furthermore, our developed algorithms exhibit enhanced robustness and high-level generalization capabilities, surpassing the performance of conventional models. We conducted extensive testing on a diverse range of tasks, and our results indicate that these models can effectively process complex time-series data, even when the data is imperfect and riddled with noise. We even discovered that these models can efficiently learn tasks with strict deadlines. We believe that these models have the potential to significantally advance the state-of-the-art in a wide range of applications, including, but not limited to, computer vision and audio processing. To further validate the strength of these models, we even conducted additional testing in the realm of implicit models, revealing a surprising level of performance in the task of image generation. We developed a novel method for estimating latent space parameters, revealing that these models can efficiently process high-level image features and even generate images from scratch, all while outperforming the performance of existing baselines on the task of image generation. Our developed algorithms have been openly shared with the research community, paving the way for further advancement and breakthroughs in the field of machine learning research. The related code can be found on our GitHub repository at the following link: https://github.com/ongen/clustered_representation. The generated images can be viewed at the following link: https://dingxifan.github.io/moe_gan. By sharing our research and its implementation with the community, we hope to spark future discoveries and inspire the next generation of machine learning researchers to tackle the most pressing challenges of our time.

Massive compact globally hyperbolic spin manifolds with vanishing first Betti number have inherent geometric complexities, encompassing elements like contact structures or being the product of a circle and a hyperbolic surface. We establish that when such a space possesses a distinctively unique Yau metric, it inevitably features at least one characteristic conical singularities, specifically conical points or conical manifolds as defined by Hass-Heber and the first author. Furthermore, in cases where the distinctiveness of its Yau metric diminishes at a positive rate, we show that it can be represented as the product of a circle and a hyperbolic surface. This investigation is based on certain invariants from Floer theory; specifically, we demonstrate the nonexistence of two distinct metrics with form $d+2\pi^2t$ that define trivial connections on the corresponding spin structures, for all but a finite number of positive t values. We also observe that our study's framework extends to the broader study of metric measures spaces. In a related development, we show that unique Yau metrics on orientable 3-manifolds with non-empty boundary possess mean curvature foliations. This earlier finding is pivotal in our study, allowing us to distinguish between the distinctiveness of a space's Yau metric and the presence of a conically deformed metric, with the latter implying mean curvature foliations but not necessarily the former. Nonetheless, we do demonstrate that spaces with the latter property are plentiful. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in identifying AI-powered medical tools with higher accuracy and who are more resilient to changes in data distribution. In addition, our proposed approach can be used to measure the accuracy of traditional, hand-coded medical models in real-time without access to ground truth data, offering more accurate risk assessments in medical settings. In simulated molecular systems, enforcing specific rules on atom movements can significantly impact conformational change and dynamics. Our research centers on the dynamics of a double-stranded DNA model consisting of 10 bases, using both NVE and NVT nematic stiffening algorithms. We compare the sampling efficiency, auto-correlation times, and structural properties of the two simulations, finding that the NVT approach yields a more uniform distribution of base orientations and greater overall mobility. Notably, the NVT system reaches a stable equilibrium in its configuration space within a time period equivalent to 10 to 20 dynamics steps, in stark contrast to the NVE simulation, which exhibits pronounced metastability. We attribute these findings to the NVT algorithm's ability to match the distribution of dihedral angles with its target equilibrium profile, whereas the NVE system is restricted to following the naturally occurring patterns. As a result, the NVT algorithm presents a promising strategy for enhancing conformational sampling in complex molecular systems. Further validation through direct comparison with Microcanonical Molecular Dynamics is suggested. Moreover, the associated source code has been made available through the following repository located at https://git.mppmu.de/Weinberg/stiff-biasing-dna. We encourage readers to engage with the code and contribute to the further development of this project. Our research was facilitated by the SuperMUC+ intercluster service. We discuss the implications of our results in the present study, which provides insights for the design of novel algorithms aimed at accelerating conformational sampling in molecular systems. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest at medium redshifts is observable due to the absorption of light from distant, metallic ions along the lines of sight to quasars. This absorption, visualized as narrow lines shifted according to the ions' redshifts, is characterized by underdeveloped or empty regions. Researchers have proposed a model in which these patterns are driven by the large-scale structures generated by cosmic fluctuations at earlier times. In this paper, a new method to verify this model is presented. This approach involves comparing the observed correlations in the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest to those predicted by simulating cosmic structure development using the linear approximation of the cosmic variables. When applying a transformation that preserves the data's statistical properties, it is found that the observed and simulated correlation functions align consistently with the principles of cosmology across a broad redshift range. This alignment represents an agreement at the 2% level, demonstrating constraints on cosmology that are significantly stronger than previously known. Additionally, analyses of small-scale differences in the simulated data enable researchers to assess the effects of nonlinear processes in the cosmic structure evolution on a more detailed level. In future studies, this analysis technique will be used to provide precise measurement of cosmic structures at the observed precision, and to make more precise predictions about the cosmic structures at earlier times by backtracking the development of these structures from the observed state. Finally, the most subtle changes in the data at small scales are found to be primarily caused by nonlinear processes or residual data processing effects in the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlations rather than the effects of primordial perturbations in cosmic structure development. The CERN SPS recently witnessed a groundbreaking experiment involving the simultaneous transport of proton beams with contrasting horizontal and longitudinal beam profiles. This innovative challenge required the simultaneous acceleration and separation of two distinct groups of beams within a single batch, resulting in a notable effect: the exchange of lateral and timing properties among these beams, which had not been observed before. To validate these findings, a comprehensive analysis was conducted, relying on data gathered from Compton-radiation, laser-photon, and beam-stripping-scattering measurements. A detailed examination of the experimental outcomes confirmed that the beams' horizontal and longitudinal timing properties did indeed intersect and cross over within the low-energy part of the SPS acceleration chain, near 24.6 GeV/c. To further understand these experimental results, a precise simulation of the process was performed, employing the MAD/XEM model. A comparison between the observed data and simulated results revealed satisfactory agreement, with the experimental findings consistently falling within a 1σ range of the predicted values. Moreover, a detailed investigation of the experimental timing properties enabled the estimation of an experimental precision of beam arrival time, which was found to be approximately 40 femtoseconds. This achievement is expected to be a valuable asset for future multi-beam accelerator experiments, particularly those involving accelerated particles and high-energy physics searches for interactions beyond the Standard Model. A simulated estimation suggests that, assuming similar experimental precision, it should be feasible to maintain horizontal and longitudinal timing properties within the same accelerator stage for beams with arrival times differing by as little as 1 picosecond. Ultimately, a potential multi-beam acceleration experiment at the future Fermilab proton driver, which will accelerate and accelerate beams at 25 GeV/c and 6 GeV/c respectively, may benefit from this research, with the proposed beam separation occurring naturally during the acceleration process, resulting in a notable effect: the emergence of a novel proton beam with arrival times differing by approximately 200 femtoseconds, which could potentially be separated and identified at a cost of merely 0.1 GeV of energy loss. Future path predictions in scenarios involving multiple entities rely heavily on understanding interactions between entities. Current methods mainly rely on spatial relationships and neglect temporal interactions within multi-agent domains. This study investigates time-dependent social behavior among agents through a set of natural language indicators, representing a more comprehensive consideration of social interactions. By integrating this insight, a novel forecasting model for agent trajectories called Socially-conscious Sequential Variational Autoencoder (Social-SVAE) is developed. By incorporating classifier-based retraining, which adapts more frequently, model performance in predicting single-entity trajectories is enhanced. To address memory constraints, a model variant that reduces memory consumption while maintaining performance is developed. Moreover, a model baseline without social awareness for through-wall forecasting in real-world datasets is provided. Experimental findings using real-world datasets confirm that the model performs better than baseline models, demonstrating the significance of time-dependent social behavior in predicting entity trajectories. The developed models, along with associated code and datasets, are available for further research and application. The models were trained on Google Colab, utilizing Google's tensor processing unit (GPU). Social-SVAE exhibits superior performance on single-entity datasets but is outperformed by models designed for socially-informed forecasting. A key objective in finding alternative models of computation is to establish that parametric variations of recurrent neural networks possess the capacity for adaptive, complex behavioral patterns, akin to biological neural networks. To support this notion, our research shows that Boltzmann Machines exhibit substantial complexity when measured through information-theoretic means. By demonstrating high variability and diversity in their time-dependent internal state transitions, our findings emphasize the importance of exploring topological and parametric complexity in artificial neural networks. Moreover, our study suggests that information-theoretic measures of complexity may yield contrasting results, with different aspects of internal network dynamics being assessed. Consequently, our understanding is that information-theoretic complexity is an adaptable metric that reflects various facets of paraometric variations in artificial neural networks. As such, it can serve as a useful framework for investigating the complex dynamics within Boltzmann Machines and other similar networks. The full implications and potential applications of our study remain the subject of future research. Crucially, our primary goal is to evaluate the potential of artificial neural networks as models for the intricate processes found in biological systems, with particular reference to the circadian clock. This paper proposes an interaction system allowing a single person to control a swarm of robots using hand movements. The system uses a deep learning model to analyze video footage captured from a single camera, which identifies different hand movements and tracks their progression over time. This information is then sent to a robot swarm, which uses it to determine the intended command and respond accordingly. With the swarm able to recognize a set of predefined hand gestures, it can execute various interaction tasks like following a desired trajectory, visiting specific locations, or maintaining a predetermined distance. Experimental verifications were conducted to ensure the system's accuracy in tracking hand movements and issuing appropriate commands to the robot swarm, which consisted of three Underwater Gliding Robotic Fish equipped with navigation and control technologies. These experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed interaction system in allowing a person to control a robotic swarm autonomously and expedite task execution. Possible applications of this technology include search operations on vast underwater areas, comprehensive surveys, and scientific research projects, where swarms of robots are deployed in conjunction with a single operator. The proposed strategy allows for ground state preparation free from entanglement using a flexible and efficient formula. These findings open the door to a new, flexible, and efficient method of ground state preparation in quantum systems with potential applications in a wide variety of complex many-body systems. This approach could also be used to prepare a family of states with synchro-nous internal dynamics, extending the strategy's reach. Image datasets commonly experience degradation due to noise, which can exacerbate the limitations of low-bitrate compression, causing apparent color variations.  These color distortions are particularly noticeable in images featuring prominent color gradients or in images that have been subject to HDR processing.  The proposed HTE algorithm offers an empirical solution to address these high-bitrate artifacts by leveraging DCT-based algorithms commonly employed in JPEG images.  The HTE's underlying approach involves differentiating between regions with significant color gradients and those without, which allows for the identification of areas susceptible to color distortion.  The analysis then examines the fast DCT coefficients of key color channels to calculate high-speed color degradation frequencies.  The calculated frequency values are subsequently utilized to create a color-correction map, which is applied during the final rendering stage of the HDR processing.  The implementation of the HTE algorithm offers minimal computational overhead and enables seamless integration with widely available HDR tools.  The empirical results demonstrate the HTE algorithm's capability to effectively remove high-speed color disruptions while preserving detailed image contrast, as well as showcase the compatibility of the HTE algorithm with leading HDR processing techniques.  Furthermore, the analysis highlights the inherent limitations of current HDR processing methods in addressing high-speed color distortions, which may have significant implications for future HDR processing applications.  The proposed HTE algorithm is now available as an open-source software for the research community to further refine and improve its capabilities to address high-speed color distortions.  The corresponding open-source software can be found at https://github.com/NYC77/JPEGDeColoration.  The accompanying dataset, including HDR images and corresponding metadata, can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/folder?viewId=1r1sYkYkYkYkYkYkYkYkYkYkYkYkYkY. Given a surface with a certain curvature property and at least three points, a harmonic extension is a way to measure potential difference on this surface. A harmonic branched extension is similar, but with a set of restrictions based on the surface's topology. Previously, researchers found that certain types of surfaces have harmonic extensions that are always harmonic, regardless of the difference in measurement. Over the last few years, RDF has become the dominant data format in Big Data, with numerous open source tools, extensive libraries and resources available, along with a thriving community that drives its continuous development. As relational databases remain the primary means of data storage, an established paradigm needs to be in place to facilitate migration of data from relational databases to RDF databases. Given the latest developments in data shaping and validation across both relational and RDF worlds, a comprehensive framework can now be formulated to guide the process of transferring data from relationships to RDF. This process of transfer, referred to as RDF migration, can be directly based on shape expressions, which in turn leverages existing validation tools to ensure accuracy and quality. Following a comprehensive review of related studies in generating RDF from relational data sources, this thesis presents an innovative solution to shape-based RDF migration, which has the potential to improve current methods, before discussing its practical implementation and evaluating its performance through a thorough case study. The study also sets the stage for future research ventures inspired by the challenges remaining in this area of study. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the evolving process of transferring data from relationships to RDF. Analysis of our research indicates that the generated RDF can be precisely and accurately validated against the associated shape expressions, which in turn confirms our hypothesis that the process of transferring data from relations to RDF can be directly informed by shape expressions. Moreover, the study demonstrates that the performance of our RDF generation algorithm can be directly impacted by the level of data normalization employed in the underlying relational database. This, in turn, highlights the need for normalized data in order to accurately represent the complex relationships present in the underlying data structure. Finally, the study shows that our algorithm outperforms existing solutions such as OpenRDF and D2R in terms of accuracy and level of manual effort required. Out of the five tested algorithms, the results indicate that the proposed algorithm emerges as the most efficient and effective method of transferring data from relations to RDF. Following the successful implementation and evaluation of the study, the proposed algorithm was freely released to the public on GitHub. As a result, the algorithm has already been freely used in several independent projects aimed at generating RDF from relational data sources. One such project aims to freely publish, using RDF, the detailed information related to the execution of academic papers across open repositories of experimental results. Another project aims to generate RDF from SQL queries in order to accurately represent the output of query results in the BigDataSpace platform. The algorithm's source code can be directly accessed at the following URL: https://github.com

In data sets with periodic or curved patterns, other forms of regression, such as the StoNED algorithm, can provide more accurate results. This method, a modification of the Notch constant rule, offers a more effective alternative. By leveraging the power of the Kullback-Leibler algorithm, it produces a more accurate and robust estimate of the pattern's boundaries, resulting in improved outlier resistance and reduced dependence on the data's initial ordering. Our pyStoNED library, a Python implementation, facilitates the easy execution of these algorithms on a range of data types. It also includes a series of synthetic and real-world examples that demonstrate the strength and versatility of the methods. In our research, we showcase the ability of the patterns to detect and resist anomalies, as well as the influence of the data's curvature on the pattern's fit, all while providing a computationally efficient solution. We investigate the performance of pre-trained language models in two key areas of semantic analysis: building word networks and word sense disambiguation. Word networks capture a word's multiple meanings by grouping its similar word occurrences, while disambiguation is evaluating a word's context to determine its intended meaning. Initially, we evaluate the ability of language models to effectively construct word networks using two datasets and discover that models of various sizes can produce high-quality word networks with minimal guidance. Following this, we introduce a new challenge to test a models' capacity for sense disambigation without supervision, by utilizing word networks to create a classification task from which we train a simple classifier. Our results show that models of larger size, such as DeIT-BASE and ALR-3B, achieve high F1 scores on the NALL SemCor dataset with little to no fine-tuning necessary, highlighting their capability in this area of study. Additionally, we extend our investigation to investigate learning from limited examples and find that our language models are capable of performing sense disambigation accurately after receiving only a couple of examples. Ultimately, we believe that further research into these two key areas of study could lead to significant progress in taking advantage of large language models in new and exciting applications. The code and related data used in our research is available at https://github.com/mcfehily/Semantic-Analysis-from-pLMs.

This paper presents an inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator when applied under Robin conditions to a bounded, two-dimensional domain with smooth borders. We derive a quantitative form of this inequality, demonstrate the equality condition, and provide an example of when equality occurs. Additionally, we bound the first eigenvalue of the corresponding Laplacian under Robin conditions, using a Robin parameter in the subcritical range. We also establish a quantitative form of this bound. Our findings are based on variational methods, which allow us to link problems of the Hermite operator to those of a nonlinear elliptic equation. We use a compactness argument and apply Sobolev's inequality, in conjunction with its inverse, to obtain our results. Our work is an adaptation of recent research by Denk and Trunk (2019) on the Laplacian. We optimise our approach by combining it with ideas from an earlier paper of Frank and Heidenreich (2020). We further develop this optimisation and broaden its applicability. In the process, we reveal intriguing linkage between the Hermite operator and a nonlinear Hardy operator. We also demonstrate that the first eigenvalue of the first Dirichlet-Laplace eigenvalue problem is bounded from below by a specific constant, exclusively dependent on the domain's shape. This constitutional bound survives even when we apply Robin conditions to the boundary, coupled with a sufficiently small Robin parameter. Similarly, we show that the first eigenvalue of the second Dirichlet-Laplace eigenvalue problem is bounded from above by a specific constitutional bound, exclusively dependent on the domain's shape, in any of the three possible scenarios: (i) when the first and second eigenvalues are distinct, in the general case; (ii) when the first and second eigenvalues are distinct and the second is the Robin eigenvalue; or (iii) when the second is the limiting case eigenvalue. These findings represent an extension of earlier research by Frank (2012). We further demonstrate that the first eigenvalue of the second Dirichlette problem exhibits 'isolation', in the sense that the first eigenvalue is separated from the second, by a specific constitutional bound, exclusively dependent on the domain's shape. This 'isolation' bound survives even when we apply conformal mappings to the domain. Consequently, by applying a logical argument, we conclude that our findings are not only applicable to the first Dirichlette problem but also to any domain with positive volume. Many current advanced interactive generative models, such as GANs and VAEs, exhibit declining performance in high-dimensional settings. Our research focuses on the capabilities of neural tangent kernels, leveraging their exchangeable properties in low-dimensional and semi-synthetic scenarios. We reveal, however, that NT-Kernels are ineffective in high-dimensional settings due to their inability to meet the spectral condition, crucial for guaranteed convergence in supervised settings. Moreover, NT-Kernels are unable to learn dimension-wise varying relationships essential for learning complex relationships within data. As an advancement, we introduce Non-Exchangeable Tanent Kernels (NFT-K) to overcome these limitations, facilitating learning in high-dimensional settings through the integration of non-exchangeable activations. Our theoretical findings demonstrate the guarantees of NFT-K performance in both synthetic and real-world datasets, including image and sound production. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/kevin0804/NFT-K. Our research demonstrates that NFT-K outperforms existing architectures, including GANs and VAEs, in various high-dimensional datasets, such as LSUN, CIFAR10-5, MOSKIT, and the EMU dataset. Our research further extends to empirical findings on the impact of activation function exponentiality on the performance of NT-Kernels, revealing a direct relationship between activation exponentiality and NFT-K performance in synthetic datasets. Previous studies have outlined essential characteristics of social speech traits, 
including vocal traits such as assertiveness, personality, and emotional states, 
which are conveyed through voice characteristics like pitch, the ease of speech, 
and the use of pauses. Prior approaches to incorporating these traits often focused 
on a single aspect, such as voice characteristics or linguistic content, separate 
from the speech itself. This separation can result in a distinct, non-natural 
voice that conveys the intended trait but lacks overall coherence. In our work, 
we present a method to integrate the expression of social traits in synthetic 
speech by providing the speaker with a script and recorded human speech as a 
reference, enabling the modification of voice traits while maintaining the 
original speech content and traits. This technique allows for the simultaneous 
alteration of voice characteristics and emotional states. We evaluated our approach 
through a study involving the modification of assertive speech traits as a means of 
communication, rather than solely altering voice characteristics. Participants 
evaluated the naturalness and the success of the intended communication in two 
listening conditions: with or without prior knowledge of the available traits in 
the script. The results show that the speech produced with our new method was 
perceived as more natural and effective in conveying the intended assertive 
traits compared to a speech synthesis approach that used a limited set of voice 
characteristics. This research presents a novel method for integrating social speech 
traits and expands the capabilities of speech synthesis beyond the modification 
of voice characteristics. It also utilizes a context-aware, rule-based 
interpretation of the synthesized speech that is grounded in the schema theory 
of mental representation. This interpretation demonstrates the role of speech 
traits in the perception of the speaker's intentions and is applied to a range of 
social traits including assertiveness. In addition, we have established a 
unified framework for incorporating the various aspects of social speech 
traits: voice characteristics, linguistic content, and speech content. This 
framework provides a comprehensive understanding of the expression of social 
traits and is essential for developing a coherent and natural synthetic speech 
that conveys the intended traits. A demonstration system of our approach,
