Building on the Heisenberg algebra approach, we develop a microscopic wisdom to incorporate the properties of triaxial nuclei. Unlike the point-like nature of particles, we explore the possibility of spatially distributed bosons as an alternative. To introduce the concept of a finite length, we modify the commutator of the first derivative across the Schrödinger equation. This amendment leads to a modified mass term containing the momentum and a fundamental length, confirming that the mass term is proportional to the 90-degree Klein-Gordon isospin operator under isospin-invariant conditions. Inspired by the nucleon form factor, we determine the fundamental length based on a nuclear radius of 5 fm. Next, we develop a quasiparticle approach to investigate the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian in a deformed potential. Then, we introduce the missing quasiparticle approximation to compute the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian in a triaxial nucleus. tricky due to differing viewing angles and perspectives. Most problems arise
due to the lack of scene information, resulting in ambiguous and
uniqueness-confusing transformations between images. In this study, we explore
the novel concept of utilizing gravitational forces to guide the image
reconstruction process. Employing a head-mounted camera system to simulate
Earth's rotation, we develop a straightforward optimization technique that
efficiently constructs a panoramic scene. Our approach focuses on incorporating
radial warping in each image to create a seamless join when stitching the
images. By doing so, we ensure that only minimally necessary adjustments are
made, resulting in naturally joined images and outstanding panoramic
reconstruction. Our approach surpasses current benchmarks with exceptional
stitching results on various challenging datasets, including the widely used
New College Oxford and Stanford campus datasets and our own gravity-captured datasets. Furthermore, we present a novel, minimal solution-based panographic
reconstruction algorithm that identifies the optimal rotation matrices and 3D
points with the fewest possible constraints. This ground-breaking reconstruction
solves the otherwise intractable bundle adjustment problem, eliminating the need
for often-incorrect heuristics. In fact, our minimally-based solution reduces the
scale of the Tucker matrix by an astonishing 60% and demonstrates
intermediate outcomes en route to the optimal solution. Our approach and code
will be publicly available at: https://github.com/aliefarooqui/GravityPanorama. (Source: arXiv.org Physicics)

Automated controller design using model-based reinforcement learning offers a high
level of flexibility, as models can be easily modified according to various system
characteristics. However, models used in this method fail to account for key system
parameters such as the effects of cyber attacks on control signals. To address this
limitation, we suggest modifying conventional model-based reinforcement learning
algorithms to take into consideration the probabilistic nature of model components.
We implement this approach on an industrial robot, incorporating characteristics
such as (1) the defense strategies employed by cyber security systems, (2) the
probability distribution of attack signals, and (3) the effectiveness of control
signals despite potential cyber attacks. By effectively combining our model with
the policy search method, we obtain controllers that not only optimize overall system
performance but also remain functional despite cyber attacks. Specifically, our
research demonstrates (1) the co-design of controllers and security measures, (2) the
probability of successful attacks against controllers, and (3) the resilience of our
controllers when subjected to actual cyber attacks. We validate the efficacy of
our proposed method using an industrial robot model, mimicking the behavior of a
Quintic motion. The results show that our approach achieves a notable level of
performance when compared to conventional design methods. For example, in the event
of a cyber attack, our controller's performance declines by 4.8% in terms of mean
squared error, while model trajectory data indicates that an attacker could have
successfully compromised the controller for at least 51.5 seconds; in contrast, our
approach enables the system to remain stable even after detection of the attack. 
In contrast, conventional design methods result in system failure upon actual
attack, while also revealing that the parameters of the security system affect the
overall system performance more so than controller parameters, while model
performance actually improves by 32.2% when the parameter value is adjusted from
0 to 0.4. Overall, our research offers co-designed security and control systems
capable of withstandng cyber attacks. Additionally, our model enables the
determination of the effects of specific security system parameters on overall system
performance, while our policy search method enables the system to adapt to cyber
attacks through data-driven search of the control policy space. Ultimately, our
research facilitates the effective management of security systems through analysis
of the effects of specific security system parameters on overall system performance.  -->

In systems that exhibit spatial and temporal change through feedback mechanisms, patterns can emerge, evolve, and persist. This research investigates how the persistent patterns in biological evolution, such as the diverse array of life forms on Earth, can arise when a variable environment drives systems in a state of constant negative entropy over time. A key finding is that a system with heritable information, which drives its own evolution, can maintain a state of dynamic equilibrium even in a constantly shifting environment. This is achieved through the selection of information patterns that resist the system's natural tendency to degrade, without the need for maximum entropy production principles, which have been shown to oversimplify the system's dynamics. Our results demonstrate that patterns with a high ability to self-improve can become entrenched, even when the system is not in a state of maximum entropy production. A model based on the system's internal and external dynamics is introduced, which accounts for the system's heritable information, its spatial structure, and the feedback mechanisms at play. This model, which is applicable to various system sizes and complexity, shows that self-improving patterns can endure, not because they maximize entropy production, but rather because their ability to adapt and evolve makes them more resilient to environmental changes. This research challenges the widespread assumption that an optimal pattern is one that maximizes entropy production. While this approach may be applicable to certain linear systems, it has been shown to fail when the system's heritable information, its spatial structure, and the system's dynamics are all accounted for. Recent years have witnessed the potential of online ongoing learning ensembles.
However, current implementations are hindered by two primary constraints.
 Firstly, they require manual specification of individual components and
their connection structure, necessitating extensive domain expertise.
 Secondly, they can only operate offline, necessitating precomputation and
buffering of isolated samples for subsequent use. This study aims to address
these limitations by introducing an innovative, fully online ensemble model,
along with a neural architecture that automates the process of building
member subsets and integrating new components.
We represent the underlying problem as a dynamic ensemble adaptation task,
and employ a neural network modification of the Greedy Ensemble Algorithm (GEE)
algorithm to tackle it. Experimental results on standard classification datasets
verify the efficacy of the dynamic ensemble model in maintaining consistent
prediction accuracy throughout ongoing learning, regardless of the evolution of
individual models. Additionally, the proposed method and source code are publicly
available for research and use. Our method Significantly outperforms top
state-of-the-art online ensemble methods (GEE, OL-ATOM, PMLR, TEE, Deep Online
Round, and Scalable Online Learning) in ongoing learning performance. This work
is an advancement towards more sophisticated and efficient neural online
ensemble algorithms for real-world learning tasks and applications. A related

Three distinct concepts are introduced: a novel, broader form of measure, generalized shapes, and differential forms. These concepts are more comprehensive than their Lagrangian counterparts, enabling us to explore new geometries. Specifically, we prove that any K\"ahler metric is also a generalized shape. Conversely, a class of generalized shapes, termed simple shapes, can be derived from K\"ahler metrics. Moreover, we establish that the metric structure of these shapes is determined solely by their complex structure. This result led us to the intriguing finding that a Ricci-flat metric exists for any simple shape defined over a complex manifold. This new metric aligns with the original when the shape is K\"ahler. Consequently, this approach enables the creation of a diverse range of Ricci-flat metrics on differentiable manifolds possessing the structure of a complex manifold. Lastly, we introduce a method for constructing new simple shapes from existing ones, including an adaptation of the Kaluza-Klein procedure. This procedure provides an additional, significant implication: for any simple shape defined over a differentiable manifold, it becomes possible to add a non-zero curvature while retaining its underlying complex structure. This result fundamentally enables the creation of a diverse set of Ricci-flat metrics with unique topological properties. These metrics can be derived from the original metric of the shape by applying a curvature transformation followed by a corresponding transformation on the shape's complex structure. Consequently, this approach yields a vast array of previously unknown metric geometries and associated holomorphic connections. This study marks the beginning of a comprehensive investigation into generalized shapes as a novel framework for differential geometry, encompassing both shape theory and metric geometry. It appears that these geometric constructs have the potential to unify disparate areas within geometry and physics, including gravity theory, the emergence of Yang-Mills fields from geometry, and the geometric interpretation of the Standard Model. A thorough exploration of this topic is beyond the scope of the current work, but it will be addressed in a companion paper.  In the companion paper, we will demonstrate that any generalized shape can be represented as a generalized symplectic structure. This discovery leads to the emergence of a vast array of Yang-Mills fields with unique topological properties at their equilibrium, characterized by exact solutions derived from the corresponding geometric equations. These findings represent an important step towards understanding the geometric unity of gauge fields within both mathematics and physics. They also mark a significant development in the theory of Yang-Mills fields, encompassing both their modern mathematical treatment and their original discovery within the context of quantum electrodynamics

This research investigates a comprehensive framework for approximating non-zero-sum stochastic differential equations driven by regime-switching Brownian motions and finite-state Markov processes. The evaluation of predictions generated by machine learning models is a highly debated topic. Traditional measures, like the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and the mean squared error, fail to account for important practical considerations. For instance, a perfect classifier can still be vulnerable to attacks on rare data points. To address these limitations, we have developed the Unfairness Notation Toolkit, a flexible tool for analyzing and understanding fairness, bias, and sensitivity in predictive models. Our toolkit provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating these concepts, which are fundamental to understanding model performance. To demonstrate the utility of the toolkit, we use it to analyze a dataset containing financial literacy survey responses. Our findings reveal that, despite their accuracy, models can still exhibit significant bias and unfairness. Moreover, our results show that mitigating bias often comes at a cost to model accuracy, which can be a concern in practical applications. Our work serves as a call to arms for the machine learning community to be more mindful of the fair and sensitive application of our models. The maximum likelihood CMB maps are typically produced as a default output by software such as SMICA and Magic, often used for cosmic microwave background data analysis. These maps, however, contain geometric distortions including ring-shaped artifacts and radial anomalies, which are the result of circular padding techniques employed to handle data gaps. Techniques like spectral presmoothing and ring adjustment can mitigate these distortions, or alternatively, implementing proper padding without rings can avoid them altogether. By combining Smica and Python's NumPy and Astropy tools, it's possible to apply this solution in CMB data analysis. In this paper, I outline a method for ring-free padding and present a tool for smoothing SMICA foreground maps. This method also preserves spherical harmonic weights, ensuring correct reconstruction of foregrounds using a multi-linear SMICA algorithm. Furthermore, it's demonstrated how to integrate this solution into the Magic software, enabling ring-free padding through setting origin-based masking radii to zero. In addition to describing this method, I've applied it to major CMB surveys including Planck, WMAP, and the Simons Observatory. Using origin-based masking radii in SMICA foreground separation can cause distortions; by setting these radii to zero, SMICA achieves better foreground separation at low multipoles, preserving the small-scale foreground pattern in these surveys. By avoiding geometric distortions through ring-free padding, it's possible to achieve small-scale foreground separation in CMB surveys more effectively. In the case of Planck, ring-free SMICA foreground maps enable slightly higher LSST foreground correlation coefficients than the standard maximum likelihood maps. This makes ring-free padding a valuable feature for CMB data analysis. In goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, agents learn to accomplish specific tasks within simulated environments that are defined by a policy written in natural language. This policy serves as a state-dependent reward function, shaping the agent's actions to achieve the desired goal. However, natural language is often ambiguous, leading to multiple possible interpretations by the agent. This study explores referential ambiguity in goal-conditioned learning, demonstrating how simple word substitutions can change an agent's ability to achieve the intended goal, even when the agent has not been trained on that specific word variation. Based on this observation, we propose two techniques for mitigating referential ambiguity: utilizing natural language processing to clarify ambiguous terms based on the context of the policy and using goal-conditioned policy feedback to train the agent for multiple possible interpretations of the same term. These methods are evaluated in a series of experiments that show the importance of addressing referential ambiguity in goal-conditioned learning. This paper is available online at https://arxiv.org/1905.03688. Additional information, including video footage and related code, can be found at https://referential-ambiguity.com.

We develop a novel method for characterizing quantum channels via unappappable interferometry. This method involves a "shadow" of the channel where its output state is its input state shifted forward in time. By measuring correlations between systems that never interact, we determine how these "shadows" transform, effectively mapping the channel's effect. This approach, using legible inputs, offers a way to fully characterize channels, recover internal properties of channels, and, most importantly, identify non-stochastic channels through noiseless channel identification. Furthermore, it has experimental implications by transforming an otherwise demanding full tomography into a more feasible partial tomography, reducing the number of necessary measurements in proportion to the channel's dimension. This method is particularly useful for near-term quantum devices due to its ability to characterize channels efficiently with near-optimal resources and resistance to noise. Finally, we extend this method to characterize quantum measurements by applying it to the inverse process of channel application, namely, quantum data reconstruction. This reconstruction is highly useful in various quantum communication tasks and, using our approach, is achieved with the same efficiency and resource independence as the channel characterization. Importantly, this method is also scalable, meaning it can be executed with minimal additional resources as the channel dimension increases. Overall, this method is now ready for implementation. Its efficiency and resource independence make it a perfect choice for execution, and when successfully deployed, will be required for generating new quantum channels. Moreover, the knowledge gained from this approach will be instrumental in enabling full characterization. Although current technology is not yet ready for full characterization, this method is essential for understanding which additional resources are required to achieve it. Finally, the knowledge and technology developed from this approach will be vital in enabling full characterization and eventually allowing us to trust it. In the future, this method, initially designed for characterizing channels, will be instrumental in extending to characterizing quantum states and, ultimately, quantum gates. Its impact will be part of a broader technological shift in characterizing quantum systems, leveraging speed and trust, and enabling the widespread utilization of quantum technology. This Cheeger constant represents the optimal ratio of optimal volume to optimal perimeter within a shape. In the case of a disk, this ratio approaches 1 as the size of the disk increases. There are existing upper and lower bounds for this constant applied across all convex shapes in 2-dimensional space, with the upper bound being at least twice the lower bound. The equality in these bounds is achieved for shapes that are symmetrical about a line. The purpose of this research is to propose new relationships between the Cheeger constant and the intrinsic mean width, with consideration of precision. In particular, a new set of inequalities states that for any convex two-dimensional shape, Cheeger constant k times the intrinsic mean width w is greater than or equal to pi times (0.785 plus 0.535k^2w) plus 0.535k times the intrinsic mean width. There is also another inequality stating that for any convex two-dimensional shape, Cheeger constant k times the intrinsic mean width w is less than or equal to pi times (1.295 plus 0.535k^2w). The shapes used in these new inequalities include a square, a regular non-square rectangle, and a gear. The work in this research reveals that these new inequalities provide tighter bounds than existing ones, with the lower bound being tighter than the upper bound. The research also demonstrates the precision of the proposed upper bound by showing that as the Cheeger constant k increases, the difference between the proposed upper bound and the lower bound decreases and becomes at least twice as small when k reaches a value of unity. Our analysis shows that in two-dimensional Coulomb systems, the corrosion process exhibits a distinctive characteristic of being influenced by the Condon effect. This gives rise to an interaction Hamiltonian that contains terms with alternating signs in an expansion series. Specifically, our findings reveal that at small scales, the leading interaction term has a repulsive property, while the next highest order has an attractive property, thus setting the stage for a variety of instability scenarios in low-energy graphene models. In particular, our application to the recently introduced honeycomb configuration in bilayer graphene reveals that this system exhibits a non-trivial phase transition resulting from the formation of triangular charge droplets. This transition is associated with an anomaly in the system's conductivity upon reaching the critical point, thus indicating the potential for this configuration to exhibit correlated metal-like behavior. Our analysis also explores the general conditions for achieving this metal-like behavior in broader families of low-energy graphene models. By doing so, we identify several open tasks for achieving the metal-like behavior in charge cones and correlation-induced metalization as an unresolved problem of graphenology. This problem reduction significantly narrows the range of parameters requiring further investigation. Finally, our analysis shows that the possibility of achieving the metal-like behavior in bilayer graphene is confined to a particular subclass of truncated models where the interaction expansion starts with the repulsive term. This provides a concrete benchmark for testing the metalization scenario in coupled graphene systems. This benchmark can be further generalized for the broader families of models yet to be explored. The scintillation properties and luminescence patterns of molecular spintronic materials, particularly certain doped fullerene derivatives on hollow carbon substrates, are highly responsive to environmental temperature variations. This work investigates how the surface supports can influence the conformational changes and resulting properties of $C$_{80} with a Sc$_{2}$TbN cluster at its center. Through a combination of computational tools, including density functional theory and time-dependent density functional theory, we analyzed the energy spectra and conformational changes of Sc$_{2}$TbN$C$_{80} when situated on hollow boron nitride (h-BN) or rhodium (Rh) surfaces. Our findings indicate that the  Dy$^{9+}$ ( D$_{5h}$ ) conformation of Sc$_{2}$TbN$C$_{80} is stabilized by covalent bonds with the substrate, whereas the$D_{2h}$ (Sc$_{2}$TbN$_{II}$) conformation is favored when the substrate and fermi level are complementary, as seen with Sc$_{2}$TbN$C$_{80}$ on h-BN. In contrast, Sc$_{2}$TbN$C$_{80}$ on a Rh(111) surface exhibits luminescence at 580 nm at room temperature and undergoes a first-order phase transition to a low-temperature $D_{5h}$ conformation accompanied by an abrupt decrease in luminescence intensity at approximately 150 K. Our studies reveal that temperature-dependent luminescence in molecular electronic/photonic materials can be intentionally modulated via the solid-substrate interface. Moreover, these results provide a theoretical foundation for the experimental observation of antiferromagnetic ordering in Sc$_{2}$TbN$C$_{80}$ with a ferrimagnetic moment of 5.0 $\mu$B below 20 K on a Rh(111) surface. Finally, these results underscore the critical role of subsurface interactions in determining the energy spectra and conformational changes of molecular electronic/photonic materials, which in turn is influenced by the electronic properties and surface geometry of the substrate solid. Therefore, these results have significant implications for the design of molecular electronic/photonic devices with adjustable molecular conformational changes. Additionally, these results provide new insights into the design of molecular electronic/photonic devices, specifically scintillation devices, which can be intentionally modulated at specific temperatures

By extending the method employed by Verlinde to other situations, we find new geometric T-duality formulas for closed, two-dimensional spacetimes that are topologically equivalent to a torus with fibre bundles exhibiting Z_N symmetry. Our research resolves T-duality transformations for various examples through explicit calculations. Geometric T-duality provides a means to construct new solutions to classical two-dimensional gravity theories from existing ones, offering a method of generating distinct solutions from a given one and demonstrating the existence of multiple solutions to the same problem. We introduce unique properties held by continuous dynamical systems and develop corresponding concepts and results for discrete-time systems. These properties ensure global analysis and consideration of equilibrium and non-equilibrium states, along with periodic and quasi-periodic orbits in the context of bifurcations. A central tool is the concept of smoothness with respect to a metric defining the system's behavior, allowing for generalizations beyond classical equilibria and allowing for system perturbations. Building upon this framework, we establish results regarding the behavior of discrete-time systems under various conditions. These include the generation of non-trivial dynamical behaviors from generic planar odd vector fields, the stability of 2-dimensional quasi-periodic motions, and the emergence of horseshoes in 3-dimensional systems. Our metric approach to modeling also facilitates an understanding of when a discrete-time system's behavior is determined solely by its initial state, enabling a generalization of a celebrated result from Kolmogorov regarding approximations of periodic orbits. A key feature of our work is the comprehensive demonstration of the ubiquitous nature of these dynamical behaviors in the context of smooth discrete-time systems, defined by compact metric spaces and shift maps with smooth additional structure. Our setting subsumes numerous well-known examples, including planar vector fields, smooth map equations, and dynamical systems defined by cobweb maps. A unifying spirit underlies our work: the widespread occurrence of robust global analysis in systems that are smoothly extended from their non-linear flow to an associated linear flow. We have sought to present our findings in a manner accessible to readers not familiar with the technical details of these dynamical systems. The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately constructing an initial wave function using VQAE can significantly impact its overall performance. By exploiting qubit excitation (QE) principles, which govern molecular transitions, it's possible to harness a broader understanding of how these systems behave. Drawing from this, we've developed an adaptive VQE (AQVQE) approach that effectively generates initial wave functions tailored to QEA patterns. We've implemented this protocol on realistic molecular examples, such as the water and acetone molecules, and compared its outcomes with traditional VQE methods. Our results indicate that AQVAE yields wave functions and computational costs comparable to standard VQE, but achieves this without needing costly initial optimization procedures. Furthermore, we've also demonstrated AQVEE's ability to be modified and tailored according to a QEA-based strategy, allowing for the inclusion of nuclear degrees of freedom. This innovation represents an important advancement in adapting AQVEE to molecular structures and serves as a key step in perfecting quantum algorithms. It opens up promising avenues for molecular chemistry applications on near-term quantum computers. Additionally, this work highlights the significance of molecular QE in understanding these systems' behaviors on the quantum spectrum. Finally, we've also begun exploring the potential for expanding AQVEE beyond molecular chemistry and material science applications. If successful, this could represent a groundbreaking shift in quantum algorithms. Further research is required to validate this promising development. A distinctive type of generative modeling called the 'profound neural network' features an intriguing property - its generative mechanism can be reversed. Typically, generic generative models use a scanner to generate new inputs, but the PNN's ability to calculate the output map of its innermost layer allows for a reverse scan, allowing new inputs to be mapped directly to the outermost layers. This study introduces a new variant of the PNN called the 'profound neural network with label supervision,' which requires predefined output labels. We modify the standard PNN to take into account these label maps and derive a reverse output map for each unit at every layer. We also develops a new method of estimating the probability distribution of each unit by using a moving window scan of the output map and calculating the most frequently occurring values. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach of reverse output map estimates in the context of the PNNS by applying it to the latent representations of a scanner trained on a dataset of hand-written digits, and show that it significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we also introduce a new approach to determine the most frequently occurring values within a continuous probability distribution, which does not require data generation. This method can be utilized in a wide range of problems involving probability density estimation. For unsupervised speech synthesis, current approaches typically involve pre-training a sequence generator with a variety of objectives including autoencoding, next word prediction, and energy modeling. Objectives like autoencoding seem necessary for developing a language model that considers the likelihood of consecutive words, yet they make the training process complicated. In contrast, this study presents a new framework called unsupervised isolation, which separates speech into distinct segments and allows for straightforward objectives in a text-to-speech system. Specifically, the isolation framework includes two main components: a text isolation model that learns to predict individual words within each sentence, and a speech isolation model that generates speech synthesis proxies using the likelihood of speech segment energies. These objectives are realized using a normalizing flow. Our experiments on the LibriSpeech corpus demonstrate that the text-to-speech proxies produced by the speech model can guide the text isolation model to produce coherent speech from topologically connected words, achieving good speech quality with a limited number of samples, outperforming previous approaches. Furthermore, the study also explores alternative pre-training objectives for unsupervised speech synthesis and discusses the reason behind the success of the proposed framework. As a result of the intricate nature of sentiment words and contextual dependence, direct object representation in neural networks often fails to capture sentiment nuances, leading to word embeddings that are far from their actual meaning in sentence context. To address this issue, we developed a novel pre-training method that leverages aspect-based sentiment analysis and exploits supervised learning, producing aspect-specific word embeddings that are rich in semantic content and dominate the representation of sentences. This approach starts with a transformer model that separates the sentence into its semantic parts based on specified aspects, using a novel supervised contrastive loss function to pull similar aspects together and push similar aspects apart. The resulting model, with its emphasis on aspect-specific representations, becomes the core of our sentiment analysis system, where we integrate it with corpus statistics through aspect-based attention to further refine the representations through a seamless fine-tuning process, ultimately leading to exceptional performance in discovering word sentiment meanings within complex sentences. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach from implicit sentiment discovery to fine-tuning effectively outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and human judges. Moreover, we successfully applied our model to various sentiment subtasks such as Sst, Sst1, and Sst2 without modifying it at all. This research investigates the secure communication challenges in a multi-user network assisted by a intelligent surface, where each user has imperfect transmitters due to hardware issues. The goal is to achieve secure communication at maximum rate while ensuring the eavesdropper remains deceived. The paper proposes a two-stage optimization approach that removes biases in the signal phase at the base station and intelligent surface. First, an optimized phase shift scheme is derived through the base station to ensure the signal remains unchanged at the base station while making it harder for the eavesdropper to decode. Next, each intelligent surface device is programmed with an optimal phase shift that minimizes the interference seen by the eavesdropper and ensures the signal is received at the intended recipient. The paper further explores scenarios of incomplete information among users. Numerical results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed solution. Additionally, the paper assesses the impact of suboptimal solutions, where users lack complete information, on the network performance. The results indicate that minor degradation in performance can be tolerated, with the base station being the most susceptible to suboptimal solutions. Furthermore, the paper's findings illustrate that even with the eavesdropper's location and the base station's transmission characteristics known to the eavesdropper, the eavesdropper can still deduce the base station's phase shift with relative precision. Consequently, the eavesdropper can potentially achieve the maximum communication capacity over the wireless network, even with the eavesdropper's location known to the legitimate users. The users can prevent this by introducing randomness in their transmission phase, resulting in reduced eavesdropper knowledge and thus the eavesdropper's communication capacity. The eavesdropper can overcome this limitation by obtaining the eavesdropper's location, which in turn requires the eavesdropper to find an optimal solution to a specific geometric issue, a problem with no simple solution. The eavesdropper can ensure the eavesdropper's transmission characteristics remain in the eavesdropper's control by verifying the eavesdropper's transmission characteristics with the eavesdropper's controller. Spectral analyses are performed on both states via the use of quasi-classical partition functions. Additionally, an empirical evidence is presented regarding a specific mass-splitting within the neutral pion sector, resulting from the decay of the quasi-scissors-mode state into two neutral pions. We have also derived the electromagnetic form factor of the quasi-scissors-mode state in a semi-classical framework. Relevant findings are expected to be applicable in a effective field theory setting that resembles the Twin-Higgs mechanism. The analysis involved calculating the strong coupling behavior of multiple mass terms that arise due to the symmetry breaking, which also includes a comparison of the ether field's theoretical heat capacity to the human body's heat capacity. The human body's heat capacity is approximately 6.7 kilowatt degrees at normal body temperature, whereas the ether heat capacity is roughly six orders of magnitude larger. The research also delved into the potential creation of an ether particle accelerator, which could be built by enclosing a superconducting material in a shape that amplifies the thermal vibrations of the ether field. The possibility of observing direct or indirect images of the ether particles or their antiparticles was also discussed, which could be feasible through extremely high temperature particle collisions. The research estimated that an ether particle with a mass of one gigaelectronvolt would result in the production of a few hundred directly visible, collimated protons and antiprotons per second. Furthermore, the possibility of using the ether field to explain the origin of cosmic matter and dark matter could be explored by introducing a matter creating mass term and a dark matter preserving mass term respectively into the corresponding ether current Lagrangians. The research however only delved into these ideas at normal space time curvature and left the exploration of their behavior at extreme curvatures for future studies. The paper's findings reveal that the ether field, when modified as suggested in this study, holds significant physical meaning and could be a means to explore the quantum gravitational realm. The research also demonstrates that an accelerated and systematic search for unconventional particle detectors, such as those described in this study, is necessary to explore the global physics landscape. A key goal in NLP is translating human language into a form that's straightforward to comprehend, both in terms of syntax and semantics. Current techniques divide this objective into two separate tasks: syntax (understanding tree-like structure) and semantics (extracting meaning), often performed in isolation. However, many challenges necessitate joint syntax- and semantics-based analysis. For instance, understanding a sentence like "Only the correct answers are evaluated," requires awareness of the modifying effect of "only" on the noun "answers." Additionally, certain crucial concepts may want to exert influence on multiple parts of a sentence. To tackle these complexities, this study presents an innovative method for collaborative syntax- and semantics-based analysis. By training a single neural module to simultaneously handle syntax and semantics while interacting via shared hidden states, this method enables information to flow and exchange between the two components. Experimental outcomes with tasks like question-answering, text-summary generation, and dependency parsing showcase the excellent performance of this approach. Furthermore, using the trained module for inference-only dependency parsing resulted in outstanding performance, surpassing state-of-the-art outcomes on the standard CoNLL-2006 dataset. Its potential applications and extensions are also explored. The developed code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/skybprime/CSSA. As an advanced project under the Linking NLP Models to Data Types initiative, this work aims to facilitate the dissemination of the state-of-the-art module to a wide range of practical applications in the linkpeda.com platform, a leading data dissemination platform. The associated documentation is accessible through the linkpeda.com CSSA page.

The ultimate fate of neutron stars merging with black holes remains unclear, particularly regarding the generation of gravitational waves and electromagnetic transients. We introduce MAGNETIC, a general-relativistic, neutrino-rich, magnetized disk simulation for postmerger black hole environments. We find that magnetic fields of sufficient strength, equivalent to the maximum energy density in a nuclear bomb, can explain the observed luminosity and mass ejection associated with MAXI J1303-620. The ejected material has a high-specific angular momentum and low metal abundance, consistent with observed polar alignment and chemical depletion. Our study reveals that the postmerger disk is dynamic, evolving over time, and is influenced by the magnetic field's initial configuration and strength. We discover two distinct phases: an initial short-lived, magnetically dominated phase lasting approximately 1-10 milliseconds, and a longer-lived, neutrino-cooled accretion phase that follows. During the second phase, the disk's evolution is primarily driven by viscosity and can result in the ejection of a large amount of material, potentially explaining the observed bright X-ray transients. However, numerical simulations using our current framework fail to successfully model MAXI J1303-620 due to the following limitations: magnetohydrodynamic numerical approximations, relativistic equation of state uncertainties, and limited simulation domain. Therefore, further studies incorporating a complete simulation of the entire magnetized disk are necessary. Our work lays the groundwork for these future investigations by outlining the MAGNETIC approach and its predicted outcomes. A more in-depth analysis is necessary to fully explore the magnetic field's impact on neutron star-black hole mergers and their potential observational signatures. Such research will significantly contribute to our understanding of the final stages in the evolution of massive binary stars and their resulting extraordinary celestial phenomena. A related movie is available at https://doi.org/10.25372/2022NWAJi.0001.01.001.

We utilized the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program to conduct a comprehensive study on tidal features of early-type galaxies. This study analyzed a sample of 349 massive galaxies in the COSMOS field with apparent masses exceeding $11.5$ magnitudes. Notably, we found that galaxy mass is inversely correlated with tidal feature frequency, as more massive galaxies exhibit fewer tidal features. This finding is consistent with the notion that massive galaxies are dynamically relaxed. Conversely, less massive galaxies are actively interacting and exhibiting orbital collisions. Furthermore, our research indicated that late-type galaxies are more susceptible to tidal interactions than their early-type counterparts. This disparity is likely a direct consequence of late-type galaxies being inherently more unstable. Notably, our study also revealed a positive correlation between galaxy mass and tidal feature complexity, as higher-mass galaxies show increased frequencies of complex two-tailed features. Interestingly, this relationship is linear for early-type galaxies but exhibits a saturating effect for late-type galaxies. These findings align with simulations predicting an exponential increase in interaction likelihood with host galaxy mass. Moreover, our study demonstrated that the probabilities of late-type galaxies experiencing two-tailed features during an interaction are roughly $0.25$ for single tails and $0.5$ for one-way features. This aligns with simulations predicting a likelihood of interaction of $0.5$ for single tails and $0.25$ for one-way features. Our study also estimated a merger rate of $0.021_{-0.013}^{+0.026}$ (1 yr)$^{-1}$ for $z<0.05$ and galaxies with masses above $11.0$ magnitudes. This rate is significantly higher than a previous study to the COSMOS field and may indicate an increased interaction likelihood in this study due to the greater mass range of our sample, as well as selecting only late-type galaxies. Notably, our study's merger rate for galaxies with masses between $11.0$ and $12.0$ is significantly higher than a simulation predicting a likelihood of interaction of $0.021_{-0.013}^{+0.026}$ (1 yr). This discrepancy may be a direct consequence of the cosmological mass bias, as the simulation predicts a likelihood of interaction of $0.021_{-0.013}^{+0.026}$ (1 yr). In recent years, advanced metrology has played a vital role in the development and optimization of high-power laser tools. These systems deliver energy through controlled absorption, generating plasma that enables scientists to study complex phenomena or drive other light with precise manipulation of the plasma's properties. The intricate interaction between the laser and plasma makes their design, operation, and response challenging to predict, necessitating experiments that are often costly and time-consuming. In this study, we introduce a practical approach that integrates computational models with physical experimentation. By combining established mathematical models describing laser and plasma behavior with an evolving neural network model, we can simulate and design high-power laser tools. The neural network model, initially trained on a combination of theoretical equations and experimental data, can then be fine-tuned through direct experiments, refining its understanding of the system's behavior and potentially uncovering previously unknown responses. This study serves as a foundation for applying our approach to other high-power laser systems, and we expect that our method could be applied to other complex light-matter interactions where first-principles models are feasible, providing a powerful feedback mechanism that could augment other optimization techniques and save valuable resources. Additionally, we demonstrate that this cycle of simulation and experimentation can be repeated in a reverse engineering scenario, and we use our technique to generate a diagram illustrating the power and pulse width trade-offs of a high-power laser tool. The data presented in the diagram can be used as a reference for other research groups looking to design and configure their own laser tools, and we anticipate that this method could be applied to other systems where such a diagram might be useful, providing a novel form of shared knowledge. The code and data used in this study can be accessed through our GitHub repository at https://github.com/ericpart/design-laser-tool, and we intend to continue developing and expanding our approach to account for additional complexity factors. Future work may involve exploring the feasibility of automating the design of laser tools, using our technique in conjunction with other optimization algorithms, and applying our method to other systems where similar trade-offs may occur. Recent studies have shown that language models possess a form of visual awareness when creating text, as evidenced by their capacity to utilize visual information when available. This study aims to investigate whether language models can integrate visual knowledge directly, rather than relying on accompanying images. To address this question, we developed a task that requires language models to generate proper scientific branch names drawn from a visual domain, despite the branch having multiple acceptable textual representations. By evaluating the generated text alongside human assessments, we found that the most accurate assessments from fine-tuned models, such as MidJumper and T0, rarely matched human standards. This suggests that the models lack a profound understanding of visual knowledge. Furthermore, we assessed how visual knowledge databases impact the task and discovered a significant improvement when using a database tailored to botanical terms. While the models demonstrated some awareness of visual knowledge, we found that the primary contributor to task performance was the model's ability to create coherent and aesthetically pleasing text. This implies that the models' ability to incorporate visual knowledge may be compromised by their overall language capabilities. Consequently, we believe that developing more sophisticated visual knowledge databases and creating controlled text creation environments is crucial for advancing the understanding of visual awareness in language models. The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of two components: an improved RingCT encryption and a token issuance mechanism, ensuring tokens are distributed fairly in support of the Delegated Proof of Stake network.
The Delegated RingCT system enables a higher level of transaction anonymity through a combined token and RingCT encryption approach.
The token issuance mechanism, combined with Ring CT encryption, ensures tokens are divisible and transaction amounts are anonymous, providing a higher level of privacy.
In contrast to previous RingCT schemes, Delegated RingCT does not hinder transaction propagation and introduces a faster and more efficient proof of concept.
A comprehensive investigation of Delegated RingCT incorporates a statistical analysis and demonstrates how Delegated RingCT's design offers a trustworthy and secure anonymity system, meeting the requirements specified in the Circular for Anonymous Transactions as outlined by the European Union. Furthermore, our research explores the prospects of Delegated RingCT in other blockchain networks.

Building reliable predictive models in fields like medicine requires accurate and comprehensive data labeling. Unfortunately, existing datasets are often restricted due to various limitations such as sample size or quality. Researchers in the field of ophthalmology are currently confronted with a particular challenge posed by retinal disease classification, which demands detailed spatial labels and further research. In an effort to address this issue, we develop innovative methods for generating labeled training data within a simulated environment. By combining statistical analysis of retinal structure with game engine tools, we create complex, detailed spatio-topographic labels for retinal diseases. Subsequently, we construct and train explainable models using this generated data, which replicates real-world results for retinal disease classification. Moreover, we recapture the essential multi-modal characteristics of retinal data through a mixture of latent features. These artificially created datasets can be utilized as standalone resources or hybridized with existing small/weak datasets through an unsupervised domain adaptation approach, leading to significant enhancements in model performance and robustness across all applied applications, including retinal disease classification, fundus segmentation, and vascular segmentation. The generated dataset, as well as our proposed approaches and code, are publicly available for research purposes in the ophthalmology and retinal field, which can also be applied to other domains. These methods are particularly suitable for fields looking to leverage synthetic data generation for topologically-relevant model training. Additionally, we make our dataset and code available for other domains at https://github.com/MULTIMED/CM2. Preliminary versions of our work have been presented at the IEEE Stable Learning Workshop 2022 and the ICML 2022 COMPGRAPH Workshop. A demonstration of our methods was also presented at the IEEE ISBI 2022. A related thesis covering this research can be found at https://pastresearch.com/thesis.pdf. Furthermore, our proposed techniques and datasets have sparked complementary research in connection to domain adaptation for retinal tools as reported in https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.13.444. Additionally, related work by other researchers can be found at https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9375/4/3/57. In recent years, substantial advancements have been made in the development of soft robotics techniques. Research in this field has primarily focused on designing innovative mechanisms of end effectors and exploring their applications. As a result, there is now a diverse range of models and strategies available to control these devices. This paper serves as an in-depth review of the state of the art in model driven control of soft robots. We also examine the challenges that remain to be addressed and identify areas that require further investigation. This assessment is grounded in a comprehensive literature survey involving over five hundred publications. We define model driven control, discuss its advantages, and outline its applications across various soft robotic systems. Furthermore, we identify and analyze the key characteristics of models used in this control type, and investigate the model realization methods, optimization techniques, and performance metrics that have been developed. Finally, based on the literature review, we pinpoint areas for further improvement and propose targeted research directions for enhancing model driven control systems. This assessment not only provides a thorough understanding of the current state of this control type but also contributes to the evolution of the field by recognizing existing limitations and potential opportunities for advancement. Our paper investigates the authentic Jacobi group $\mathrm{GU}(2,2)$ with minimal
characteristic $p$, focusing on $p$-stable and $p$-reducible, but not
$p$-stable, representations of the group. We build on Hayat-Guillou's framework
by extending $\mathrm{GU}(2,2)$ to $\mathrm{GU}(2,N)$ for any $N \in \mathbb{Z}$.
This allows us to extend the construction to $\mathrm{GU}(n,N)$ for
$n, N \in \mathbb{Z}}$ and provides a foundation for future research. For $\mathrm{GU}(2,N)$
with $|N| > p$ when $p$ is an odd prime, we establish the classification of
$p$-representations by coupling their irreducible $p$-representations.
Furthermore, the representation theory of $\mathrm{GU}(2,N)$ with $|N| \equiv
p \mod ~2$ is also explored. For $\mathrm{GU}(2,N)$ with $|N| \equiv 1 \mod ~p$
when $p$ is an odd prime, we delve into the properties of $p$-stable and
$p$-reducible, but $p$-stable, representations. The representation theory of
$\mathrm{GU}(2,N)$ with $|N| = p$ is another area of research. Finally, the
$\mathrm{GU}(2,N)$-groups that are $p$-simple and the extension of the
framework to $\mathrm{GU}(n,N)$ for $n, N \in \mathbb{Z}}$ are discussed. This
invites the reader to a future and intriguing study of a $p$-admissible group
extending the authentic Jacobi group. Ultimately, the method employed here can
be used to investigate the representation theory of a $p$-admissible group
extending the authentic Jacobi group. This presents an exciting prospect for
further research. (Abstract of PhD thesis)

Recent studies demonstrate the effectiveness of Conditional GANs in generating realistic results across various fields. However, using a conditional layer to pass inputs to these networks can be problematic due to the potential for inaccurate representations, like when working with image modulations in genetics. In such cases, a structured representation cannot be directly achieved through a conventional conditional layer. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Hidden Space Conditioning (HSC) layer for HCGANs, allowing the latent representation to extract relevant features from hidden inputs. Our research conducts a thorough analysis on the HSC in more complex networks and evaluates its performance in two common scenarios, image reconstruction and image generation. The results reveal that HSC offers better stability and performance than traditional conditional layers. Moreover, HSC has the ability to successfully process complex structural and sequential inputs, making it a more suitable option for datasets with intricate relationships, like images associated with genetic data. We achieve this by establishing a reference operator with a resolvent that is bounded for all values within the positive half of the complex plane. This achievement enables us to utilize a nonlinear resolvent algebra to verify the existence of solutions to the equation. The methods employed rely on the specification of specific boundary conditions, varying depending on whether the equation is considered in reference or curved geometry. When considering the equation within curved geometry, we take into account the geometry's evolution as part of a nonlinear hydrodynamics system, which adds an additional complexity to the problem. Detecting out-of-distribution data is essential for most deep learning models to prevent incorrect predictions. Previous research shows that normal processes in NCP layers have high in-distribution detection performance. In this study, we numerically demonstrate that the location parameter of the normal process in MCD models is the key to performing out-of-distribution detection. Based on this insight, we develop a simple and efficient out-of-distribution detection method by minimizing the variance of the location parameter, without requiring training data from the target distribution. Our experimental results show that the proposed method achieves a significant reduction of at most 40% in the number of required clean data samples, while demonstrating test performance comparable to the existing benchmark approach. Furthermore, the OOD detection method presented in this study can be easily integrated into existing deep learning models without additional computational costs, and we validate this in our models retrained with our OOD detection criterion only. Moreover, the models retrained with our OOD detection criterion not only excel in out-of-distribution detection but also demonstrate an improvement in out-of-distribution detection robustness, as proven by theoretical justification. Our theoretical results show a lower bound on the out-of-distribution detection error rate, and through numerical simulations, we confirm that this lower bound tightly bounds the observed out-of-distribution detection performance of our models retrained with our OOD detection criterion. Our work opens up possibilities for multiple novel OOD detection methods to be developed based on minimizing the variance of the location parameter, and one such method has been experimentally validated in this study. This research centers on a distributed edge computing framework within a software-defined network environment. The objective is to achieve optimal energy efficiency while ensuring the timely processing of services in a distributed architecture. A novel protocol, named FEDC, has been proposed to achieve efficient service delivery through close collaboration between the service delivery entity and the network infrastructure. FEDC manages the allocation of fog resources via a centralized server that also handles service requests and mitigates faults while overseeing the restoration of services. A key component of FEDC is its adaptive fault-treatment strategy which comprises a contextualized fault type recognition mechanism and deep learning-based fault-mitigation and restoration technique. A simulation study has demonstrated the enhanced performance of FEDC in comparison to the current best practice algorithms in terms of energy efficiency and service restoration speed. In addition, the research has validated the optimality of the FEDC protocol in its current form and discussed the scope for further optimization. Notably, the average service restoration speed for FEDC is approximately two orders of magnitude faster than the current best practice algorithms. By allowing participants to make in-scenario choices at set times, four distinct scenario phases were created, enabling the extraction of critical moments in each scenario. This resulting dataset, called SceNDD, comprises over 8,000 scenarios with over 160,000 time points, giving it nearly four times more data than existing large-scale datasets. Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted wireless communication has gained significant interest due to its potential in modifying the characteristics of wireless signals. Yet, the complexity of RIS-related channel estimation poses a major hurdle in its practical implementation. To address this challenge, we develop an enhanced Extreme Learning Machine (ELM)-based channel estimation model for RIS-supported Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems. By taking into account the limited availability of channel estimation data and the negative effects of inaccurate model inputs, our proposed model first establishes a time-dependent non-linear regression model that leverages historical channel estimation data to predict the values of subsequent timeframes. Subsequently, we design a linear regression model that utilizes the predicted channel estimates from the non-linear model and current receive signal values as inputs to estimate the actual channel in-flight. Our simulation results indicate that the proposed methods significantly outperform the existing single-model approaches in terms of accurate channel estimation, minimal hardware failure resistance, and simplified model implementations. To illustrate this point, our results show that the proposed models achieve an impressive 90% reduction in estimated channel accuracy loss when subjected to 10% sensor failure and 40% shortened CP conditions, respectively. The effectiveness of the Integral Fluctuation Theorem in the single energy assessment is examined. This theoretical framework addresses a critical issue: confirming the presence of entropy production in a system using a single energy monitor. Historically, non-diverging trajectories have been observed in experiments constrained by thermodynamic laws. However, but it has been claimed that the Integral Fluctuation Theorem remains valid even with such constraints. We examine this assertion, considering a system connected to heat sources and detectors, with the application of the Integral Fluctuation Theorem. Although the theoretical framework assumes no limitations, we find that entropy production cannot be confirmed in a system meeting necessary conditions and if the monitored energy remains within its natural range. Furthermore, we verify that the critical issue of confirmable and measurable entropy production does not exist in a system equipped with an entropic sensor, even with the absence of additional constraints. Therefore, we suggest the integration of sensors capable of measuring entropic values to validate the presence of entropy production in a system using a single energy monitor. This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems. The tool is built upon the concept of a shallow embedding of C within ACL2. Unlike traditional deep embeddings, this approach separates the implementation of C's syntax and semantics, allowing for additional abstractions to be applied. A detailed explanation of the tool's underlying architecture and methodology is provided, including its implementation details available online. Furthermore, this paper showcases the effectiveness of the tool by utilizing the ACL2 automatically generated C code to teach students and demonstrate runtime interoperability between ACL2 and C. Its ability to produce correct results is consistently verified. The generated C code is compiled in an offline environment and the resulting executables are then run within ACL2 by specifying input values and verifying their outputs. This approach allows users to verify the tool's output in a holistic manner, ensuring both logical and practical correctness. The generated C code is confined to utilize only fundamental C features, specifically function definitions, macros, static variable declarations, and basic arithmetic operations. This restriction ensures the generated C code is uncomplicated and susceptible to the tool's verifiable ACL2 translations. The tool's potential extensions are also discussed to broaden its capabilities, including support for additional C elements such as pointers and multi-threading. Similar concepts have been explored in the context of a different programming language, but the research remains in an early stage and the specific results are currently unavailable. Ultimately, this study contributes to the expansion of available programming languages that can be represented within ACL2 and provides a valuable resource for implementing shallow embeddings of languages for the purposes of verification. The tool itself is anticipated to serve as a useful learning tool for programming and the underlying technology could potentially be applied in other contexts, specifically in the development of a compiler for a programming language aimed at a beginner level. The tool can translate ACL2 expressions approximately 10-20 times more complex than those of standard C in a matter of seconds. This remarkable efficiency is attributed to the use of an optimized implementation in both ACL2 and C languages. The tool's performance is particularly remarkable given that it is capable of translating code with a level of complexity similar to that of a loop-driven algorithm for sorting a list of n elements. Our research delves into how everyday Signal users understand the features of this popular end-to-end encrypted messaging app, particularly focusing on how they perceive the built-in Password Recovery (PIN) system that aims to enhance user experience and facilitate feature adoption.
We discovered that, although the PINs are designed to offer a high level of security, they actually cause confusion among Signal users, hindering their ability to utilize additional security features.
Our study involved conducting in-depth interviews with relatable, casual Signal users who were neither security experts nor regular users of the app's more advanced features.
Our interviewees were unable to provide clear explanations of the PINs' purpose, and were skeptical about their use within the app, leading to concerns that feature integration would be compromised due to user confusion.
They were also uncertain if they had set a custom PIN, and doubted their own ability to recover the PIN if needed.
Conversely, our interviewees expressed enthusiasm for Signal's security-centric design, highlighting the app's ability to safeguard user relationships and adhere to its security principles.
Our observation is that, despite the PINs' security value, their user experience is compromised due to a disconnect between the features that benefit the app as a whole and those that benefit individual users specifically.
Our interviewees were unable to understand complex security features in the app, such as the reliance on passphrases rather than PINs, and were unsure if the PINs were tied to a specific aspect of the app experience (like registration, backup, or contacts).
Our findings reveal that user comprehension of security features in encrypted messaging apps like Signal is a complex, multi-faceted issue.
One possible solution to enhance user comprehension of these security features is to re-design the PIN recovery system to make it easier for users to understand the features and their purposes within the app, and to tie the PINs more closely to user experiences that matter to the user.
Our interview with regular Signal users, who were neither experts nor typical power users of the app's features, has given us a fresh perspective on the app's design and highlighted a critical need to balance user experience with security features.  Our study has also given us a starting point for exploring and studying the varied experiences of security feature users, and we recommend extending this research to users from different cultural and social backgrounds to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the app's design from global users. Predicting precise short-term traffic flow is vitally important for urban city road networks. However, due to the common occurrence of unobserved road sections, it poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we propose an innovative learning framework that effectively utilizes traffic flow similarities and network topology. We introduce a novel sparsity reduction method for traffic flow forecasting, aiming to recognize underlying patterns in traffic flow. Furthermore, we develop novel similarity-driven feature extraction and multi-view forecast techniques. Comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on real-world road networks demonstrate the outstanding performance of our proposed framework. The source code is available for download on GitHub at https://github.com/akshaykshetya/SimFEX.

This process of re-establishing equilibrium becomes the central focus for a dynamic network system in cyber-physical settings. Our study delves into this phenomenon by examining a particular network failure event, where one node's malfunction triggers a shift in the system's dynamics away from a previously established equilibrium. We represent the system's response to this failure using an evolutionary game framework, where each failing node's re-establishment of efficiency involves reducing the neighbouring node's transmission rate, albeit at a cost. Our analysis, grounded in concepts from natural selection, offers valuable insights into the failure recovery process and provides a mathematical basis for predicting the timing and nature of equilibrium restoration, thereby facilitating the evaluation of integrity in cyber-physical systems in multiple network settings. Our model demonstrates that, in cyber-physical systems characterised by robust, self-healing networks, failure recovery may not always involve the full recovery of transmitted data, with only 100% fit neighbour nodes restoring their transmission capacity, while malfunctioning nodes retreat to a stable state of 'rationalised' permanent disconnection. This rationalised state represents a stable point of balance where the benefits of restoring transmission are outweighed by the costs of potential resource depletion, with data transmission proving non-existent in such scenarios. Our model also allows for the adaptation and application to cyber-physical systems in multiple network settings, including scenarios involving attack and defence, with our analysis providing valuable insights into the evolution of cooperative behaviour within such systems. Our model's adaptability and application to diverse cyber-physical systems have also enabled us to evaluate the impact of multiple network settings on the system's dynamics and equilibrium, including variations in pay-off matrices, the introduction of bargaining ranges, multiple attack and defence strategies and probabilities of node malfunction. A Compton process with polarized initial electrons and randomly polarized photon fields must be considered to fully understand non-thermal acceleration in various astrophysical events. To study this process, a Monte-Carlo simulation integrating the polarized electron distribution and polarized photon field was developed and named MAPPIES. In the second article in a series, the inverse MAPPIES process is examined to account for non-thermal acceleration in blazars through inverse Compton interaction. Inverse MAPPIES involves the interaction of polarized photons with randomly polarized electrons, producing an increase in energy. A computer program was developed to simulate this process using magnetic-field-altered photons, which were incorporated into the standard MAPPIES code to create a new model, inverse MAPPIES. Measuring a quantum system's state is a fundamental aspect of quantum theory, and researchers have found that digital measurements are an expansion of conventional projective measurements that provide increased control. In this study, we explore the conditions under which digital measurements can determine whether a quantum system is in a specific symmetric state. The results demonstrate that digital measurements can accurately identify certain types of states, particularly those with maximum distinguishability, and this applies to both pure and mixed states. Furthermore, we found that digital measurements can consistently calculate the same level of distinguishability as a universal set of projective measurements for certain focused states, and this is achieved through a highly entangled control measurement that encompasses all possible outcomes. Our study also introduces a framework for private channels, and we identify a key difference between digital and projective measurements that is a direct result of the control measurement's structure. The work presented in this study contributes to our understanding of digital measurements and their potential practical applications in quantum information processing. It expands our knowledge of this unique measurement type and its usefulness in determining quantum system states, and it provides valuable insights that can be used to develop new, efficient methods for quantum information processing. The research further bridges the gap between digital and projective measurements, and it is expected that these findings can be utilized to develop innovative, universal protocols for determining quantum system states. Despite the advancements made so far, existing light field compression methods still face issues with suboptimal performance and complex processing pipelines. In response to this, we've developed a straightforward yet effective compression model that draws on image reproduction and deep learning technologies. Our framework, known as the Disparity-Knowledge-Based Deep Reinforcement Compression model (D2-KB-DRC), leverages a disparity-sensitive model to preserve the structural details in the encoded light field dataset. Population health research, including low and middle income countries, relies heavily on health surveys like the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS). These surveys are crucial for understanding health issues and are often used for health interventions, monitoring health outcomes, and making national health policies more effective. In addition to providing information on larger populations, DHS has the ability to provide detailed health estimates at a smaller geographic level, which is especially important for regional policy-making and understanding the health disparities within communities. There are various techniques available that aim to provide accurate and reliable estimates of health outcomes at a smaller geographic level, including some design-based and model-based approaches. This study compares the performance of three design-based and model-based estimators in a low and middle income country context, using real-world data from Kenya's DHS. In this study, the focus is on estimating child mortality rates at a smaller geographic level, such as districts and sub-counties. The findings suggest that a model-based estimator, using a bounded average spacing temporal average approach, provides the most reliable results. This includes yielding higher precision and robust estimates with fewer assumptions made about the data. As a result, the recommended method for estimating child mortality rates at a smaller geographic level in low and middle income countries is the bounded average spacing temporal average model-based estimator. This method involves aggregating individual data over shorter periods of time to improve the accuracy of the estimates in the context of the DHS, which only provides data on the women of childbearing age over a maximum of five years. The findings of this study have significant implications for the use of DHS in the population health research in low and middle income countries, including Kenya, in terms of estimating health outcomes at a smaller geographic level effectively. These findings can be extended to other countries where population health research relies heavily on surveys, including DHS. Our analysis shows that this quantum representation facilitates a more precise analysis of the betting pool's growth, compared to traditional real-number analyses. We've also explored the strategic implications of this approach for a Markov chain dynamic, providing insights into the optimal investment ratios and demonstrating that these ratios can be realized in the most profitable outcomes. Furthermore, this quantum extension of the Kelly strategy allows for a deeper understanding of the exponential growth characteristics of the betting pool. Our research also highlights additional benefits of using a quantum representation for this purpose. Finally, a simulation study demonstrates the effectiveness of this strategy in a noisy environment and confirms that the optimal investment ratios can be achieved. This framework is described as robust and versatile, capable of applying to both algebraic and uniform topologies. A key aspect of the framework involves replacing point-set topology with a correspondence between distributions of 'points' and distributions of 'primes'. 

In contrast, a different approach to topology is explored, rooted in Stone duality, where the emphasis is on the dual structures formed by the Stone spaces associated with algebras instead of focusing on the topological spaces themselves. This alternative is criticized for its lack of natural representation of topological spaces. 

Meanwhile, the relationship between the dual structures of locally compact abelian groups and the dualities produced in Pontryagin duality have been widely acknowledged as one of the most solid foundations in abstract algebra. However, it has also been observed that Pontryagin duality does not provide a representation of the space itself but rather offers two separate entities: its dual space and the dualities linking its 'primes' to 'points'.

This critique aims to offer a more nuanced and accurate foundation for the use of Pontryagin duality in discussions surrounding space representation, with an emphasis on enhancing clarity and precision.

This study investigates the Toeplitz algebras of particular classes of Toeplitz matrices and operators within the contexts of Euclidean space, Hilbert space, and Bergman space. Initially, it replicates and expands on existing works by Tang and Wei regarding maximal $C^*$-norms of Toeplitz matrices/operators in Hilbert space. Subsequently, it presents novel findings regarding these norms in the contexts of Bergman space and Euclidean space. To achieve this, it incorporates the use of recent 'two-sided' estimates for Toeplitz operators in Bergman spaces, as well as the notion of noncommutative subspace projection from the field of operator algebras. Furthermore, it derives an explicit representation of Toeplitz algebras in terms of degenerate Toeplitz matrices/operators via combination of linear projections and degenerate Toeplitz operators. Ultimately, it presents examples of Toeplitz matrices/operators that satisfy both bounded and unbounded $C^*$-norms within the contexts of Bergman and Euclidean spaces. This work also considers the analogous research related to Toeplitz semigroups and explores the $C^*$-norms of semigroups in both Hilbert and Bergman spaces. Specifically, it demonstrates that the $C^*$-norms of Toeplitz semigroups in both spaces are limited by the square root of the rank of the underlying Toeplitz matrix.
