A well-designed Neural Architecture Search (NAS) method can greatly improve high-performing neural architectures. Despite this, existing NAS methods are often hindered by the interference problem, which causes previously well-performing components to deteriorate when combined in the same architecture. To tackle this issue, this study introduces two novel approaches: 1) a novel evaluation technique to measure component performance; 2) an innovative training method that helps reduce interference and allows architectures to generalize better when trained and tested independently.

The experiments conducted on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets reveal that NAS' ability to find top-performing architectures is greatly hindered by interference, yet this drawback can be effectively mitigated using the proposed component evaluation and training methods. Specifically, the results show that:

  1) These approaches significantly alleviate the interference problem and enable NAS to find top-performing architectures even when trained and tested independently.
  2) Component evaluation enables NAS to generalize better when trained and tested independently, and also leads to more adaptable component designs that require less modification when reused across different datasets.
  3) Training with "swalation" helps eliminate interference and allows architectures to generalize better when trained and tested independently, and also results in more accurate and robust inferences from smaller and larger random top-performing architectures.

All source code and experimental results are available on GitHub at https://github.com/danihechler/interference-free-nas. Recent advancements in Remote Sensing and IoT fields have created time series datasets that are growing at an rapid pace, causing time series analysis to become an increasingly vital task in both research and applications. One key aspect of analyzing time series data is identifying how different features or attributes correlate within a series. Current methods for examining time series often involve summary statistics or unsupervised machine learning techniques, but these methods lack the ability to make meaningful comparisons between time series that are based on specific attributes. To address this need, a new R package named theft was developed. The theft package provides a compact collection of functions that make it easier to compare time series based on attributes such as daily patterns, weather conditions, or water quality. The package was demonstrated through a real-world example using data from the Florida Keys, where it was used to detect violations of the Mandatory Marine Zone regulation by comparing the diving behavior of wild dolphins. We apply the proposed system to evaluate the trustworthiness of two scientific translators and present the results. To investigate the influence of individual electron-phonon coupling components on valley behavior in two-dimensional materials, our previous work involved conducting ab-initio calculations based on microcanonical density functional theory. A novel numerical approach was developed to handle the simultaneous participation of multiple electron-phonon coupling mechanisms. By considering a concrete case involving graphene and silicon carbide, our research demonstrated that the participation of a wide range of phonon frequencies in electron-phonon interactions has a substantial impact on valley dynamics. Notably, our results showed that the presence of a particular electron-phonon interaction mechanism unique to a specific valley can cause inversion of the drag force, where the slower valley is accelerated by the faster one. A comprehensive comparison between graphene and silicon carbide highlighted the potential for exploring and understanding the complex interplay of various electron-phonon interaction mechanisms affecting valley behavior. Furthermore, our research encouraged the use of electron-phonon interaction mechanisms as a means to manipulate and control valley dynamics in two-dimensional materials. A theoretical framework was developed to explain how valley polarization can be caused by the difference in electron-phonon interactions across valleys. Our research also identified silicon carbide as a material which, due to its specific characteristics, facilitates the realisation of long-lived valley qubits. t-SNE is a widely employed method for creating low-dimensional visualizations in data with high dimensionality. Its use of heavy-tailed Gaussian distributions enhances similar data points' proximity in embedding space. However, its implementation assumes data points follow a Gaussian distribution and are defined within a Cartesian space. As a result, it can be ill-suited and poorly effective for data sets with spherical structures, producing inaccurate and misleading results. To address this, we have developed a generalized version of t-SNE that can accurately analyze and visualize spherical data sets while identifying the symmetrical pattern inherent in spherical distributions. This generalized version, VMF-SNE, uses the von Mises-Fisher distribution in place of the heavy-tailed Gaussian, and has been proven effective on data sets including hominid skull shapes, bird skull orientations, and data sets with high-dimensional spherical structures. By comparing its performance to Cartesian t-SNE, our method has demonstrated superior performance across these applications. Moreover, our method has been shown to retain its geometric and semantic properties in low-dimensional visualizations. A graph trait is a concept that assigns a polynomial to a labeled graph, and several instances have been introduced in the literature, often giving rise to various series of polynomials. This paper explores the possibility of constructing a graph trait that would yield a specific series of polynomials, such as the chromatic polynomial or the Tutte polynomial, by establishing a connection between the traits and iterated edge contractions. This connection also enables the development of a graph trait for colored graphs, which provides additional flexibility. While the traits are typically defined recursively or implicitly, our work demonstrates that certain well-known polynomials can be expressed as rational functions of others, revealing a complex relationship between them. This insight also enables the computation of certain polynomials using polynomial division instead of recursion. Our work also contributes to a deeper understanding of the properties shared by various series of polynomials connected to graph invariants. These series include the chromatic polynomials, Tutte polynomials, flow polynomials, and others, which share common characteristics such as positivity, evaluations, and intersection properties. These shared properties refine the characteristics previously identified (such as those for the chromatic polynomials) and provide a unified framework for understanding the polynomials associated with graph invariants. This knowledge may inspire the development of new graph invariants, which could be utilized in diverse applications. Additionally, our work confirms that several published series of polynomials are in fact series of graph invariants, providing explicit examples in the process. These include the series comprising the homomorphism polynomials, Tutte polynomials, and the polynomials associated with the Bollobas-Riordan category. In contrast, our work also indicates that the series of Tutte polynomials for non-planar graphs whose Tutte polynomials have positive entries is a series of graph traits, rather than graph invariants. The Strauss process is a bivariate point process that forms a Poisson random field with a non-negative intensity function. It is a combination of two independently simulated Poisson processes with a combined area equal to one. Although simple in concept, simulating this process efficiently can be challenging. We present a new, easy-to-implement method for generating Strauss model realizations. Our approach uses two independently simulated Poisson processes and a'stitching' technique to construct the realizations. We compare this method with two existing techniques and provide a calculation of the computational cost for each. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the new method is comparable to or superior to established techniques in terms of computational efficiency. We verify the accuracy of the new method through simulations and theoretical analysis. A practical application of the new method is provided in the form of a C++ code for simulating Cressie-Williams Cressie-Williams process realizations, which is included in the supplementary information. A comprehensive R package for simulating a range of Strauss process simulations is also available from the website: https://github.com/Neera-Sim/Strauss-process-simulation. The R package provides users with the option to select different simulation methods, multiple seed options, and various simulation parameter values. Each simulation is recorded as a time series in a data frame, which is provided as output. Users can specify the lambda and beta parameters, as well as other optional parameters, to customize the simulations. The stitch method has several potential applications in Bayesian settings, where it can be used to sample from a posterior distribution consisting of sets of Strauss process realizations. For example, in a joint space-time intrinsic coregional law model, simulating the space-time residual covariance matrix using the stitch method yields significantly faster computation times compared to the standard methods. A supplementary information document includes additional information on this model. The methods presented in this study can be easily extended to simulate other bivariate and multivariate point processes, such as the doubly stochastic Poisson-Dirichlet process, which is the conditional distribution of a homogenous Markov process given a partition of the underlying space. A separate R package is available for simulating this process from the website: https://github.com/Neera-Sim/POD-CD- simulation. In real-world systems with multiple processing facilities, it's common for tasks to be distributed across these facilities to optimize overall performance. For task distribution in timetabling systems with multiple facilities, we develop a decision-making framework that balances efficient use of facilities and task requirements. We introduce a new solution method for this problem, based on alternating improvements, and demonstrate its effectiveness through comprehensive experimental analysis, comparing it to a previously existing approach. Key findings reveal that our proposed technique yields superior outcomes in various scenarios, notably outperforming the previous method by a significant margin in some cases. Additionally, we show that, unlike other methods, our approach is capable of making feasible decisions in practical multi-facility, multi-task systems. Based on this success, we apply our technique to a new version of the Multitasking Timetabling problem to find high-quality solutions for task allocation problems. Furthermore, we extend our approach to address uncertain task requirements in uncertain multitasking timetabling systems. Through systematic experimentation, we establish a comprehensive understanding of the performance of our methods in diverse timetabling systems and facilities, and provide valuable insights for generalization to other related problems. The proposed techniques are now being used in various real-world applications, including scheduling jobs across multiple factories and assignment problems in network-based systems. This complexity is characterized by a scaling exponent of the energy at the critical point, but the nature of this exponent remains unclear. By computing the Fock space propagator and its squared magnitude over an infinite period of time, and then determining the lattice spacing scales over which energy fluctuations occur, we are able to assess the critical dimensionality of the complex energy landscape that forms at the many-body localization critical point. Our results show that the landscape is highly fragmented and expansive, with critical dimensionality equal to or greater than two, indicating that it is highly intricate. This highly intricate nature of the energy landscape is responsible for hindering the return time of the Fock space propagator and slowing down the entire system. Furthermore, we have discovered that the complexity of the energy landscape, measured by the exponent of its scaling factor and the fractal dimensions obtained from its scales, increases upon entering the many-body localization phase, but decreases upon entering this phase when systems of one and two dimensions are compared. This implies that many-body localization does not solely occur within areas of high disorder and that the critical properties of one-dimensional systems cannot be directly applied to two-dimensional systems. Finally, the nature of the energy landscape of an imaginary phase of a one-dimensional quantum system under imaginary time evolution is investigated, with our findings revealing that this landscape is characterized by unique and different fractal properties. This information may prove useful for further researching and understanding the behavior of quantum systems under imaginary time evolution. Our data also confirm the connection between logarithmic growth and the time it takes for eigenfunctions to become localized, with our fractal dimensions in one-dimensional systems matching theoretical expectations that include a degree of universality. This includes accounting for the average disorder $h$ experienced by the quantum systems, the system size $L$, and a universal critical exponent $\nu$, where $n_L = \log L + \nu \log h$. The problem of budget-constrained multi-target interactive search is defined where the goal is to find and detect multiple hidden targets within a bounded area using a device with limited range and a signal transmission restriction. Each movement allows the detection of at most one target, and the target's existence in a given location is determined by a binary indication function, which may vary from one location to another within the area. The success criterion is based on finding and detecting 'C' targets within the area, where 'C' is either equal to a specified constant value or equals 'C' due to an unbounded value. A near-optimal strategy with a limited number of steps (close to 'C' plus the cost of the area's perimeter divided by 2) exists under certain conditions, and in cases of both constant and variable 'C', a polynomial-time solution exists to determine whether a budget allows the detection of at least 'C' targets. Furthermore, a approximation algorithm for the problem of budget-constrained multi-target interactive search is presented, which is based on a budget-constrained single-target search approach. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using performance guarantees, specifically relative loss and regret bounds. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is efficient in practice and outperforms a random tree search method. The proposed approach is applicable to various real-world scenarios such as search and rescue, search for a minimal Steiner tree problem, and the etching of microstructures using a conical tip. In modern cellular networks, accurate prediction of signal strength is crucial for managing frequency resources and ensuring high network quality. This requirement is particularly pressing as networks expand to cover a greater area. Traditionally, engineers have relied on empirical models, like the Winkler-Hata model, which provide a basic understanding of signal propagation. However, these models are often inadequate, and inaccurate at times. With the advancement of computational methods, alternative approaches like artificial neural networks are now available. In this study, we explore the use of deep convolutional neural networks, trained on data from real-world cellular towers, as a means to enhance signal propagation prediction. We analyze the key factors driving signal strength, including the transmitter's altitude and power, as well as its distance from the measurement point. Additional environmental influences, like terrain complexity and the presence of buildings, are also automatically encoded in the model through convolutional and recursive components. We compare the performance of our proposed model with the Winkler-Hata model, using measurement data from over 6000 sites across the United States. The results show that our cellular propagation model surpasses the Winkler-Hata model by as much as 15%, providing over 90% accuracy in a best-case scenario. This model offers a data-driven solution, as its performance adapts to the changing installed base of antennas. In summary, this research presents a performance-driven approach for frequency resource planning and high-quality cellular network design. In the future, we intend to supplement this model with additional environmental data, including satellite imagery, to create an advanced and highly sophisticated model capable of simulating the intricate effects of building shapes and other complex factors on signal propagation. Such a model has the potential to greatly benefit a wide range of applications, from cellular network design to emergency response, in areas with a high degree of environmental complexity. With the advent of more accurate models like this, we can create a better future for mobile network design. This research was supported by grant 2000168 from the U.S. National Science Foundation. Despite significant advancements in natural language processing, the task of categorizing multi-label document topics in Science remains challenging and contentious. Existing methods employ textual features extracted from raw documents, but the performance gap stems from omitting inherent structural characteristics within these texts. We introduce a new method called stable pairing, which determines proposal pairs in attention-based models by ensuring the approximation of a quadratic function as a piecewise linear one. This technique has the following benefits: Firstly, it prevents sudden changes in optimization loss during training, resulting in more consistent convergence. Secondly, the model's output becomes predictable and improves consistently throughout, characterized by smoother and more gradual changes. Thirdly, the model's proposals become more distinguishable, reducing the likelihood of duplicate proposals and resulting in more precise ranking and value estimation. Our findings show that stable pairing's inherent regularization has a positive impact on both optimization convergence and final model performance. When applied to RNNs, the model shows consistent convergence and slightly improved final performance according to both average ranking and final model performance. Similarly, the model exhibits predictable and improved convergence and performance on vision tasks such as VQA, VFE, and Visual Commonsense Reasoning, and its performance surpasses strong baselines on VQA by 2.0 points. Previous studies on metrics for assessing summary quality are plagued by issues: 
    - They can't cross-verbalize summary and reference text for enhanced understanding, 
       limited to only extracting similar surface information.
    - They often fail to generalise outside of the training domain.
    - Their evaluation is based solely on word-level similarities rather than meaning-based relevance.
    - There is no single robust metric capable of comprehensively capturing the entire spectrum of summary quality.

To address these challenges, we develop a new, comprehensive assessment metric called SummScore, capable of offering a complete evaluation of summary quality by quantifying similarity at both word and sense levels through the utilization of cross-encoder. 
Our method also incorporates a training data enhancement approach, training the model with augmented data in an end-to-end manner, thereby enabling it to withstand out-of-domain tests and maintain consistency with human evaluation metrics. 
By comparing our model with existing metrics, we conduct out-of-domain tests and perform sensitive analyses, thereby showcasing its robust and reliable performance. 
Furthermore, SummScore outperforms other existing metrics in out-of-domain tests and offers single-number simplicity along with theoretical backing, making it a pioneering research in the field of summary evaluation. 
You can access the code for SummScore at https://github.com/MITIE/SummScore. 
Additionally, an online tool for generating summary evaluation reports can be found at https://summ-score.mit.edu.

A crucial method to pinpoint a substantial number of loop diagrams and IR divergent integrals in loop amplitude expansions has been developed. This method is particularly essential for scalar three-point functions in effective field theories. By utilizing this technique, it is possible to generate extensively off-shell one-loop integrals through top and bottom structures without resorting to residue techniques, a method known as non-resonant graph calculation. Typically, this approach requires the application of reverse unitarity constraints for identifying loop integrals through cross mutations and recursive structures. Here, we demonstrate that this can be bypassed and propose a novel method to generate three-loop form factors via a combination of cross mutations and disjoint graph structures. This strategy allows for the reconstruction of form factors at the three-loop level without necessitating resonant diagrams and IR divergent integrals can be identified through subtractions at the one-loop level. Additionally, we propose a simplified approach in the context of generic renormalizable field theories to construct subtraction terms for loop integrals, empowering the reconstruction of on-shell amplitudes across a wide range of processes involving massive particles and on-shell configurations. Artificial Intelligence's capability to mimic human perception has made significant progress, particularly in processing natural images. Yet, humans possess an adaptability that machine learning often can't replicate. To investigate this disparity, we conducted a study to understand how severe image distortions affect both human observers and a cutting-edge Visual Transformer model. By running a user survey and employing a benchmark dataset, we found that humans have a higher tolerance for extreme alterations in images than the Visual Transformer model. These results indicate that AI's limitations in image interpretation can be identified by analyzing the effects of extreme distortions, which has important implications for evaluating AI's performance in practical applications. Furthermore, we found that humans have a greater ability than the Visual Transformer model to utilize contextual information in an image, which the model struggles to do, especially when dealing with severe image distortions. Our research suggests that testing AI's performance using intensely distorted images can provide valuable insights into its limitations in natural image processing. Additionally, we found that AI's performance can be improved or at least mitigated by training the model on distorted images, which is an efficient approach for limited computational resources. Overall, our study demonstrates that intensely distorted images can reveal intriguing and useful differences in how both human vision and machine vision analyze images. You can see an illustration of these results by visiting https://intensevision.github.io. The related code and datasets for our study have been made available on the GitHub site at https://github.com/nkornaree/IntenseImageTransformation. Please note that our study was initially an extension of our previous work as described in the report titled "Can AI Read Distorted Images Like Humans?" published at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR 2021), where we found that AI's performance can be evaluated by analyzing the effects of moderately distorted images. The current study builds upon that research by focusing on extreme distortions. The related press release about our study can be accessed at https://tinyurl.com/Intense-Vision.

Large graph analysis systems depend on node representation techniques like Node-Physics and DeepWalk to predict links in complex networks. These methods create a random walk-based representation for nodes, leveraging local and global network characteristics, which is then used for link forecasting. However, these approaches are inefficient in sparse networks, as they discard valuable information about network structure. To address this issue, a new method called SSNE has been proposed. SSNE efficiently generates node representations for link forecasting in sparse networks, using a hybrid of local and global network characteristics. This allows for the creation of targeted memory views and more efficient processing of network edges. Initial experiments using networks from various domains have validated the effectiveness of SSNE, as well as its performance advantages compared to existing link forecasting methods. Additionally, a key innovation, the SSNE optimizer, has been developed for optimized node representation training. This innovative approach enables significant memory reductions and accelerates training times, outperforming existing optimizers. Finally, a demonstration of SSNE's capabilities for visualizing network structure, an application of node representation, has been demonstrated using a network of US air travel routes. The proposed method achieves timescale-dependent node representation accuracy, unlike prior hybrid approaches. Furthermore, SSNE's effectiveness for predicting links in networks beyond link prediction applications has also been validated. To facilitate adoption, a fast and scalable SSNE implementation for distributed network processing has been developed and made publicly available. This implementation, which uses a novel memory layout for efficient network edge processing, can process very large networks efficiently, even on modest hardware. For example, the implementation easily handles networks with millions of nodes and edges, requiring only a few gigabytes of memory. This efficient scalability further supports SSNE's potential as a tool for network analysis, beyond its initial application in link forecasting. To enable widespread adoption, the SSNE library has been created and released as an open-source contribution to the network analysis community. This implementation, which is fully scalable and flexible, has been publicly released under a permissive open-source license, allowing others to reproduce the results, modify the approach, and use SSNE freely in various network applications. As a result, SSNE is expected to serve as a valuable tool for the network analysis and machine learning communities, empowering researchers and practitioners to accurately predict links, represent nodes effectively, and apply these approaches to various network applications. The approach, implementation, and tools enabling SSNE have been thoroughly described, facilitating adoption, which in turn, is expected to lead to a broader range of research applications and tools in node representation and link forecasting

Advanced technologies like Advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar and visible spectrum imaging can capture large areas quickly, under harsh weather conditions, despite the limitations of visible spectrum sensors in remote forest settings. However, combining infrared and visible spectral imaging data requires significant expertise and often hinders real-time decision making in wildfire surveillance systems. To bridge this gap, our research introduces FIRe-GAN, an innovative infrared-visible fusion method, leveraging a Context Encoder and multi-scale feature fusion framework and aided by Generative Adversarial Networks. Through extensive testing with the ESA M-SARAD dataset, our results show that FIre-GAN produces high-quality in-real-time panoramic, snow-free, and snow-revealing visibility comparisons during the summer season. Moreover, Panorama-GAN, a core component of FIre-GAN, enables the fusion of infrared and visible spectral data to create snow-free and snow-revealing panoramas with an impressive Level of Detail. By applying our framework, which is grounded in the theory of reversible Markov chains, we can determine the exact, calculable optimal hedge and temporary profit or loss expected from reversible derivative financial instruments. In addition to explaining the connection between the framework's coefficients and the traditional stochastic models used for pricing derivatives, we also show the convergence of our framework's coefficients to their static counterparts as transaction volumes become infinitely large. We effectively provide a practical method for deriving derivative prices and temporary profits or losses without needing to rely on time-consuming numerical simulations or sophisticated machine learning algorithms. To demonstrate the applicability and efficiency of our framework, we use reversible Markov chain methods to calculate the prices and temporary profits or losses of vanilla European put and call options. Compared to machine learning-based methods, we also achieve a significant performance improvement by avoiding the need to train huge neural networks. A finite-step solution can be obtained through convex relaxation, applying a method called the alternating minimization technique. Our results show that, under certain conditions, this system exhibits complex behaviors similar to those observed in models of predator-prey or parasite-host interactions. However, when these conditions are not present, our model's dynamics are similar to those seen in models of gene selection. Depending on various factors, including the environmental impact and complexity of the ecological interactions, our model is able to predict the emergence of these complex dynamics, even when these factors are quite slight. Advancements in self-supervised learning (SSL) have significantly enhanced performance in various tasks such as speech and vision. SSL's efficacy in speech is particularly evident in its low resource applications, like speech recognition. Research into SSL's impact on speech samples is crucial to its practical use. Past studies were conducted in ideal environments and failed to account for the emotional and psychological impact on speakers. This research aims to characterize the emotional and psychological susceptibility of SSL models, especially their response to distress-related speech, and explore the relationships between speech properties and SSL's performance. A 28-participant panel evaluated speech samples, including normative and distress-related conditions, from participants who had just received a life-alternating cancer diagnosis. Two prominent SSL models were used: ResTran and SSL-WAS. Analysis revealed significant performance discrepancies in speech samples with emotional and psychological complexity, including increased rates of errors and decreased confidence in SSL models for such speech. This study is a comprehensive investigation into SSL's susceptibility to emotional and psychological factors, exploring its practical applications in real-world environments. A parallel clinical study is in progress to assess the therapeutic effects of working with SSL models. This research is part of a larger research initiative, the EMOS Project (Emotional and Psychological Susceptibility), driven by the necessity to understand emotional and psychological susceptibility in various areas of expertise, including healthcare, law, and artificial intelligence. Past studies were conducted in ideal settings, failing to account for emotional and psychological susceptibility in real-world applications. This study marks the first instance of SSL's susceptibility being characterized in speech samples, offering valuable insights for future research in this field. A database of 28 individuals who have undergone various forms of stress and distress is available for download at https://mosaiclearlearning.github.io/EESSL/. This database, named EESSL, can be utilized for research purposes, with the aim of advancing the field of emotional and psychological susceptibility in speech. In many cases, data analysis involves incomplete data, and researchers often conduct a sensitivity analysis to assess how the outcome changes in response to specific assumptions. This study develops a sensitivity analysis approach that enables researchers to make confident inferences about incomplete data under uncertainty. The E-value is a established measure of uncertainty that serves as a threshold for uninformative probabilities. This paper proposes a new type of E-value designed for missing data, and utilizes a Bayesian approach to derive it. The E-value is characterized mathematically and demonstrated to be equivalent to the conjugate prior covariance matrix under a specific Bayesian assumption. Building on this approach, we define the E-sensitivity analysis, and show that E-sensitivity is more conservative than classical sensitivity analysis. The E-sensitivity approach is illustrated through the use of two example studies. The first study examines the impact of incomplete data on a Bayesian inference about a population mean, and the second study investigates how the outcome may be affected by missing data in a Bayesian mediation analysis. The results confirm that the E-sensitivity analysis provides a reliable and conservative assessment of the sensitivity to assumptions regarding missing data in both scenarios. The proposed E-sensitivity analysis is shown to be a useful and reliable tool for conducting sensitive analysis in the context of incomplete data. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques within Internet of Vehicles is becoming increasingly popular, with a notable focus on Federated Learning, which is highly suitable for IoT applications due to concerns over data security and communication limitations. As Internet of Vehicles generates vast amounts of sensitive data, encompassing routes, environments, and equipment, maintaining the confidentiality of this data is of paramount importance. Additionally, the need to analyze vehicle-generated data necessates collaborative efforts among organizations, including governments and private companies, to pool their resources. Conversely, data sharing often leads to potential data leaks, raising concerns underpinning the reliability of service and data privacy. To address these challenges, the literature has devised various privacy preservation methods for Federated Learning, prompting a comprehensive review of existing frameworks, particularly those employing Blockchain technology. This survey aims to provide a detailed analysis of the current state of Blockchain-based Privacy Preserving Frameworks for FL in IoT, evaluating their strengths, weaknesses, and comparing them against conventional methods. Furthermore, this review identifies gaps within existing research and suggests potential avenues for exploration by the IoT and FL communities, including an assessment of the feasibility and challenges of implementing Blockchain-based Privacy Preserving Frameworks for Federated Learning in IoT. With a view to promoting replication and offering guidance to researchers and practitioners, this review showcases notable milestones, delves into current limitations, and highlights future research directions, thereby contributing to the advancement of Blockchain-based Privacy Preserving Frameworks for Federated Learning in IoT. Our survey has been recognized through the Award for Outstanding Literature Review at the 2022 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Intelligent Cloud Computing and Artificial Intelligence (IC2AI). Lastly, due to the wide range of Blockchain consensus algorithms, we present a unified classification of these algorithms, thereby contributing to the literature and offering a systematic approach to classifying these algorithms. Moreover, due to the growing interest in Blockchain among researchers, we present a Literature Review on Blockchain Consensus Algorithms within the Internet of Things. Previous studies have analyzed and understood the mistakes made by users when abusing open-source cryptographic libraries, but there is a lack of research on how to detect and prevent these errors. To bridge this gap, we conducted a comprehensive study of how developers handle cryptographic functionality in Python, a widely used programming language. Our research, which involved examining real-world Python code from GitHub and PyPI, as well as artificially generated code, revealed common mistakes made by Python developers when using cryptographic functions. We discovered that more than 13% of Python projects on GitHub contain insecure code, and that new code is also prone to vulnerabilities. Our research also showed that while Python developers tend to avoid using low-level cryptographic functions, they often misuse higher-level libraries in various ways. To help prevent cryptographic errors, we developed a tool called PyCheck, which uses static code analysis to identify and report potential issues in Python code. Our results demonstrate that such a tool can effectively identify and prevent cryptographic errors in real-world code. Our research is available at https://crypto-abuses.com. Additionally, PyCheck can be downloaded from https://github.com/mateusresende/pycheck. The source code of our study, including all data and code, can be found at https://github.com/mateusresende/crypto-abuses. Furthermore, a video summary of our research can be found at https://youtu.be/4hYU2lo2u9k. Our research was supported by the EC funding, grant number 825302, and the Government of Portugal, grant number UID/EEA/05058/2013. We would like to express our gratitude to the developers for sharing their code with the community, as well as three anonymous reviewers for their feedback. Finally, further research is needed to address the challenges of securely using cryptographic functions in Python code. In particular, it is essential to investigate the circumstances that lead developers to misuse the `hashlib` function, as well as the reasons for the limited use of higher-level cryptographic functions in Python code. Our research can serve as a foundation for such future studies. The common themes observed in this research, such as the challenges of securely using cryptographic functions in real-world code, could be the focus of future investigations. Furthermore, although our research primarily centered on Python code, it is possible that similar patterns and challenges exist in other programming languages. In seismic imaging, various deconvolution tasks are crucial and frequently encounter situations of sparse noise in signals. A common approach involves making the convolution operation invertible and applying l1 regularization to retrieve the underlying signal. However, standard inversion and sparsity-based methods are often hampered by the shift-variant characteristic of two-dimensional convolution, as well as non-uniform sparse noise that causes salt and pepper noises distorting the optimization process and leading to incomplete recovery of the signals. Existing salt and pepper removal techniques are not very effective in seismic applications. A novel network, called Proximal Mean Network (NuSPAN), is proposed to tackle the issues of two-dimensional convolution and non-uniform sparse noise by directly learning the deconvolution and desalting operations through the lens of deep neural networks. A primary benefit of NuSPAN lies in its ability to handle complex scenarios, such as salt and pepper noises, without making assumptions about their origins. A different type of layer, Proximal Layer, is also introduced, which applies l1 regularization to the convolution operation while reflecting the characteristics of two-dimensional convolution, thereby eliminating the need for artificial padding. A pre-trained NuSPAN can further enhance the performance of other convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by integrating it into the backbones for seismic imaging tasks. The effectiveness of NuSPAN is demonstrated in the form of numerical examples, such as seismic reflectivity reconstruction and interpolation. In these examples, NuSPAN outperforms other methods by means of visual and metrics such as the Structural-Similarity-Measure and the Multi-scale-Scale-Structure-Measure. In comparison to pre-trained NuSPAN, the results reveal that it can bring about notable improvements in the quality of seismic images for CNNs, thus reducing the time and cost associated with retraining the networks. Additionally, NuSPAN also shows its potential in other fields, such as deblurring tasks. A future research direction, which involves extending the method to other areas, is presented in the spare paper. In this work, the potential of NuSPAN in other fields, such as blind deconvolution, is tested and the results show that it is effective even in cases where the blurring operations are unknown. With the ability to handle various types of deconvolution tasks, NuSPAN is a versatile method that can be applied in other domains with similar requirements. In this study, the method has been successfully employed in the fields of seismic, medical, and scientific image reconstruction, thereby verifying its wide range of applications. The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within medicine has been well-documented, with the use of ML being successful in redefining diagnosis and treatment across various clinical practices.  Despite the pivotal role of ML in medical imaging, there is currently no standardized output format that allows for the encoding of model outputs in ways that are interpretable by clinicians.  This lack of standardization complicates the evaluation and validation of ML models, with a key challenge being the need to establish a clear comparison between expected outcomes (based on clinical expertise) and the actual model outputs.  To address this issue, we have developed Highdicom, an open-source Python framework that enables the efficient conversion of image-based ML model outputs into standardized digital formats.  By leveraging Highdicom, it is now possible to seamlessly integrate model outputs that are rooted in multidimensional image data with widely-established formats like DICOM and CSV.  This, in turn, enables the easy visualization and analysis of model outputs using a variety of specialized image viewers and browsers.  To showcase the capabilities and potential applications of Highdicom, we have undertaken a collaborative project aimed at developing an actionable model output visualization and validation tool for use in digital pathology with the primary goal of promoting efficient tool development for model validation, management and compliance.  This article introduces the core components and functionalities of Highdicom, highlighting its key applications and potential uses within the medical imaging community.  By enabling the standardization of model outputs, Highdicom holds the potential to greatly enhance model development, evaluation, visualization and compliance across a wide array of imaging modalities and pathology and radiology applications.  This, in turn, represents an important step towards advancing the development of accurate and reliable ML models in medical imaging.  Ultimately, the proposed tools and techniques will facilitate the efficient integration of model outputs that are understandable by computers into clinical practices, thereby paving the way for digital-based, computer-optimized diagnostic decision-support systems in medical imaging.  Highdicom, as a key enabling technology, plays a crucial role in enabling this critical transition. The chromatic symmetric polynomial of a graph G is a mathematical expression that captures its unique graphical properties utilizing the chromatic variables. This paper explores related concepts for two specific types of graphs: Dyck paths and zigzag graphs, specifically through their relationship with the $q$-version of the standard concept of the chromatic polynomial. A key tool in this study is the application of a $q$-analogue of the standard algebraic combinatorial structure known as the rook coverage system, which has been extended for the purposes of generalizing $q$-analysis to the study of Dyck paths. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the resulting formula for chromatic symmetric polynomials of Dyck paths has a specific generating function that is equitable in terms of a particular class of graph patterns, known as alternating M\"obius lattices. These results build on prior research, specifically in the field of $q$-analysis, as well as the study of the generating functions for Dyck paths and related concepts. Ultimately, the paper provides new insights, extensions, and expansions of existing theories in the fields of $q$-analysis and the study of Dyck paths, while also revealing implicit connections to the theory of graph patterns. This paper is an extended version of a presentation from the Theory Days hosted by the Fields Institute. The corresponding $q$-analogue tool used in this study is novel and has been published for the first time. The paper's formula for chromatic symmetric polynomials of Dyck paths, via rook coverage, is also an original concept. The paper establishes a new link between Dyck paths and alternating M\"obius lattices through its main result, which provides an analysis and extension of the study's underlying theories. The paper's approach to $q$-analysis is consistent but the original formula for chromatic symmetric polynomials of Dyck paths has a level of generality not seen in the field. The study's approach to the generating functions for Dyck paths is also new. The paper's study has significant implications for the ongoing research in the study of $q$-analysis and the study of Dyck paths. The paper's approach to the study of graph patterns is also an area for potential future research. The corresponding data for the study was compiled but is not included in the paper's text. The study's theory has the potential to be extended to the study of more complex graphs, specifically via the study's approach to the study of alternating M\"obius lattices.

Inspired by the success of circular convolutions in adaptive orientation sampling, we introduce Orientation Convolutive Networks (OC-Net), a streamlined architecture composed of a circular convolution layer and a shared convolutional network. Unlike traditional convolutional networks with a fixed grid, OC-Net adapts to image orientation by sampling a circular 2D grid, effectively doubling its resolution. This leads to a 50% increase in parameters, a more efficient detector. Comparative studies using ResNet, DenseNet, and MobileNet architectures demonstrate that OC-Net models with these components outperform their traditional counterparts in orientation sensitivity, achieving better results on image classification tasks. Our findings also show that the gain in orientation robustness comes with minimal increase in parameter overhead. When combined with data augmentation, the performance advantage of OC-Net models expands to include fixed-oriented baseline cases, resulting in faster training times and more efficient inference. We conduct in-depth analysis on the effect of circular convolution on feature representation, offering a deeper understanding of orientation adaptability. Additionally, an accompanying Python package is available for easy replication of our experiments. With these foundations, the potential of OC-Net lies in extended applications, such as unsupervised domain adaptation, low-resource domain detection, and more. Such extensions are planned but have not yet been implemented. A new method for determining the top quark mass from hadronic top quark decays is presented, focusing on the longitudinal momentum of the decay products in the laboratory frame. The analysis uses the road-map of the top quark's energy distribution outlined in CTEQ6 parton distributions and shows that the decay structure is insensitive to the flavor type of the initial proton. Therefore, top quark mass measurements can be performed independently of the proton's flavor composition. A crucial role in this process is played by the internal gauge interactions that ensure consistency between the measured top quark mass at different energy scales. The method's results reveal a significant dependence of the top quark mass on the substance making up the proton from which the top quarks are formed. Specifically, a variation of the top quark mass measured in proton-proton collisions with respect to the measurements obtained from proton-lead and lead-lead collisions at the LHC is found to be -56 GeV and 67 GeV, respectively. These measurements are consistent with the variation of the top quark mass measured at different energy scales, which is estimated to be -10, 20 and 33 GeV from QCD calculations based on the CTEQ6 parton distributions. These measurements are further confirmed through simulations of the formation processes of top quark-antitop quark pairs at various energy scales. Given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, "sequential $k$-edge-dyeing" of $G$ involves assigning a color to each node in $G$, such that any two adjacent nodes receiving the same color are separated by at most $k$ edges. This problem is an extension of the well-known vertex coloring in graph theory. Research on sequential $k$-edge-dyeing has focused on determining the minimal number of colors necessary to apply to the nodes of a given graph. In our study, we examine the problem of sequentially $k$-edge-dyeing a subset of nodes in a certain type of irregular graph called "near-rigid graphs". A near-rigid graph is defined as a graph that, when excluding its vertices with a specific degree $r$, has a minimal degree of $r-1$. We show that these graphs have unique properties which enable us to apply an optimal number of colors to a subset of their nodes. This study contributes to the graph theory literature by expanding our understanding of sequential $k$-edge-dyeing in near-rigid graphs and illustrates the connection between this problem and the distinctability of vertices with specific degrees in these graphs. Additionally, we examine how our findings can be applied to more complex irregular graphs and provide relevant illustrations. A pioneering research project is aiming to make ground-level, high-resolution imaging possible from any location in low-Earth orbit. By developing an innovative satellite bus, researchers hope to create a cost-effective platform for various spacecraft designs. Key aspects of this project include designing the satellite's structure and developing its propulsion system, which utilizes a hybrid microthruster setup. A novel 3D printing technique has been employed to optimize the structure's layout, resulting in a highly efficient and lightweight framework. In conjunction, three different microthruster types – based on femtosecond laser treatment, heat expansion, and polymerization — have been integrated to provide 50 millinewtons of thrust. By combining these innovations, researchers aim to create a versatile and flexible satellite bus suitable for a wide range of applications. For instance, equipping the satellite with a hyperspectral camera could facilitate the reduction of a harsh environment's impact on spacecraft materials. In addition, the satellite's modular design would enable significant reductions in the financial costs typically associated with spacecraft development. In particular, a study found that financial risks could be mitigated by up to 67% and hardware failures to at least 51%. This study aims to lay the groundwork for future development by outlining the various components and their functionalities of this revolutionary satellite bus. Furthermore, the research demonstrates the potential benefits of this platform through an in-depth analysis of a hyperspectral experiment. By identifying the key advantages of this platform and the steps taken to address associated technical challenges, researchers demonstrate the feasibility of this highly innovative and adaptable satellite bus. In the future, the project's findings could potentially contribute to the expansion of commercial activities in space and may even pave the way for a future lunar base. A related patent has been filed with the US Patent and Trademark Office under the title '3D printed primary structure of a satellite.' Additionally, the project has inspired the creation of two spin-off companies, 'Laserpowered' and 'Poliplus,' which are further advancing the technological aspects and applications of this pioneering concept. A documentary based on this project has also been produced in collaboration with the German Broadcasting Corporation (DR). The project's website, which serves as a central information hub, provides in-depth details and visualizations of the innovative concepts and their applications. In 2020, the project received the 'Innovation Award' at the ILA Berlin trade fair and the 'Start-up Award' at the SpaceTech Capital space investment fair in Berlin. In addition, the project's findings and outcomes have been presented at various conferences worldwide

To efficiently generate large, high-order quadrilateral grids from complex computer-aided design (CAD) models, researchers have been exploring alternative path reduction methods. Unlike traditional approaches that construct refined grids through repeated refinements, new techniques aim to directly generate high-quality coarsened grids from fine meshes, but often result in low-resolution grids with many DOFs. The issue is addressed by developing quad grids on CAD models using integer linear programming, where the optimal grid topology and node placement are determined simultaneously, building upon the successful application of this approach in triangular grid generation. The proposed method is complemented by a new constraint, which enforces the generation of quadrilateral grids with a specified number of DOs through the introduction of ‘fake nodes’. The effectiveness of this approach is evaluated through numerical analysis, which demonstrates the efficacy of this method in generating accurate and efficient results, but notes that the need for a high-ranked linear programming solver limits its further optimization. The addition of approximate local refinement is also explored as a potential future development. The generated grids are utilized in the high-fidelity numerical simulations of Navier-Stokes equations for aerodynamic calculations, where the authors demonstrate the benefits of this method in balancing computation cost and accuracy with the example of supersonic airflow around the RAE M9 airfoil. The results show that high-fidelity simulations can be achieved at reduced computational cost through the combination of this grid generation method with approximate solvers for Navier-Stokes equations. The paper concludes by highlighting the promising future developments, which could further optimize the performance of this method, for example by integrating generative modeling to accommodate topological changes, or adapting generative adversarial networks, especially generative adversarial networks for geometry generator, to bypass the need for path reduction altogether. The authors also express their intention to contribute to the open-source code for grid generation via path reduction via integer linear programming, which has been successfully applied in various industries such as aerospace and automotive. The description of the method is hoped to inspire further advancements in this field. The generated grids are also visualized through 2D and 3D representations, which demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of this method and serve as a starting point for further research in quad grid generation. The paper's findings are further developed in two related publications by the same authors, where generative modeling and generative adversarial networks are leveraged to generate quadrilateral grids with a specified topology and distribute nodes efficiently. We provide a concise overview of an innovative approach to derive the general theory of relativity and generalize it, which is centered on an analytical formula for an $S$-matrix that incorporates a general background metric. The derivation of Einstein's theory is straightforward when the effect of the metric on the $S$-matrix is interpreted as an energy-momentum tensor, with the realization that particles are emergent phenomena lacking definite energies and momenta. Utilizing the weak-field approximation, we extend general relativity to develop theories that account for loops of excitations and these effects are expressed through novel functionals of density and current. Additionally, we establish that effective field theories are natural applications of the $S$-matrix formula and we verify this principle by conservatively utilizing the existing symmetry associated with a general background metric to isolate the action. We conclude with a perspective on potential future developments, including the possibility of identifying a unique theory through the completion of emergent particles and we suggest that quantum gravity may be discovered by analyzing the properties of light in strong gravitational fields. The theory developed here is testable and, if it passes our expectations, it would represent a significant breakthrough in understanding the gravitational effects on the behavior of particles and matter. We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. This model takes into account an external force and a control parameter, also known as an "actuator". Our work is centered on establishing the uniform stabilization of solutions in a specific space of functions (L^q _\omega). This space, denoted as B^s_{q,s} (over the torus), encompasses a wide variety of critical norm types including s=1 and q=2. In the case of a confined domain with boundary conditions imposing zero velocity, we utilize a finite-dimensional feedback control. This work is an enhancement over the previous research by J. L. Lions in 1986, which demonstrated the ability to achieve exponential decay through feedback controls acting externally. Our model, however, requires a more complex approach due to the absence of a specific structural property in the partial differential equation, namely the dissipativity property. Additionally, in the case of a confined domain with boundary conditions imposing zero velocity, we overcame the challenge of quantifying the proximity between smooth functions and finite-dimensional subspaces, an issue that had stumped us in the past. This work is an extension of our previous research on the finite-dimensional feedback control in the case of a specifically dissipative model (the 2D heat equation) presented in 2019. Our approach for establishing the uniform stabilization of Navier-Stokes flows in the case of a confined domain with zero velocity boundary conditions involves a novel extension of the resonant gap technique, which was first introduced in 2020 for the case of a specifically dissipative model. We explore novel view generation in a dynamic environment using a single-view input. Traditional approaches struggle with generalizing due to limited training data and dynamic scenes, making learned perception challenging and view generation unreliable. To address this, we introduce a conditional image generation task, generating a rear view from a forward view. By modeling perception and novel view generation within a unified conditional image generation framework, advancements in both can concurrently progress. To achieve this, we develop a conditional diffusion model-based novel view generation method, called DiffDreamer, capturing the essence of perception and novel view generation through the lens of image generation. Despite not directly modeling the underlying perception, DiffDreamer's performance surpasses existing methods due to an efficient data-driven approach. Furthermore, we establish a baseline for novel view generation and reveal trade-offs between representation learning and novel view accuracy, highlighting the importance of perception-quality representations for successful novel view generation. Our implementation of DiffDreamer is available online.

Notably, the robotic ultrasound technique coupled with automated image analysis yielded excellent results, effectively tracking the spinal curve and correcting for errors. The reliability of these measurements far exceeded the minimum required standards. These findings suggest that robotic ultrasound imaging, facilitated by the Intelliscan software, presents a reliable and efficient method for scoliosis evaluations. This non-invasive procedure offers the potential to automatically and consistently assess scoliosis in patients, as well as aid in the development of corrective treatments. The combined use of these technological advances may expand the scope of digital rheumatology and orthopedics. The study further explores the practical implications of using robotic ultrasound imaging in clinical settings, including the possibility of remote monitoring through digital platforms. Our research focuses on detecting hate speech in these platforms by utilizing a characteristic extraction-based model that incorporates Hatewatch, a leading global hate speech database. Through a detailed analysis of the baseline models and their shortcomings, we identified key features necessary for hate speech detection, ultimately adapting and refining the FastText model with our derived characteristics to establish a new standard for baseline performance. In recent times, Multi-Input-Multi-Output (MIMO) networks have emerged as promising candidates for handling various vision-based tasks due to their inherent capacity for accommodating large amounts of nonlinear interactions. Despite their potential, MIMO's structural design also introduces challenges such as the tendency for individual sub-networks to develop separate, independently fragmented feature representations, which hinders the networks' overall performance. In response to this limitation, we have developed a novel method for enhancing MIMO network efficiency by retaining the advantages of network depth and depth-wise feature sharing. Our proposed framework for optimizing feature sharing in MIMO networks involves identifying a latent structure for the network's composite feature representation through Clustering Analysis, which yields a more cohesive set of features. We then apply Weight Sharing-based Clustering (WS-CLUSTER) to constrain individual sub-networks to learn from one another, thus reinforcing the shared feature representation. In addition, we have incorporated an Error-Based CLUSTERing (E-CLUSTER) approach for scenarios where the initial feature representations are unknown. This technique determines a more effective feature sharing strategy by simulating the error propagation through the network and introducing a soft clustering strategy. Our experiments, encompassing multiple vision-based tasks, have validated the significant practical value of our approach for optimizing MIMO network performance. Our code is available for review at this link: https://github.com/azee/wsccluster. With this methodology in place, we are poised to further refine MIMO network architecture design and unlock their full potential for achieving state-of-the-art performance. Our findings suggest that fine-tuning feature sharing can lead to MIMO network performance that is several percent better than current benchmarks, which presents an exciting area of further research. Moreover, as the code for our architecture is now openly accessible using this GitHub link: https://github.com/azee/mimo-features-sharing, we are eager to collaborate with fellow researchers and contribute to the advancement of MIMO network architecture design. Furthermore, as the current implementation of our approach can handle ImageNet V2, ImageNet-C, and other downstream tasks, including classification, segmentation, object detection, and generative vision-based tasks, we are prepared to facilitate potential future advancements in these areas. Finally, as MIMO structures also hold promise for expanding into other areas such as time-series prediction, healthcare, and speech processing, which presents a promising avenue for further research. Local government archives contain vast amounts of historical documentation, such as scanned images, which have received relatively little research in the field of Optical Character Recognition (OCR). The primary obstacle hindering the application of OCR systems in this context is the lack of suitable evaluation tools and comprehensive datasets. This problem can be overcome by leveraging datasets composed of images from historical records, which have been annotated by OCR systems to assess their performance. This study aims to provide an in-depth analysis of existing datasets. A key distinction between the selected datasets is the level of preprocessing they have undergone, ranging from basic image filtering to the automatic identification and removal of layout components. The complexity of the chosen layouts, which can vary significantly, also differentiates the datasets, along with the presence of varied textual orientations (portrait or landscape mode) and the presence of white background separation from the page layout. The relevant dataset creation tools, data distribution links, and the employed annotation information (ground truth) are also documented. The datasets have been utilized in the official competitions of the Technical Chamber of Greece and have been published in the proceedings of the workshops as descriptive reports. A corresponding testing platform has also been developed, which enables the simultaneous comparison of OCR systems' performances on the selected datasets, drawing from the field of Document Image Recognition and Handwritten Document Recognition. The purpose of this study is to promote the development of effective OCR systems capable of handling the complex datasets in question, while also contributing to the expansion of the related field, specifically Adaptive OCR Systems, which requires further research in the field of Local Government Record Image Recognition. The selected datasets have been found to share common characteristics, such as the presence of archaic or outdated text formats, which may pose challenges for OCR systems, as well as the presence of unique layout components, such as certificates, which may need to be automatically removed or can be bypassed. A new dataset has also been created, drawing from the decisions of the Greek Courts, which can be accessed via the corresponding repository. The study documents the creation process of this new dataset in detail and presents the results of the testing platform on the selected datasets, including the recognition rates of the baseline system, which is based on a standard document image preprocessing and feature extraction. The results also demonstrate that the most powerful system, which is based on a suitable document image pre-processing and layout feature extraction, as well as a support vector machine-based classifier, achieves a high recognition rate, specifically 73.65%, on the selected datasets. A future extension of the study could involve the creation of a new testing platform

Discrete position measurements from an N-axis measurement system are insufficient for maintaining smooth motion in multi-degree-of-freedom robots. Additional position sensors, also called auxiliary encoders, are required to enhance the characteristics of the motion. A precise algorithm is presented for calculating the velocity and position of each axis based on the measurement of one selected degree of freedom and the characteristics of the desired position trajectory. The proposed method adjusts the position of each additional axis to align with the optical measurements, thereby optimizing the parameters of the tracking error. Due to the presence of dynamic uncertainty and disturbances, a calculated position may deviate from the actual position, resulting in steady-state error. The presented control algorithm includes a compensator designed to eliminate dynamic error, thereby ensuring that the actual position and desired position converge over time. A critical factor for achieving convergence is the correct setting of the controller gain, which requires an in-depth analysis of the system's characteristics. The properties of the system can be estimated through numerical methods based on a designed model of the system, providing an alternative for identifying the system's characteristics experimentally. The presented model is a multi-body model, incorporating both rigid and flexible elements. The characteristics of the system are then extracted from the model's eigenvalues, representing key indicators of the system's stability and response to disturbances. The presented algorithm is substantiated through both simulated and actual experiments, demonstrating its capabilities in optimizing the characteristics of multi-axis motion control systems using auxiliary sensors. A position trajectory with a significant amount of noise was also used in the presented study to evaluate the system's noise resistance capabilities. The presented findings demonstrate that by setting the gain based on the system's characteristics, the actual position and desired position converge in the steady-state phase of the system's response. Consequently, the presented algorithm ensures that even a discrete position measurement system can maintain smooth properties through the effective use of additional sensors and an optimized algorithm. The presented research provides a critical foundation for the development of more sophisticated algorithms in the optimization of multi-axis motion control systems' characteristics. The presented study is a comprehensive solution to the problem of maintaining smooth properties in multi-axis measurement systems with discrete position measurements. The presented algorithm is one of the few published methods for optimizing the characteristics of such systems, which has significant practical applications in various fields. The presented study is a ground-breaking contribution in the area of multi-axis motion control, which has important implications for industrial robotics. This paper explores a statistical model that considers various health states for a person over time and examines the probability distributions of state transitions to understand their disease progression. This framework is particularly suited for analyzing cardiovascular diseases like myocardial infarction, which often exhibit complex and variable patterns of occurrence. A proposed method for estimating the model involves combining myocordial infarction data from multiple sources, including clinical files and genetic research, which can provide valuable information on risk factors, familial tendencies, and overall health. This approach allows for a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of individuals' health trajectories and and disease progression, which can inform the development of effective prevention and treatment strategies in the medical field. A simulation study has validated the method and assessed its practical implications. This study also shows that only a small proportion of individuals who have not had a myocardial infarction die over a given time period. This study provides important new knowledge on the progression of cardiovascular diseases. A number of potential research directions related to these results are presented. The molecular continuum method, also known as matched asymptotics, breaks down a gas flow into two regions: one where kinetic and potential energy are equally significant and another where viscous effects dominate. Typically, this method has been implemented using globally averaged equations within the slip boundary layer region, albeit with recent advances allowing for the preservation of local flow characteristics. Nevertheless, this study presents an alternative approach where instead of averaging governing equations, numerical solutions are interpolated from the inner region to the outer region using multi-site Gaussian quadrature techniques. Evaluating solutions at multiple points yields improved accuracy when interpolated to other points compared to traditional averaging methods, particularly when dealing with non-uniform grids. This method was then evaluated using theoretical flat plate and circular cylinder flows before being applied to the simulation of a cylindrical cylinder in the transonic regime. Results showed that this method could effectively simulate global flow patterns as well as microscopic flow characteristics around cylinders at Reynolds numbers exceeding 500. Furthermore, this method offers the advantage of preserving local flow characteristics, unlike globally averaged methods. We also demonstrated that accurately modeling turbulent flows corresponding to wide distributions of velocity and wall shear rate requires the use of a large number of quadrature points, especially points near the boundary layer region. Consequently, this method presents an alternative solution to the averaging method and enables the simulation of turbulent flows using relatively simple equations representing regions with high kinetic energy. Moreover, implementing smoothing procedures at low Reynolds numbers can effectively reduce turbulent eddies, mimicking kinetic energy distributions characteristic of turbulent flows across multiple scales. Using a smoothing kernel based on the von Karman viscosity profile, we successfully simulated drag reductions of turbulent flows due to coherent structures at moderate Reynolds numbers exceeding 200. This work provides the groundwork for the development of efficient drag reduction technologies across various engineering applications corresponding to both low and high Reynolds numbers. Finally, implementing smoothing kernels within the molecular continuum framework effectively reduces turbulent fluctuations in sparse grid simulations of kinetic models, also known as Carleman schemes. Nevertheless, this method may lead to an increase in computational drift, a potential shortcoming of flow simulation. Therefore, implementing smoothing kernels within the molecular continuum framework effectively reduces turbulent fluctuations in sparse grid simulations, but a future work is needed to develop recipes for the complete elimination of thermal noise. Multinational missions like the European Space Agency's ExoMars and NASA's Mars 2020 project are working together to examine the Martian surface and provide valuable information for understanding the environment and searching for signs of life. Researchers are particularly interested in finding out how liquid water interacts with the Martian surface and surface chemistry, especially in environments that could have supported life in the past. We've established a twistor action for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and various Yang-Mills theories of higher spin. When specialized in a twistor space with a small radius, the action translates into a simple, self-explanatory description of these higher spin theories, drawing comparisons to a well-known action for self-dual gravity formulated by Penrose. Similar to self-dual gravity, the action for higher spin theories incorporates Penrose operator boxes, generating new fields of higher spin twistor as well as field constraints. We demonstrate that these field constraints originate from the expansion of a generalized Suslov operator on the restricted twistor space of a self-dual complex, effectively playing the role of Lagrange multipliers in the action. We provide mathematical proof that the resulting equations of motion are equivalent to those derived from the original Yang-Mills equations of higher spin through a procedure of conformal twistorization. We've also extended our method to apply to general Yang-Mills theory of any spin by employing the spinor component of a self-dual complex, dubbed the Penrose operator cube, in the corresponding action. This results in a new class of field equations. We show that these new equations of motion are equivalent to the original Yang-Mills theory equations when expressed through the spinor component of a self-dual complex, drawing connections to a well-known action for self-dual gravity formulated by Deser-Zerillo. Our method allows for the action for higher spin theories to be translated into the radius of a much larger space, namely 16d, 24d, and 24d Euclidean spaces, by incorporating additional non-linear field interactions based on the Penrose operator boxes. This is made possible by a new procedure we've developed for the non-linear extension of twistor actions. We've also shown in the companion paper "Higher spin theories of Yang-Mills extensions and cosmic string spaces" that these higher spin theories can be translated into the geometry of these larger spaces. In that work, we demonstrate, by employing the mathematical framework established here, that these higher spin theories can be resolved into the geometries of type-JII gravitational theories. Furthermore, our method and resulting theories exhibit a number of striking applications to physics that we will describe in a separate work. Despite the existence of various methods for addressing label noise, the field of supervised learning remains understudied in this context, particularly within the realm of supervised learning models designed for medical image applications. To address this gap in knowledge, this paper introduces a new mechanism for addressing label noise based on Bayesian statistics, thereby enhancing the accuracy of medical image categorization models. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed mechanism significantly improves the accuracy of models trained on noisy data, retaining high levels of accuracy even after extensive noise introduction. Our study utilizes two standard datasets for medical image categorization: CSLI and Pneumonia detection.
