However, when defining positive recursive functions over data with a temporal aspect, 
such as real numbers or dates, non-uniform timing of operations in hardware and software 
poses an issue, as it often goes unconsidered in formal definitions.
This often results in definitions that are either imprecise or excessively complex.
This paper presents an approach to specifying the timing requirements of functions explicitly.
It involves introducing a new definition domain, allowing for timing information to be associated 
with functions through a relation that links a function's input and output to their respective timings.
By utilizing this approach, definitions can be tailored to match a function's actual implementation and, 
as a result, its timing requirements can be explicitly stated, enabling reasoning about its timing as well.
As a demonstration, various practical applications of explicit timing specifications have been exhibited.
These include abstractions and validations of timing information, as well as the use of timing specifications 
in conjunction with other domain-specific principles, such as state and resources management. Furthermore, 
as an illustration of its practical utility, the approach was applied in a formal verification of a widely used but 
error-prone function, known as the "double" function, in widely available programming languages. 
As expected, the verification process was found to be extremely laborious without the explicit timing specification. 
As a next step, the possibility of extending the approach to other essential programming elements, 
including higher-order functions and object-oriented programming, is being considered. Such an extension 
would involve the use of subtyping in conjunction with the definition of the timing relation, allowing for 
a smooth integration of timing specifications into existing formal definitions. 
As a result, the approach could be applied not only in the verification of the "double" function but also in the 
validation of many other crucial timing-related properties of high-level programming functions. 
As an initial step in this direction, the essential principles of subtyping have already been formulated in the 
presence of recursive definitions, paving the way for further research in this area. 
As an important next stage, the development of automatic verification tools, including 
model checkers and interactive proof assistants, is being considered. 
Such tools are already highly effective in facilitating advancements in verification and 
are, in fact, heavily utilized in the HOL Light theory development environment in which the approach was applied.

Our results show that in systems with weak molecule-surface interactions, the underlayer has no significant effect on the properties of the molecule. In contrast, molecules exhibiting strong interactions with the underlayer exhibit altered electronic properties, specifically involving the formation of a backbonding energy minimum. Additionally, incorporating manganese into the center of the silicene ring results in the stabilization of a quadrupole electrically charged state, with manganese being able to accept an extra electron when in contact with boron nitride. Notably, manganese-based systems exhibit distinctive charge transfer patterns between the molecule and underlayer. In particular, manganese can lose an electron in systems with weak molecule-surface interactions but can transfer an electron in systems with strong interactions. Our findings contribute to the advancement of theoretical silicene models and provide valuable insights for designing experimental studies of manganese-based systems. The goal of text categorization is to assign one or more labels to a given document based on its content. Since most machine learning algorithms can't handle datasets with multiple class labels, a common technique used for multi-class text categorization is to use a one-vs-all method. However, this approach has been shown to have limitations, particularly when dealing with a large number of classes. A more recent method overcomes this issue but requires a large amount of data. To address this issue, we experimented with artificially increasing the size of a text categorization dataset using different techniques and measured the effect on accuracy. The results showed that two specific methods, adding synthetic samples and reducing word counts, performed significantly better than the standard method used in similar studies. The improved method achieved a 2% higher accuracy than the one-vs-all method. Furthermore, our findings revealed that under-sampling data from dominant classes can be an efficient alternative to one-vs-all modeling. The reason behind this improvement is that the added samples are drawn from a more diverse set of classes, thus resulting in better model performance. We have made our implementation available under an open-source license for other researchers to use. The findings from our study could help other scholars working on similar text categorization issues. News media play a vital role in keeping the public informed about the current COVID-19 pandemic and its various effects. To understand the impact of different news media outlets and their audiences, we analyzed the online content of seven media regions within the U.S. from April to July 2021. This involved studying the COVID-related topics covered by each region, as well as the number of articles, words, and social media engagement generated in response. Our findings show that news regions with higher case and death rates tend to have a greater number of COVID-related topics, yet not a greater word count. Additionally, we discovered that the COVID-related topics covered by each region are often consistent, both within and between regions. What's more, social media engagement is more influenced by the word count than the number of articles. These results provide insight into the complex relationships between news coverage, COVID cases and deaths, and audience engagement. They offer a fresh perspective on news dissemination and the role of media in shaping public perception of the COVID-19 pandemic's progression. Such understanding is essential for developing a more comprehensive model of news coverage and its implications for public health. With the ability to digitally access news media, we can now rapidly respond to public health crises like the COVID pandemic, facilitating novel research discoveries. Moreover, such findings can contribute to a better-informed public health policy and communication. Finally, our research delves into the digital footprint of the COVID pandemic and its effects on the news media, ultimately influencing the world's ever-interconnected digital landscape. As a reflexive and data-driven study, we also examine the ethical and societal implications of news media research and their digital subjects. While considering research benefits and biases, we reflect on our own positionality and how it might impact our findings and study participants. Ultimately, we reflect on the broader consequences of our research and encourage audiences to think critically about the digital world, acknowledging the inherent complexities and uncertainties of our research environment. In the case of the Yukawa potential, which models a point mass's interaction with surrounding masses within a sphere defined by a specific radius and angle of deviation, we found that a modified version of the algorithm can ensure conservation of angular momentum by adjusting the quadrature method and resolving boundary contact points. Our modified version of the algorithm achieves this by either using a four-point Hermite-Simpson quadrature with specially modified kernel functions or by correcting for boundary contact effects through additional calculations. In our simulation tests, both of these methods were found to successfully conserve angular momentum to a high degree of precision. For energy conservation, we found that a simple adjustment to the quadrature method was enough to achieve precise conservation in our tests. Our solution maintains the algorithm's high level of efficiency, taking no more than three times the original number of time steps while still ensuring precise conservation of both energy and angular momentum. In environments where direct data is scarce but indirect data is plentiful, we develop a method to utilize this information effectively. A key challenge is that some sources may be unreliable or provide skewed information. We address this by designing a robust data augmentation technique that selects and combines credible examples to support a model's training. The proposed approach involves a Bayesian framework that evaluates the reliability of a teacher model, determines the credibility of local examples, and uses this information to improve the performance of a student model through effective data augmentation. The method also enables adaptive teacher selection and can be employed in settings where teacher models are limited. Notably, our method offers a wide range of applications that extend beyond the classic setting of having a single teacher model. Such diverse applications include image processing tasks like data augmentation for blind image denormalization and low-dose X-ray reconstruction, as well as other tasks like generating labeled CBAM maps for attention-aware block attention networks. The findings are in line with the standard model predictions. The challenge of finding a polynomial-time algorithm to approximate a network's genus has been a persistent issue in the field of graph theory for a long time. A network's genus represents the minimum number of planes necessary to separate a network's embedded graphs. Previous methods, such as the Tomita algorithm, aim to calculate a network's genus in polynomial time but often fail, resulting in a time complexity of n^O(1/4) in the best case. A recent study proposed a new method that significantly improves efficiency, achieving a time complexity of n^O(1/5), close to the previously best result of n^O(1/6). In this study, a new efficient polynomial-time algorithm is proposed to approximate a network's genus with a specified level of accuracy, making use of the Euler method for numerical computation and achieving a time complexity of n^O(ω^2), where ω represents the square root of a network's size. This algorithm can be modified to run in a time complexity of n^O(1/ω) on single-threaded systems. Furthermore, a corresponding algorithm is proposed for approximating a network's embedding genus, resulting in a time complexity of n^O(1/ω). In order to demonstrate the efficiency of these algorithms, a new experimental method is proposed that validates the performance of these algorithms on real-world network data. A comprehensive testing of these algorithms on a range of network data types demonstrates the accuracy and time complexity of these algorithms. A network with 20,000 nodes and an average degree of 50 was found to take approximately 0.18 seconds to calculate its genus using the new efficient polynomial-time algorithm. In comparison, a Tomita-based approach took approximately 1.5 seconds to calculate the genus of the same network. These results confirm that the new efficient polynomial-time algorithm outperforms the Tomita approach by a factor of nearly 8 in terms of time complexity. This study contributes to the development of technology to recognize hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali languages, representing the most widely spoken languages in India and Bangladesh, respectively. Due to the scarcity of a comprehensive public dataset for these languages, we created a highly effective classifier using a novel approach that combines a neural network with a sequential model. The framework begins with a text normalization process, followed by the application of a neural network. To address the issue of limited training data, we explore the feasibility of transferring knowledge from English models, showcasing through experiments the significance of text pre-processing and knowledge transfer in identifying hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali. On the one hand, we achieved an accuracy of 65.96% using our customized classifier on the newly created Hindi hate-speech dataset 'Offensiveness: Identification of Hate Slang', resulting in 40.6% accuracy improvement over the baseline model. On the other hand, we successfully demonstrated the applicability of transfer learning from English to Hindi/Bengali models and also made public the 'Bengali Hate-Speech' dataset, an unlabelled dataset collected from social media platforms that specialize in online abuse and hate-speech discussion forums. Moreover, we briefly discuss how our research can be expanded to other low-resource Indian languages including Gujarati, Kannada, and Oriya, as well as the Bangladeshis languages Urdu, Sanskrit, and Sanskrit Sign Language. Finally, we highlight the societal implications of identifying hate-speech through neural networks. In the field of Commercial Driving, expert agents evaluate and guide self-driving vehicles for optimal performance. Our research focuses on expert supervision as a crucial tool for system assessment, uncovering various roles experts play and how they impact robot-assisted driving evaluations. We introduce a novel method for automated assessment, considering not only technical performance but also safety and responsiveness to situations. By integrating this approach with an advanced decision-making system, experts can provide more accurate and comprehensive feedback on system behavior in real-world applications. The proposed method achieves optimal results when integrated with a tree decomposition-based decision model and is currently being used in commercial evaluation services of autonomous driving systems. Our research demonstrates how expert supervision can enhance self-driving vehicle performance assessments and is currently transforming industry practices. Furthermore, from the perspective of decision-making, we categorize expert evaluation processes and develop a method to automate most of the assessment, freeing more complex and nuanced judging for human experts to focus on. The additional complexity of expert evaluation is associated with incomplete information and uncertain probabilities in various situations. We introduce a novel information theoretic measure to quantify and optimize this incomplete information and illustrate its application in automated evaluation systems. Our research also explores time-based assessment evaluations but finds they do not directly relate to optimal system performance. By integrating time and information-based evaluation, however, we uncover a link between the two and show that optimal information-based evaluations can result in equitable and efficient time-based assessments. The proposed evaluation framework is currently being used in commercial settings, and our research provides a theoretical basis for its development, showcasing expert supervision as a critical component of self-driving vehicle assessments. The method's current implementation is available for public download. Future work could focus on incorporating more information theoretic elements and automated assessment, potentially transforming the development and assessment of self-driving vehicles. The proposed model is compatible with current machine learning and automated assessment technologies and is grounded in commercial self-driving vehicle practice, providing a link between AI system evaluation and human expert decision-making. As a result, our research could have a significant impact on the development of reliable and efficient autonomous vehicle systems. The evaluation framework balance, fairness, and sensitivity were thoroughly examined, and the corresponding code is publicly available for other researchers to access. The time-based evaluation was explored but was found not to offer added system benefits, and the proposed information-based evaluation provides a unique contribution to the field, differing from existing research and seamlessly integrating with current self-driving vehicle technologies and practices. The long-term implications of this research could lie in autonomous vehicle manufacturing and could potentially transform the development and assessment of self-driving vehicles.

This paper represents The Metals in AI at CMU team in the Out-of-Context challenge, where we achieved a ranking of 5th out of 79 submissions. Our approach relies on a V5 detection model to extract objects from the environment, which we then utilize a variant of the FRODOco model to link these objects to their relevant descriptions. We develop and implement a novel strategy, dubbed ROAR, to tackle the test collection problem, which entails selecting the most relevant descriptions for each detected object and ensuring temporal coherence. We meticulously examined the two leading submission by CogNet, which employed a similar object detection and linking methodology but a distinct model and a different ranking strategy, and Optima, which relied on a different problem formulation and a different model. In the qualification phase of the challenge, we achieved a ranking of 8th out of 67 submissions. Our results imply that a straightforward extension of a model optimized for vision-and-language pretraining, coupled with a conventional ranking strategy, may not suffice to solve the problem, and that a more sophisticated technique like ROAR is necessary to yield substantial improvements. A stochastic process is considered a manifold of Gaussian fields when its regression function is everywhere curved. The paper explores the geodesic properties of this specific manifold, demonstrating that the regression function's curvature determines whether these geodesics align with straight lines. A distinguishing feature of the Gaussian field manifold is that it has a single optimal point when optimized under minimum mutual information criteria, and in this optimal point, geodesic paths exhibit linearity. Moreover, the paper presents a non-parametric approach to estimating the optimal point and calculating the geodesic coordinates. This method involves first fitting a Gaussian process regression model and then evaluating the geodesic paths based on the resulting mean function. The approach is validated using synthetic data and applied to two real-world datasets. One of the datasets is from a study involving infant caregiving activities, and another is a clinical dataset analyzing treatment effectiveness across multiple disease states. The methodology is also compared to a similar method developed by (Fistric et al., 2020) for the Gaussian field manifold. A distinguishing feature of the presented method is its requirement for zero-dimensional Gaussian process regression. This makes the new method more scalable and powerful than the existing method, and it demonstrates strong alignment with the underlying Gaussian field properties. Lastly, the research outlines potential future applications of the Gaussian field manifold in the context of Gaussian process regression. The calculated geodesic paths have a geometric interpretation that could be relevant to topics such as infrastructural link analysis and molecular cluster structure modeling, and the optimal point could be seen as a form of multivariate density representation. Moreover, the geometric interpretation of the Gaussian field manifold, combined with its connection to the core principles of Gaussian process regression, makes it an attractive tool for machine learning applications, and the optimization problem associated with the manifold is related to the optimal transport problem as first introduced by Kantorovich. Consequently, additional research could focus on the potential use of the Gaussian field manifold as a tool for optimal transport-based image analysis and other related topics. Nonetheless, the current implementation of the methodology is limited to cases where the Gaussian process regression model has a dimension of at most two. This is because the underlying optimization algorithm for minimum mutual information criteria, which is based on the expectation minimization algorithm, experiences numerical instability in higher dimensions. In practice, this means that the methodology can only be applied effectively to features such as image pixels, gene expression levels, and the different states of a disease progression. This research explores electron transport in graphene nanostructures with specific molecular sp sp2 bonds, utilizing the self-consistent tight-binding model. The study examined both non-magnetic and exchange interaction-based Hamiltonians to determine their influence on the device's electrical properties. Results showed that devices featuring exchange interaction between graphene and ferromagnetic contacts exhibit a predictable, on-off transport behavior indicative of a spin filter device. Additionally, devices with non-magnetic contacts exhibited random, non-reproducible current patterns due to charge transport. By replacing the ferromagnetic contacts with a p-orbital contact, the device's electrical properties remained unchanged, demonstrating the device's potential for efficient spin filtering and controllable transport through graphene nanostructures. Moreover, analyzing the spin polarization revealed that the device's spin-filtering performance could be adjusted by modifying the central barrier's height. This device's simple fabrication and efficient spin filtering capabilities make it well-suited for versatile spintronics applications. The study's findings also provide valuable insights into the device's transport behavior at the quantum level and demonstrate the device's potential as a reliable spin filter. Furthermore, introducing a quantum contact model enabled the exploration of quantum transport and revealed the device's potential as a rectifier due to its predictable current patterns under different voltage polarities. The device's current patterns were found to be more stable as temperature increased, indicating its robustness against environmental conditions. The study also explored the device's performance under laser irradiation, revealing enhanced spin filtering capabilities. The device's efficient spin filtering was found to correlate with specific laser frequencies and polarizations, as well as the presence of spin-polarized electrons. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the device's transport phenomena and sheds light on its potential as a spin filter. The study's findings can be applied to explain recent experimental results and provide a foundation for exploring quantum transport in graphene systems. Furthermore, exploring quantum transport using a quantum contact model enabled the exploration of graphene devices at the nanoscale and uncovered novel quantum effects. The study's findings reveal that graphene systems exhibit robust and versatile properties and hold the potential for producing quantum devices with predictable electrical properties. The study's exploration of quantum transport using a quantum contact model in conjunction with tight-binding models may provide valuable insights into the quantum behavior of one-dimensional systems. This review focuses on the application of the outward complex scaling technique in computational physics, specifically highlighting its use in quantum mechanical treatments of atoms and molecules under the influence of strong direct currents. The outward complex scaling approach involves wrapping the boundary of the computational domain in a complex direction, resulting in an advantageous mathematical representation for dealing with far-field conditions. The method's fundamental nature and variations are explored in the context of time-independent quantum mechanics. It provides an alternative to the finite element method, particularly useful in the presence of strong DC fields that complicate conventional scaling procedures. The output wave functions and energies resulting from this method correctly describe physical properties, albeit influenced by finite volume effects that depend on the complex scaling parameter. The approach's versatility is reflected in the variety of methods employed to determine the optimal scaling parameter value. We also delves into the use of non-orthogonal basis sets in this method and recent developments aimed at expanding the output domain's real-axis reach. Lastly, a concise overview is offered of current outcomes and planned investigations. The aim is to present an extensive and detailed overview of this method, and by doing so, inspire further research and development. The associated Fortran source code, available through the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.764063, serves as a flexible and expandable numerical tool that can be modified to suit different applications. The code's scope is broader than the outward complex scaling technique, incorporating a comprehensive DC field implementation that can be used independently. The review's purpose is to facilitate future developments by highlighting existing achievements and opening up new paths for continued method enhancement and application expansion. Measurements of the $t\bar{t}$ production cross-section have been conducted in 5.02 TeV $pp$ collisions, utilizing 250 nanobarns of data with the ATLAS detector. Differential cross-sections for total $t\bar{t}$ cross-sections are reported at the visible stage and after correcting for detector inefficiencies. Simulations of soft radiation by the parton shower model and additional $t\bar{t}$ events by matrix element calculations help address residual corrections. Total and differential $t\bar{t}$ cross-sections, with various kinematic cuts, including lepton, parton-to-lepton efficiency corrections, are presented in this study. Data and simulation results are compared using a least-squares fit from top quark pair rapidity distributions, showing good agreement between ATLAS data and simulated simulations after efficiency corrections, revealing no significant residual bias in total $t\bar{t}$ cross-section measurements across different dilepton decay channels. Total $t\bar{t}$ cross-section measurements in all channels were found to be 75.2 $\pm$ 1.3 ± 2.8 ± 2.8 pb, with visible and reconstructed $t\bar{t}$ differential cross-sections agreeing with QCD predictions. This study had the highest precision, with a total uncertainty of 5.5% for a measurement of the total $t\bar{t}$ cross-section. Moreover, this study showed promising potential for improved precision in various $t\bar{t}$ differential cross-section measurements at 5.02 TeV with the ATLAS detector at LHC. It was also found that, despite not having the track-based reconstruction of the top quark decay, there was still sufficient sensitivity in total $t\bar{t}$ cross-section measurements with the ATLAS detector. This study laid the groundwork for future measurements of the top quark pair production cross-section and polarization in experiments at the 5 and 13 TeV LHC with the ATLAS and CMS detectors, with the 5 TeV LHC providing a valuable test of the LHC's energy range and a distinct work environment. This study was particularly significant in determining the $t\bar{t}$ production cross-section measurements in a specific energy range not yet addressed in previous experiments. Furthermore, this study marked the first utilization of the ATLAS detector at LHC in measuring $t\bar{t}$ cross-section measurements in a 5 TeV $pp$ collisions

Past research indicates that individuals with higher incomes tend to exhibit more proactive urban interaction behaviors. To understand the impact of the pandemic on urban spatial interactions, this study investigates how the shift in spatial interaction patterns among varying income groups affects the diversity of areas and areas' level of homogeneity. Analyzing Chicago's interaction data from 2020 and 2019, the results indicate that higher-income areas experienced a greater increase in diversity following the pandemic, whereas lower-income areas became more uniform in their diversity. Consequently, the gap in diversity levels between high-income and low-income areas widened during this period. To verify that the increased homogeneity of low-income areas was not the result of a natural shift, simulations of pre-pandemic conditions using the same data are performed. These simulations reveal that a reduction in urban diversity would have occurred in low-income areas under normal circumstances, implying that the pandemic had a profound effect on the diversity of urban spaces and income inequality. Therefore, the study concludes that the pandemic exacerbated income disparity of urban spaces and may have long-term effects on the distribution of urban diversity. Moreover, the study's findings highlight the significance of continuing to examine the impact of extraordinary events like the pandemic on urban planning. To facilitate replication of the study's methods, all data sources and code used in this research are available on a publicly accessible repository.

In our investigation, we have evaluated multiple preconditioning techniques for solving two-phase flow equations within heterogeneous porous media under steady-state conditions. These preconditioning methods can be categorized into two types: linear and nonlinear approaches. The linear techniques, such as coarse-grid scale fully factorized Jacobi and Fast Off-Grid Data-Driven Preconditioners, show faster convergence rates in the first few iterations but struggle with deep or large-scale linear systems. On the other hand, nonlinear techniques, like field-split preconditioners (based on Schur complement), offer superior performance despite more complicated computations. However, their effectiveness heavily relies on pre and post conditioning processes, such as Jacobian matrix calculations. To further improve their performance, we have implemented an innovative system of equations known as field-split Schur forms. Through our thorough analysis and extensive numerical comparison, we have quantitatively demonstrated the superior performance of our new nonlinear field-split preconditioning method. Moreover, this technique has been successfully tested on real-world 3d coal bed methane injection models, where it outperformed existing field-split preconditioning methods by orders of magnitude. Our results also highlight the critical impact of pre and post conditioning on field-split Schur forms performance and propose several areas for future enhancement. Ultimately, this research aims to accelerate the development of efficient reservoir simulation models, paving the way for faster simulations through accelerated field scanning and optimization. TERS is a highly sensitive imaging technique that offers profound insights into the electronic and geometric properties of nanoscale materials. Although its resolution is significantly limited by the size of the tip-apex probe, the method's precision could be further impeded by the subtle interactions between the tip and sample, as well as unwanted laser scattering. Our comprehensive study draws on cutting-edge quantum mechanical methods, including ab initio calculations and density functional theory, to thoroughly examine the chemical and electromagnetic interactions involved in TERS. By focusing on the key factors that contribute to the signal strength, tip-sample interaction, and laser scattering, we identify the essential parameters that determine the sample's photoemission yield, tip-sample ripples, and laser beam focusing, respectively. Our investigation reveals that the sample's yield plays a dominant role in determining the TERS signal strength, followed by the intensity of the localized electromagnetic field at the probe tip and then the effects of tip-sample ripples on the signal. Furthermore, we illustrate various scenarios in which the tip-sample interactions can compromise TERS resolution and signal strength. Our work addresses a pressing need to rectify the chemical and electromagnetic interferences distorting TERS's nanoscale imaging and spectroscopy outcomes. It is our hope that this study inspires the development of new experiments aimed at correcting these interferences, thereby unleashing the full potential of TERS. Additionally, we present an innovative idea for rectifying the ripples' adverse impact on TERS by employing probe tips coated with thin insulating materials. Such probe tips can significantly reduce the chemical reactivity of the tip's active regions, thereby preserving the sample's chemical and electromagnetic properties. Our analysis also demonstrates that these insulating coated probe tips can maintain a high level of localized electromagnetic field intensity while minimizing the related sample's photoemission yield. Consequently, they present promising possibilities for enhancing the overall performance of TERS. It is our intention that this study contributes to the ongoing efforts to perfect TERS and other similar scanning probe techniques such as SNOM and APT. Please note that the related source codes for the quantum mechanical methods employed in this study can be accessed at https://github.com/Fatemeh-Najafi/TERS-Quantum-Influences. Furthermore, this code also enables the simulation of various probes made from monolayer materials and is named MLProbe. It is our hope that this code can be utilized in the exploration of new probe materials to further elevate the capabilities of TERS and related techniques. Time series close neighbor search involves determining the closest or one of the closest time series within a specified distance threshold from a query time series. Several approximate search algorithms have been proposed, and we examine their speed versus accuracy tradeoffs using the Frechet distance as a benchmark. We highlight limitations in existing bounds and present new theoretical limits for two variants of the problem. We also provide experimental validation of these limits and show how these bounds can be applied to other distances as well. Additionally, we provide a framework for converting time series approximations to the Frechet distance to limits applicable under other distances as well. This framework is demonstrated with the example of the edit distance. We conclude by discussing ways to optimize the balance between speed and accuracy in time series close neighbor search. Our work offers the first rigorous theoretical limits for time series close neighbor search using the Frechet distance and related distances. These limits can serve as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of time series close neighbor search algorithms. However, the situation is different for the edit distance, and we show that it is possible to achieve the identified limits of the Frechet distance while still providing better results for the edit distance. Thus, the distance metric used in time series close neighbor search plays a significant role in determining the efficiency of approximate search algorithms. This work offers key insights into the design of efficient and scalable time series close neighbor search algorithms, and it can be applied to develop optimized algorithms for the edit distance and other distances as well. Finally, the tradeoffs between speed and accuracy can be optimized using indexing techniques such as trees and partitions. Although our analysis is for exact search, the same concepts can be used for approximate search as well. This work is more comprehensive as it involves various distances including Frechet distance, and it is also applicable to the edit distance and other distances as well. Although practical issues generally prefer precision over precision-corrected values, theoretical analyses benefit from taking into consideration these uncertainties. We then establish conditions under which this method is reliable and provide a systematic technique for its implementation. For tasks like delivery or maintenance work in indoor environments, developing navigation systems that utilize building layouts is crucial, especially in unfamiliar premises. Unfortunately, accessing or creating detailed layout plans for these areas often isn't possible, which limits the performance of layout-based navigation systems. In response, we've created HiTMap - a space representation system that organizes locations into areas and sub-regions based on the layout's topological structure. This approach reduces reliance on detailed layout details, focusing instead on the overall layout pattern, which can be easily transferred between adjacent locations. In contrast to standard grid-world representations, HiTMap enables agents to leverage their experience in one location to improve navigation in others, while maintaining efficient planning capabilities. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of HiTMap in our accompanying paper. In particular, in retrieval-based navigation experiments, a agent trained with HiTMap-aided reinforcement learning successfully retrieved a target location 52.75% of the time, outperforming naive and grid-world-based agents, who achieved 20% and 40.12% retrieval success rates respectively. Furthermore, the agent trained with HiTMap was able to transfer its knowledge across multiple locations more successfully than those trained within each location in isolation. Our results highlight the practicality of integrating topological structure into reinforcement learning-based navigation, even in the absence of detailed environmental information. This research was enabled through integration with the 2D-VO system for visual observation and mapping in indoor environments. This work introduces a novel variational model for simultaneously reconstructing CT images from polychromatic X-ray sources, filtering out measurement noise and separating material compositions within an object. An existing model we built upon relies on the regularization of a system consisting of differentiation, Laplacian, and convolution operations, which makes image reconstruction difficult due to the presence of matrices and functions of matrices. By decoupling the cost function, we break down the optimization problem into smaller components with well-structured matrices, making the problem more tractable. We provide comprehensive mathematical analyses justifying the new optimization path and propose an efficient iterative algorithm with fast convergence.Numerical simulations confirm our analytical findings. Furthermore, we showcase the practical efficacy of our approach using real-world data provided by a CT scanner. Our results indicate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in terms of both quantitative measures and the quality of the resulting images, particularly for a material separation task. An added benefit of our method is its ability to automatically determine the number of material components within an object without prior knowledge. Based on these outcomes, we believe that our method holds significant potential for real-world applications in material analysis, such as applications in the fields of medicine, materials science and industrial manufacturing. An implementation of our algorithm is freely available for other researchers on the GitHub platform. The implementation of electronic health records has generated vast amounts of data that can be leveraged for clinical research purposes. Nonetheless, mining this data presents challenges due to its structural complexity, which necessitates the application of complex computational techniques. Graph neural networks have recently emerged as a highly effective tool for analyzing this data, particularly in predictive modeling tasks. Nevertheless, the current approaches to graph neural networks are limited in several ways: they often aggregate node features using a global method, which fails to preserve the distinct characteristics of individual patients; and by employing a fixed, pre-trained graph structure that is incapable of adapting to the dynamic medical condition of each individual. In an attempt to address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel graph neural network model known as the diverse similarity graph neural network (DSGNN), which dynamically aggregates graph structure information based on the similarity between patients, utilizing either clustering or medical correlation analysis methods. This innovative model can be applied to various applications such as the extraction of text data from ehr records and the analysis of medical tabular data using a combination of DSGNN and transformer encoder layers. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed model significantly enhances the performance of typical baselines across multiple evaluation metrics, thereby showcasing its utility as a robust tool for clinical data analysis. Moreover, the various applications of the DSGNN model, which can be easily adapted to other use cases, can help to accelerate the discovery of insights from massive digital health repositories by clinical data scientists. These repositories include publicly accessible datasets such as eicu, medico, and MIMIC-IV as well as the privately owned Informatics of Sugery after Discharge dataset. We consider a soft interface with a position-dependent profile that can be modified by an external solvent influence, allowing us to compare the responses of a neutral solvent and a solvent that can be polarized. We investigate the electrical behavior, charging process, and solvent polarization at the interfaces of a capacitor, nanotubes, and nanocylinders. Our analysis shows that solvent polarization has a significant impact on the soft interface's electric behavior, while also influencing the ion distribution and potential profile according to the geometry of the system. We found that solvent polarization may lead to a decrease in the capacitance of the soft interface, and we discuss the implications of the charging time in different geometries of the system. Our model provides a framework for understanding various electrochemical processes involving soft interfaces and highlights the importance of solvent polarization in their modeling. This research targets energy-efficient wireless communications by optimizing a multi-user system using network coding, where data is combined at intermediate nodes, reducing overall transmission time, but at the cost of consuming power. To achieve this goal, we formulated a more efficient problem by combining power allocation and relay selection, translating it into a mixed-integer non-convex optimization issue. To resolve this challenge, we introduced an innovative algorithm: an iterative solution for selecting optimal relays and optimizing power distribution. Notably, this method requires no prior knowledge of channel conditions or initialization. We demonstrated via simulation that our proposed approach enables significant reductions in transmission power with minimal impact on transmission time. Moreover, this method outperforms comparable solutions by optimized, uni-modal network coding. Additionally, it offers greater flexibility in system design with the capacity of decoding at intermediate nodes. An interesting finding is that, in certain configurations, fully orthogonal configurations can be as effective as nearly-achievable bounds for network coding. These findings emphasize the potential advantages of combining network coding and power allocation in optimizing wireless communications. Finally, we compared the energy efficiency of different coding and decoding methods and introduced a new network coding scheme with improved energy efficiency. Notably, this innovation requires only a single packet transmission at the destination to recover the original information, whereas previous schemes require two packets. Our simulations demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions in energy efficiency. Notably, it achieves a comparable success rate with significantly fewer transmission attempts, reducing the energy consumption per successful reception. This significant improvement in energy efficiency corresponds to two key factors. Firstly, our proposed algorithm requires only a simple initialization, unlike convex optimization algorithms that need specific channel information or initialization. Secondly, it's a more efficient problem, which means it's easier to find solutions, which in turn reduces computational delays, as our algorithm can run freely without the need for internal optimization tools. Notably, these properties make our proposed algorithm an attractive solution for real-time wireless communications, which prioritize energy efficiency, simplicity, and speed above other factors. In this study, we focus on eliminating biases in distribution-to-distribution matching by employing a neural network filter. Various data sets of laser and sonar scans from different environments and platforms have been used to develop and test the algorithm, which is based on a multi-layer neural network trained with the mean squared error as its loss function.  The results show that the algorithm is effective in removing time-based distortions caused by moving platforms, like a quadrotor, as well as spatial discrepancies generated by simulated sonar data.  Furthermore, in collaboration with human observers, the information obtained from sonar data is separated into useful and useless components, enabling the development of a bias filter trained on these new labels. However, their use in critical systems is compromised by their vulnerability to manipulated inputs. Previous studies have shown methods to counter SVM attacks, primarily focusing on data manipulation techniques. This study introduces novel, blended attacks on SVM classifications, specifically targeting modulation categorization, and showcases their effectiveness in compromising performance. In response, this research incorporates techniques from generative adversarial networks and ensemble methods to enhance the robustness of SVM models against these blended assaults. The analysis includes evaluations of relevant physical characteristics and considers an active defense approach utilizing noise addition as a countermeasure. The study evaluates the techniques through a comprehensive analysis of various metrics, including accuracy, receiver operating characteristic curves, and feature influence, to understand the behavior of the methods and their accuracy variations. The study finds that blended attacks can significantly compromise SVM performance, but also effective countermeasures can be employed to mitigate these vulnerabilities. Moreover, a combination of methods, in this case, the hybridization of an SVM with a gradient-enhanced extrema point detector, is sufficient to protect against the blended assaults, and that noise addition is an eligible countermeasure that can be exploited to safeguard critical systems. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that has been constant for decades. Given the significant time and resources required for data collection, the challenge lies in developing models that can adapt to new patterns without compromising earlier knowledge. In this research, the problem of supervised segmentation models 'forgetting' previous knowledge when trained on new datasets is explored. A comprehensive analysis is provided on two publicly available datasets from different imaging sources, revealing the issue of knowledge retention as it relates to data origin and institutional variability. A novel approach called InterSession Contrastive Learning is proposed, allowing models to retain earlier knowledge while adapting to new patterns through self-comparison during the training process. The results show that this method can effectively maintain the accuracy of previous sessions while improving cross-session and cross-dataset accuracy by 8-15%, thus outperforming the standard approach and surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. The research also highlights underlying architectural and temporal knowledge issues in conventional models and presents a framework for integrating inter-session contrastive learning into existing segmentation methods. The data, implementation, and results are available on the MS-Net GitHub repository. A related demonstration can be found at https://cisl-demo.org. (Figure presented as a Figur8 contribution.)

A filamentary network of dust and gas stretches across the sky, with dense cores forming within them and giving birth to new massive stars. To understand the evolution of these cores, researchers are studying their properties and growth patterns. One such core, located within the Dragon filament, was investigated using a combination of radio and infrared observations - but radio data proved inaccurate due to nearby strong sources, while infrared data revealed the core's structure and mass but left its radio appearance uncertain. Therefore, the core's evolution process and the impact of activation by a massive star remain unclear. To resolve these questions, researchers are using a novel numerical model for core development to analyze the core's dynamics and growth patterns at different times, and they are also exploring ways to correct the core's irregular radio appearance to predict its patterns of chemical development more accurately. By studying the core's patterns of growth and the chemicals it contains, researchers can better understand how these cores form and how massive stars are created. One such pathway is currently being investigated further in the development series.

The emergence of First Principles-based models for dark energy is crucial in understanding the expansion of the universe. In this report, we incorporate a model that includes both dark matter and dark energy in the form of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs), which serves as an alternative to other theoretical dark energy models. This model is based on a computer code called PopSyCLE, which we have expanded upon by introducing a new (PBH) particle type and modifying existing equations to represent PBH interactions. This enhanced code allows for the simulation of PBH dark energy, which conforms to four fundamental laws: the conservation of energy, the laws of gravity, thermodynamics, and electromagnetic interactions. Our simulations comprise two types: cosmic structure formation and fundamental particle interactions, which enable us to investigate PBH dark energy concepts, including decay, annihilation, and gravitational constraints on PBHs, as well as detecting them through gravitational wave events. Furthermore, we have made the modified PopSyCLE code available for public use, which facilitates efficient and reliable numerical simulations of PBH dark energy. This work serves as a foundation for future studies of PBH dark energy, which may lead to new insights into cosmological phenomena. The modified PopSyCLE code is available upon request. A related Python package 'pbh-cosmology' is available at https://github.com/kaihinc/cosmology, which provides an implementation of PBH dark energy models. This Python package is further supplemented by a JAX-based framework 'pbh-sim' at https://github.com/kaihinc/simulations for running dark energy simulations efficiently using the PBH models. Specifically, the minimum viable prototype (MVP) 'pbh-ignite' at https://github.com/kaihinc/ignite serves as a benchmarking tool for testing and benchmarking PBH dark energy simulations across various hardware and software platforms. A two-dimensional model comprising rigid triangular plates formed from uniform spheres was studied in a strictly planar configuration. Each "wedge" in this model has an inherent triangular structure, with the "grain boundaries" connecting them maintaining exact angles, maintaining a completely planar configuration. The spheres were then allowed to move at room temperature, resulting in the creation of unique, irregularly shaped domains that spread through the network. These micro-spheres can adopt varying levels of freedom, ranging from zero to fifty-nine degrees, resulting in the emergence of distinct phases. The partial flexibility of the grains led to the formation of twisted grains and changing angles at grain boundaries, resulting in the creation of unique, non-crystalline structures. The system's phase diagram was found to be largely determined by the degrees of freedom of the spheres, with the absence of additional parameters. The system demonstrated a unique splay modulation that arose in the twisted grain region, in addition to the existing twist and twist-shear phases already observed in similar systems. The presence of this modulation led to a type of supermodulation that emerged due to the interaction between the twisted and twisted-shear phases, with the most common phase being the twist phase due to the prevalence of small grains with low degrees of freedom. The system's behavior can be explained using a simplified model based on the twist-grain interaction, with the resulting phase diagram displaying distinct regions corresponding to the twist, twist-shear, and twist-splay phases, with the last being characterized by the presence of the supermodulation effect. The corresponding phase diagram demonstrates that the twist-splay region emerges when the periods of the twist and twist-shear phases align, resulting in the creation of two distinct types of phases: a concave and a convex phase. The system's behavior can be described using a modified twist-grain model that incorporates an additional term accounting for the flexural elasticity of the grains, with the corresponding period of the twist-shear phase dependent on the curvature of the grains, with the corresponding phase diagram displaying distinct regions corresponding to the twist, twist-shear, and twist-shear-splay phases. The system's behavior can also be described using a model based on the flexibility of the grains, with the corresponding period of the twist-shear-splay phase emerging due to the interaction between the twist and twist-shear phases. Language model pre-training has been extensively studied through the lens of efficient utilization of computing resources. Advancements in scaled-down models for transfer learning have particularly garnered significant interest in facilitating model development across various tasks. Current research into efficient models is predominantly confined to adapting pre-trained models for unique tasks by fine-tuning or meta-learning techniques, overlooking the complexities involved in ensuring models remain within defined parameter boundaries. This study presents an innovative method for constrained model adaptation, incorporating token-specific adjustments to address parameter limit constraints, and demonstrates its adaptability to encompass diverse parameter adjustment techniques and convergence acceleration. Experimental evaluations conducted on the MNIST and IMDB datasets showcase the efficacy of the proposed method in achieving successful model adaptation within defined parameter constraints. Furthermore, the study examines the theoretical underpinnings of the proposed method, and its implications are discussed. This research is expected to facilitate development of innovative models within established parameter constraints, driving progress towards the creation of lean, efficient language models. Potential applications of these models encompass deployment on resource-restricted edge devices and development of multi-model frameworks, enhancing the overall efficiency of computing resources. The proposed method is anticipated to foster advancements in model efficiency, contributing to the development of adversarially trained models for virtual adversarial training. Lastly, the study presents a variety of parameter adjustment techniques, enhancing model robustness against perturbations and encouraging the exploration of efficient model adversarial training. The code for this research has been made available for public access at https://github.com/zhang-yanjie/PEAA.

We propose a preference ordering model, specifically designed for set addition problems, which combines contextual and non-contextual elements. The contextual aspect is modelled by introducing a domain-specific search protocol to gather preference information. The non-contextual aspect is represented by an expert who provides preference judgments without consideration for specific situations. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through set synthesis problems from real-world domains such as planning and information systems. Compared to a fully contextual model, our method yields substantial reductions in preference information requirements, resulting in around 71.4% fewer preference judgments for plan set addition and 62.5% for database schema set addition. The trade-off comes at the expense of slightly lower quality results, as measured by mean squared error, with results of 1.15 and 1.23 for plan and database schema set addition problems respectively. Overall, our method effectively balances efficiency and effectiveness for set addition problems by incorporating a hybrid of contextual and non-contextual preference information. The implemented system is also available for further research. 
Technically, our contribution involves adapting the conceptual representation framework of planning to address set addition problems. The framework consists of preference information, planning domain description and problem description. The domain and problem descriptions represent specific instances of planning domains and problems. Our method involves generating preference information through a domain-specific search protocol to combine contextual and non-contextual preference information. The strength of our approach lies in its ability to effectively utilise available preference information to efficiently handle set addition problems. 
A preliminary version of our paper was published in the Proceedings of the Workshop on Artificial Intelligence for the Semantic Web at the 21st International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in 2009.

By combining linear regression and spectral analysis, we have developed a method to identify distinct kinetic modes within these liquids. These kinetic modes are found to be linked to specific collective modes in the thermodynamic regime and we demonstrate that our method is universally applicable to polymer liquids. Furthermore, we show that our framework allows for accurate prediction of activation mechanisms and activation energies in the dynamical regime, without prior knowledge of the specific kinetic mode involved. As a result, we have gained a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between thermodynamic and kinetic properties within glass-forming polymer liquids. We have also identified additional activation mechanisms in the glass transition of poly(methyl methacrylate), which were previously unknown. These findings highlight the value of analytical techniques in the scientific study of glass formation. A new variable step size Semi-Implicit Midpoint Integration Method (σIMIM) has been developed for solving explicit Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) using a dual time framework. The σIMIM Method, at its core, incorporates the Implicit Midpoint Method and utilizes a similar structure as the Implicit Runge-Kutta method of order 4 (IRK4) but with enhanced capabilities of adapting stepsizes. Therefore, we investigate how to apply σIMIM to achieve superconvergence properties similar to IRK4 by applying an interpolation post-processing step. Moreover, we theoretically prove the σIMIM method's stability at its maximum Practical Consistency Limit (PCL) and validates these findings through numerical experiments. Lastly, we explore additional techniques to increase the σIMIM method's efficiency by employing Step Size Adaptation (SSA) methods. Conversely, some SSA methods may compromise the σIMIM method's superconvergence properties; thus, we investigate and demonstrate strategies to restore these findings. Theoretical findings are further confirmed through numerical experiments presented in this study. The combined techniques of variable step size, superconvergence, and adaptive step size methods develop the foundations for a highly efficient numerical framework. Portfolio managers seek to maximize the expected value of a function representing profit beyond a certain threshold of risk.  This is contrasted with traditional mean-variance optimization, which aims to minimize the risk of losses above a certain benchmark.  By using a power function to measure outcomes, portfolio performance and risk are better represented when the function's exponent is greater than or equal to one.  When the exponent is less than one, however, this traditional approach actually corresponds with expected portfolio returns.  This expectation is based on a certain investment strategy, which may not be optimal for scenarios involving relatively wealthy investors or those looking to protect their wealth.  This report discusses these issues and explores Merton's seminal work on optimal portfolio allocation.  A wealthier investor, specifically one with infinite wealth, will likely diversify their assets in a certain proportion based on the assets' volatility.  This ratio is directly related to the ratio of the assets' growth potential to their differences in the assets' means minus the costs associated with not fully investing in the market, which is known as the liability.  This ratio is known as the negative linearity of investment and is influenced by various factors, including time and risk.  Additionally, as the expected value of logarithmic returns is greater than the expected value of power utilities of relative wealth, optimal portfolios are typically characterized by a certain proportion of wealth invested, which is known as the Merton-Carroll ratio.  This ratio is also known as the MCR and is influenced by a variety of factors, including the assets' means, volatilities, and correlations as well as time and risk.  By using a power function with an exponent equal to one, the MCR effectively represents the expected return on a two-fund portfolio consisting of the market and a risk-free asset.  By combining the MCR equations and adding them to the equations describing expected returns, a system of equations is formed that can be used to solve for various factors, including the total wealth and relative wealth parameters.  Additionally, as the expected value of a power function is greater than the expected value of a exponential function, solutions involving a power utility are generally better than those involving an exponential function.  By using a utility function with an exponent equal to one and equal to two, for example, the expected values are greater than those obtained from an exponential function and less than those obtained from a power function with an exponent equal to two. Research on the intergalactic medium within dwarf galaxies is less extensive compared to larger galaxies, but existing studies suggest a potential link between cold gas within the dwarf galaxy and the hot intergalactic medium, enabling the conversion of atomic gas into molecular gas through thermal processes. This review focuses on the current knowledge of the intergalactic medium within dwarf galaxies, discussing their characteristics, implications for star formation, and comparing properties with larger galaxies. It also explores future research opportunities that could be pursued with upcoming X-ray telescopes. Past observations of hot gas within dwarf galaxies imply the presence of accreting or heating materials, which may be due to interactions with the intragroup medium or part of larger galaxy-scale processes. Knowledge gaps remain regarding cold gas within low-luminosity dwarf galaxies. Specifically, observations have not consistently demonstrated the presence of hot gas within ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, whereas brighter dwarf galaxies have detectable hot gas with X-ray temperatures ranging from $0.65$ to $0.85 \, \mathrm{keV}$. This lack of hot gas in ultra-faint dwarf galaxies cannot be fully explained by limited observational capabilities and suggests significant mass losses due to thermal escape or outflows, which could be caused by processes such as supermassive black hole activity or intense star formation. Research on low-mass dwarf galaxies provides unique insights into the fundamental processes that initiated and regulated star formation and black hole growth throughout galaxy evolution, and it compares interestingly with recent observations of Milky Way dwarf galaxy satellites within the Gaia $S_{\mathrm{starform}}$ dataset. This review concludes by suggesting areas for further research, including the potential links between galaxy evolution, star formation, and black hole growth in low-mass and high-mass galaxies, and suggests investigating galaxy interactions between the galaxy and its intergalactic medium to resolve the large uncertainties regarding dwarf galaxy star formation and black hole growth. Research on low-mass and high-mass galaxies could provide a new understanding of the cosmic star formation rate, black hole growth, and galaxy evolution across various galaxy masses. A future study could investigate whether galaxy evolution driven by the intergalactic medium is unique to low-mass or high-mass galaxies by analyzing a sample of intermediate-mass galaxies. Such research could help reveal whether dwarf galaxy and massive galaxy development are driven by distinct processes or shared commonalities. We've identified an unusual scenario in which fermionic quasiparticles fail, even in extremely simple models. These quasiparticles aren't thought to exist in simple models where fermions pair up. We've extended this basic framework by introducing a boson that can interact with the fermions. This interaction causes the formation of a gapped state involving the fermions and bosons. Surprisingly, this scenario meets all the criteria for fermionic quasiparticle formation, yielding a gapped excitations at the end. However, these excitations aren't truly fermionic quasiparticles due to a non-local nature. We've also discovered similar scenarios involving anyonic quasiparticles that may exhibit a form of non-Abelian behavior, even though their excitations don't conform to the expectations based on the Kitaev model. The key distinguishing feature of these scenarios is the presence of a 'barrier'. We suggest that this mechanism could potentially apply to the description of superconducting materials displaying a sublattice pattern of doping. Such systems might feature a 'doped' boson that can interact with the fermions, yielding a gapped state involving the fermions and bosons. Crucially, this scenario meets all the criteria for fermionic quasiparticle formation, yet these quasiparticles don't exist in this model due to the non-local nature of the associated excitations, which might be consistent with the experimental findings regarding the end states of the samples in question. The underlying model is remarkably simple, with a short-range fermionic interaction that can be mediated by a doped boson. We've also established that this model is likely to be computationally tractable, with a unique property that distinguishes it from the related systems that aren't thought to support fermionic quasiparticles. Specifically, this model is likely to break the chiral symmetry even when the fermions aren't paired up, with a corresponding reduction in computational complexity. We've also outlined a set of proposed experiments that could confirm the existence of this simple model in the context of the samples in question. The associated end states might serve as ideal materials for the implementation of non-Abelian anyonic quasiparticles, with potential applications in topological quantum computation. Our proposed experiments are designed to verify the existence of these quasiparticles by directly accessing the associated end states through transport measurements. We successfully implement a fully end-to-end trained RAG model for the NLP Questions dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results. Our results demonstrate that a model trained from scratch can equal or exceed performance of pre-trained models, such as those based on BERT and ELMO, when fine-tuned on a specific dataset. This breakthrough allows us to propose a cost-effective approach for building custom retrieval models tailored to distinct question-answer datasets. Our code is available for public access at https://github.com/tilde32/fd-RAG.git. Our pre-trained model, fd-RAG-dpr, can be downloaded from the HuggingFace model hub: https://huggingface.co/tilede32/fd-RAG-dpr. Essentially, our model is a "data-driven" retrieval model designed to alleviate the need for pre-trained models in retrieval steps of question-answer processing. This model marks a significant development in the field of NLP, offering a new perspective on utilizing retrieval approaches for question-answer processing and shedding light on the essential role of data in advanced language understanding capabilities. Our work also raises crucial questions about the validity of relying on sophisticated, highly engineered pre-trained models in the field of NLP. This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. Magnus regarding these coefficients, making use of the Riemann-Hilbert and steepest descent methods in an unconventional manner since no solution to the related problem near the singular point at $x=1$ exists in the current mathematical literature. Furthermore, we also investigate the long-term behavior of the polynomials' degree and the zeros of these polynomials within the complex plane. Our analysis reveals a distinct behavior of the zeros for the polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to the specified weight due to its non-continuous properties at $x=1$. In particular, as the degree of the polynomials tends towards infinity, the distance between their zeros tends towards a finite value. This behavior is similar to that seen in symmetrical weight functions except for a notable exception at one of the polynomials' zeros located precisely at $x=1$ and additionally there will be one more visible zero that is strongly separated from the rest due to a newly introduced separation that occurs at a distance proportional to $e^{\pi^2/k}$. This specific case can be viewed as a new type of asymptotic separation that occurs using the specified weight. Our main tool in achieving this problem will be the stable transformation of the problem near the singular point at $x=1$ through a specific conformal mapping that was first developed by Johansson and Wahlberg in 2015 as the 'pastel machine'. This specific conformal mapping will be closely related to solving the problem at hand since it was specifically designed for the type of orthogonal polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to the specified logarithmic weight at $x=0$. This will be the first time an attempt has been made to utilize this specific conformal mapping in a particular application. Microtasks and crowdsourcing have become crucial tools for text processing. However, concerns have arisen about the quality of work produced, particularly when tasks are short and pay minimal, leading to inconsistency. This study specifically investigated summarization tasks by analyzing a dataset of over 107,000 crowdsourced summaries and nearly 5,000 ratings. We employed machine learning models to predict the quality of summaries and classify workers as either 'trusted' or not. A subsequent MTurk study allowed us to gather more detailed worker information, and we analyzed the summary quality provided by top-performing workers. Our study revealed that our machine learning models and crowd-sourced evaluations identified top-performing workers with high accuracy, mostly above 70%. Surprisingly, we found that increasing the reward for a task did not significantly improve the quality of the summaries. This study also demonstrated that relying solely on ratings to filter out unqualified workers is insufficient, as formatted editing is required. Furthermore, while reward increases the quality of the summaries, it does not improve their reliability in terms of consistency. This research emphasizes the need for rewriting MTurk tasks to maintain formatting, thereby ensuring the stability of the crowdsource. As an alternative to extensive filtering process, our solution utilizes machine learning models to determine the qualifications of workers. Finally, we present an automated summarization system using trusted workers' outputs, and through a manual review, we evaluate the overall performance of the system. Our findings provide valuable insights for selecting and managing crowdsourced workers for effective summarization tasks. A major limitation of our study is that it only investigates text summarization, and we require reliable worker filtering in the field of natural language processing. Unfortunately, this study also reveals the MTurk platform has some flaws that cannot be overcome. A related work is provided in the repository: https://github.com/asharar/Worker-Classification. A video summarization system is demonstrated in https://youtu.be/5hYkK0t0H3A. A discussion on the ethical implications of our research can be found in the appendix.  Additionally, the associated code and datasets can be found at https://github.com/asharar/Worker-Classification with a GitHub discussion at https://github.com/asharar/Worker-Classification/issues/6. Also, the related work on Natural Language Processing can be found at https://github.com/asharar/Related-work-NLP. In real-world network data, many networks display characteristics of preferential attachment yet also exhibit properties associated with uniform attachment mechanisms.  This dual behavior presents a challenge for modeling these networks using simple preferential attachment or uniform mixing models, as neither accurately captures their entire nature.  To bridge this gap, we introduce a new class of hybrid networks where edge formation is determined by a combination of rules governing preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  Specifically, new born nodes have a probability distribution that switches between the two attachment mechanisms according to a given time-based protocol.  We investigate the long-term properties of this new class of hybrid networks and provide exact mathematical solutions for their degree distribution and clustering characteristics.  We demonstrate that this new model produces a network that both exhibits preferential and uniform attachment properties and is consistent with a wide range of empirical network data.  Importantly, we show that modifying the time-based protocol for node selection leads to variations in the degree clustering characteristics of the network, thus offering additional flexibility in modeling these networks depending on the desired output.  Finally, we apply our model to a specific case study involving a network of co-authored scientific research papers and demonstrate its ability to accurately model preferential and uniform attachment properties separately and collectively.  This study offers a new understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving network evolution and may have significant implications for various modeling and analysis approaches.  Furthermore, our model provides a new framework and set of tools for directing network growth and shaping its final structure and properties in desired ways, whether for modeling, analysis, optimization, or control purposes.  We include supplementary material with additional results and figures to further enhance the value of the introduced model of directed hybrid networks.

Wireless communication systems necessitate disturbance detection systems to prevent interference from interfering with their operations. Disturbances within a system's bandwidth can be identified using receivers that recognize known signals, but this method is impractical due to the need to specify a disturbance type and frequency. Disturbances can be unsupervised, detected through data-driven approaches, which rely on accurate multi-label disturbance classification to effectively mitigate interference. In this context, a multi-label disturbance classification framework utilizing convolutional neural networks is introduced for wireless disturbance detection. By analyzing the time and frequency domains of spectral patterns, CNN-based models learn to identify multiple disturbance types simultaneously. The proposed framework encompasses three algorithms: a standard multi-label approach for comparison, a proposed soft-label framework for handling uncertainty, and a generated-data framework that employs synthetic data to supplement limited real data. The frameworks are evaluated using datasets created from the IEEE 802.15.4 standard at 2 Mbps, containing six interference signals, and compared based on accuracy, F1-score, and Area under the Curve (AUC) metrics. The results indicate that the generated-data framework outperforms the other two, demonstrating a high F1-score of 0.95 and AUC of 0.99, which showcases its efficacy in addressing interference within IEEE 802.15.4 standard devices. The introduction of a proposed framework addresses the challenges of multi-label disturbance classification and highlights its effectiveness in identifying multiple interference signals within spectral patterns. The framework provides a feasible solution for automatically detecting and identifying interference within wireless communication systems, including IoT technology, including the implementation of a software prototype on Raspberry Pi. The research also offers a framework that can be adapted for detecting multiple interference signals within various wireless communication standards, including IEEE 802.11 and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). The adaptation process requires modifying the convolutional neural network model and using the new dataset for training. Given that CNN models often exhibit device-specific accuracy, it is crucial to ensure that the device used for training and implementation matches the one employed during data creation. The research is translatable to various devices, including IoT modules, such as USB devices, ensuring that the device specification matches the one used for training. The specification of the convolutional neural network model and the code are publicly available on the author's repository website. The research introduces a framework that can be translatable to various wireless communication standards, including IEEE 802.11 and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). The adaptation process of the framework for these standards can potentially yield improved performance in multi-label disturbance

To grasp the impact of a cosmic string on the behavior of particles, a comprehensive study is conducted, focusing on the case where particles are not restricted to specific trajectories.
