This method is founded on the principle of stochastic gradient ascent, and we've demonstrated its capability to estimate the contribution of a single tensor factor to the total tensor variance. By combining the generated estimates for each factor, we've created a method that produces an approximate solution for the tensor SVD. Our method is capable of producing an exact solution if desired, and we've also identified a strategy for reducing the required number of passes if an approximate solution is sufficient. The proposed method can be executed in parallel without the need for communication between processes, and we've shown that it shares an analytical connection to the tensor SVD as a whole. We've also provided initial experimental evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method on a large classification dataset. Our results suggest that the proposed method is capable of achieving competitive results with a significantly reduced number of passes. For instance, we've observed that the proposed method is capable of achieving 80% accuracy with a reduced number of passes, and further reducing the number of passes only serves to improve efficiency while still maintaining an accuracy of at least 70%. Accurate results have also been achieved for various other datasets in the experimental study. Our research demonstrates the need for further testing the proposed method on additional datasets to confirm its robustness and reliability across diverse applications. The source code for the proposed method has been made publicly available at the following GitHub link: https://github.com/ashar122/TensorSVD. We introduce a method that takes a sequence of evolving graphs as input, using the message-passing network to learn an edge-aware and node-aware latent representation of each graph in the sequence. The final graph in the sequence is compared against a specialized contrastive loss function that checks for similarities between nodes and edges across different graphs. Our evolvable graph embeddings are versatile and can be used across various tasks such as bridge detection, classification, and more. Building upon the success of inverse reinforcement learning in mimicking expert behavior, we investigate its counterpart, reverse constrained reinforcement learning (RCRI). This problem focuses on a setting where an AI observes a constraint being enforced in real-world interactions with an environment. By limiting the AI's policy options while allowing it to make choices, an expert can impose a specific performance constraint on the AI. RCRI aims to determine the underlying reward function that guides an expert's behavior when constrained by a specific, predetermined constraint. We define a candidate reward function as locally optimal if it closely mirrors the expert's chosen actions under the given constraint. We then develop local and global optimization methods to identify the most suitable reward function, using constraint-invariant dynamics as a key component. Furthermore, we provide quantitative assessments of our approach through both theoretical analysis and a comprehensive set of experiments. While our results show that local optimization can yield high performance, it may not lead to a comprehensive understanding of the reward function. Conversely, global optimization guarantees the existence of a locally optimal solution but often relies on an excessive computational burden. By combining the two methods, we create a hybrid strategy that effectively balances the trade-off between performance and computational efficiency. The outcomes of our approach are independently validated through both automated testing and human-based evaluation. We conduct a thorough investigation into the limitations of our method in a diverse array of scenarios, revealing that assumptions regarding the invertibility of the constraint play a vital role in determining its performance. Ultimately, we demonstrate how RCRI can serve as a powerful tool for automating various tasks, including converting a vehicle's safety rules into an understandable format and transforming a robot's operational limitations into an intelligent policy framework. Unlike prior work assuming similar action spaces for all decision-making steps, we established that no algorithm can perfectly solve the identification problem when action sets differ. Our method utilizes two key techniques - within-action mean reward model for estimation purposes and between-action regression for identification. With the ability to balance estimation and identification, UNES exhibits improved performance in both new and existing linear bandit scenarios. Our algorithm's effectiveness is further illustrated through application in linear bandit settings with various other constraints, including bell-shaped and polyhedral action sets. Even in the most complex scenario of polyhedral sets, UNES achieves sub-linear regret with bounding regret at C sqrt(K). Furthermore, we extended UNES for simultaneous online learning and offline prediction tasks and established that its bound is at least an order of magnitude better than the best offline prediction algorithms alone. Specifically, our method achieves a dimension free regret with O(1 / sqrt(K)) regret in the case of various action sets with bounded action norms. Our method's efficiency and performance are further demonstrated through bell-shaped and polyhedral set experiments. Analysis of UNES's performance also led to several theoretical contributions some of which are proven to be tight. These results include that no algorithm can achieve the same level of estimation accuracy as UNES without knowledge of gamma, that no algorithm can achieve the same level of identification accuracy as UNES without knowledge of delta, and that no algorithm can achieve the same level of both identification and estimation accuracy as UNES without knowledge of delta and gamma. Our method also led to the development of a new bound on regret in the case of identifiable but unbounded action sets with the rate of n^{-1/4} + ( lambda_2 / lambda_1 )^2 n^-1, where lambda_1 and lambda_2 are the smallest and second smallest eigenvalues of X^T X. This bound is at least 4 times better than the best prior work in the case of various action sets with bounded action norms. In this research, additional photometric information is used to enhance the matching process between catalogs by increasing the weight of well-understood objects, while objects with unclear identities are assigned a weight based on how well their photometric properties match those of other objects.  This method prioritizes objects based on their photometric consistency as well as their astrometric accuracy, resulting in a significant 50,000-fold decrease in the number of ambiguous objects to be examined manually within the photometric catalogs of the Southern sky.  This new approach is demonstrated using a set of photometric catalogs of variable stars, which are part of an ongoing project to create a unified variable star catalog known as the Southern Variability Catalogue, based on data from the SuperNova-Accelerating-Dragnets Project.  This new approach allows for the efficient matching of objects, streamlining the manual examination process and ultimately facilitating the examination of only the objects that require human intervention in order to obtain accurate results.  This method is not limited to the available data and can be effectively applied to the matching of objects within the universe, regardless of their origin. If no such finite $\mathcal{C}$ exists, we say $\mathcal{H}$ has no infinite edge covers of minimal size. We introduce an novel approach to semi-supervised speech recognition that leverages CycleGAN to address inter-domain disparities between manually annotated text and spoken audio. This method is integrated with a specially designed inter-domain penalty to ensure that the learned speech-text mapping remains consistent across the training and testing phases. We evaluate our proposed framework, which combines end-to-end automatic speech recognition with manual transcription, using the WSJ, Librispeech, and Switchboard datasets. By optimizing the cycle loss and incorporating an inter-domain penalty, we have achieved significant improvements in speech recognition accuracy across all datasets used in this research. Specifically, we have observed performance enhancements of 6.3%, 5.5%, and 4.8% in speech recognition tasks conducted on the WSJ, Librispeech, and Switchboard datasets, respectively, using our proposed framework that incorporates both cycle loss and inter-domain penalty. The Soret effect is a temperature difference caused when a temperature gradient crosses a multicomponent mixture containing molecules that are not rigidly connected, leading to the gradual exchange of pure components. The Soret effect has been observed in various mixtures of molecules, with applications in self-regulating systems and thermosensitive materials. Traditional theories of the Soret effect consider the movement of large molecules within a mixture as a result of the difference in their average speeds relative to the surrounding fluid. In this context, we provide a mathematical description of the Soret effect based on the movement of large molecules through the internal movements available to them, with a focus on flexible molecules that are not necessarily linear in shape. Theoretical results are developed for a mixture of two fluids containing molecules that can rotate around a central axis, with external and internal movements mimicked by spherical and ellipsoidal particle shapes. Computational model simulations of the Soret effect in mixtures of freely moving polyphenol molecules through nitrogen at room temperature also support our theoretical findings. Our study sets the foundation for further research into the relationship between internal freedom of movement and Soret effect strength. To develop an effective evaluation system, we first determined the best approach to represent student compositions, contrasting a token-based model that sequences words and a byte-based model that sequences characters. Subsequently, we trained a series of transformer-based language models on samples of student compositions, both with and without guidance from existing evaluation frameworks. Notably, byte-based models performed better than their token-based counterparts. Furthermore, models trained on student compositions exhibited lower scores than models trained on monolingual English text. Interestingly, models trained on student compositions scored higher when the student compositions were of lower quality, indicating some level of adaptation to the students' writing style. Lastly, byte-based models performed more reliably when the input is byte-level translation, as evidenced by their success in an offline evaluation where we simulated student composition translations. This study delves into the consequences of incorrect throwing mechanics, specifically how they impact perception and expectations of observers. Traditional approaches to analyzing throwing motions, whether from human observation or through machine learning, generally assume that the ball's trajectory accurately represents the thrower's intended motion. Realistic simulations of throwing, however, depend on complex factors such as arm position, velocity, and acceleration, making it difficult to create authentic motions when required to specify a point of release. To better understand the consequences of this limitation, we investigated how viewers interpret throwing motions with both authentic and artificial dynamics. Our research found that when watching a throw, viewers tend to overestimate the impact of forces acting on the thrower, especially early in the motion, and make incorrect assumptions about the thrower's point of release based on this interpretation. This implies that artificial or falsified throwing motions with proper dynamics can appear more authentic to observers. To improve the authenticity of throwing mechanics in both machine learning and simulation contexts, we identified key indicators that viewers use to interpret throwing motions and suggested more advanced methods for analyzing and generating throwing motions that better match human perception. Our research was conducted as part of a broader virtual reality study that examined the behavior of users participating in a game, and it offers insights into the potential consequences of this limitation for authentic and realistic interactions, not just in the context of games. Our research was conducted as part of a broader VR study, and it provides new perspectives and data on this topic as well. These findings have significant implications for the creation of realistic and interactive models of human movement, especially in 3D and immersive environments. This method builds upon existing work by leveraging syntactic links to guide translation during the decoding process. Syntactic links are learned using a neural parser, and we present two techniques to optimize its performance: one uses target-side syntax as an additional learning criterion, and the other employs transfer learning to port the source language's syntax to the target language's syntax. Furthermore, we present a method to abstract away from syntax by modeling tree structure through a simple decoding process, and we provide benchmark scores for standard tree structure decoding without syntax. Using multilingual training data can sometimes lead to biases in translation, 
which can be mitigated by decreasing model sensitivity to individual words.
Post-training quantization and word dropout are two methods to achieve this goal, 
although their effectiveness and ease of use with existing translation models vary.
This study compares the two methods in terms of their impact on the quality and 
stability of low-resource MT performance, using a Chinese-English model as a test case.
The findings suggest that word dropout produces slightly better translation 
quality, but its reliability is compromised by occasional severe degradation.
On the other hand, quantization produces consistent translation quality with 
the added benefit of reducing model size and computational cost. 
Ultimately, the choice between the two methods and their potential hyperparameter configurations depends on the priority between consistent, though subpar performance and occasional, potentially top-notch results. 
To reconcile this trade-off, a hybrid approach was developed, combining quantization and word dropout with a pre-training and fine-tuning protocol tailored to mitigating the risks associated with word dropout. 
As a result, the proposed mechanism achieves translation leakage only when encountering unknown words, thereby preserving consistency in translation quality while eliminating dependence on hyperparameters. 
This result sets a new performance standard for the subject matter and establishes a performance baseline for future models. 
Moreover, due to its ability to handle unknown words, the model opens a new pathway for potential future extensions to handle out-of-vocabulary neurons. 
Ultimately, the added benefit of this model stems from its ability to expand the scope of existing translation models and leverage the advantages of quantization to reduce model size and computational cost. 
The associated code for replicating our findings is available at https://github.com/fhatshare/Too-Fragile-To-Touch. 
A demo link for the proposed model is accessible at https://hatshare.github.io/Too-Fragile-To-Touch. 
Lastly, the corresponding publication can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.corr.2022.04.001.

In medical image analysis, data scarcity often hampers performance due to costly and time-consuming annotation processes typically required for machine learning model development. This challenge is particularly severe in fields like radiology, where high-quality image annotation necessitates expert radiologists. This research investigates whether image enhancement techniques can decrease this necessity by leveraging pre-trained models initially trained with minimally labeled data. Our study applied two such autoencoder models, originally trained on 40 labeled images, on three sets of augmented images (original, image enlargement, and image inversion). Our results reveal that these models can effectively segment augmented images not seen during training, including when subjected to pathological transformations. Furthermore, the models trained with augmented data surpassed the performance of those trained solely with original images, despite having seen fewer labeled annotations. This suggests that augmenting data can allow for a substantial decrease in the required number of labeled images needed for high-quality pneumonia detection and segmentation. The current standard approach to detecting COVID-19 in chest CT scans relies on finding lung fields or lesion areas, which are heavily influenced by previous knowledge and tends to mistake healthy areas for infected areas. This leads to a significant challenge in getting accurate COVID-19 diagnosis from automatic systems. To overcome this problem, we developed a new technique by using annotation of infected areas with a simplified mask representation of infected areas for guidance, which allows for a greater degree of freedom and less bias in detection. This technique leads to better accuracy in detecting COVID-19 and reduces the difference between different operators who provide annotations. Numerical studies show our method outperforms others with a difference of more than 1% in the accuracy of detecting infected areas and significantly improves the consistency in the results for different operators. By integrating an optimal controller, the movement policy is efficiently translated into actionable commands for each actuator, taking into account the properties of the elastic actuators, which lack clear definitions of position, velocity, and torque. As a result, the combined approach effectively exploits the advantages offered by these actuators to reduce energy consumption while maintaining the robot's movement speed and stability. A key challenge in fashion search lies in identifying relevant items based on a description, where images are often diverse and require context such as season and style to understand meaning. Unlike standard image retrieval tasks, fashion images must incorporate semantic traits like sleeve type and neck style, implying that a search query represents a set of characteristics rather than a fixed entity. Building upon this understanding, our research introduces a novel paradigm for fashion image retrieval: Feature-Level Trait Manipulation. By employing Feature-Level Trait Manipulation, the characteristics of a query can be modified, allowing the model to distinguish between identical images with varying semantic traits and thus enhance the overall retrieval process. Since labeling fashion images with precise attributes is costly and time-consuming, our method also uses pseudo-labeling with feature-level constraint to train the model in an unsupervised manner, minimizing the impact of noisy labels in the process. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques on three prominent fashion datasets: Fashion2012, ApparelGoogle and Datasift. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of our method reveals that it accurately captures trait manipulations both visually and semantically, resulting in improved retrieval quality. Our research is documented on the GitHub platform. When trained with sufficient data, our method significantly surpasses the performance of a baseline model without feature-level trait manipulation, with a mean average precision rate of up to 75% compared to 50% for the baseline model. Moreover, our method performs competitively with state-of-the-art image retrieval models not specifically designed for fashion, such as GLIM, achieving a mean average precision rate of 66.87%. These results showcase the effectiveness of our semi-supervised feature-level trait manipulation method in the fashion context. Our research is available on the GitHub platform at this link. What is unique about our method is that it accurately captures feature-level trait manipulation in fashion images, resulting in state-of-the-art performance on fashion image retrieval tasks. To further enhance the retrieval process, our method integrates attribute information into the feature-level manipulation task. By doing so, our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques and establishes a new benchmark for fashion image retrieval tasks. What is also notable about our work is that it uses unsupervised pseudo-labeling with feature-level constraint training to minimize the impact of noisy labels in the model. As a result, our method performs competitively with state-of-theart image retrieval models not specifically designed for fashion, setting a new standard for fashion image retrieval tasks. Finally, our method is documented on the GitHub platform.

The task of solving systems of linear equations with poorly posed matrices is a critical issue in various disciplines, involving large-scale equations and sparse patterns. Unfortunately, typical numerical methods like Newton's method or primal gradient descent may not be able to handle all types of ill-posed systems. This work introduces a new approach, dual gradient descent, tailored to tackle ill-posed systems in complex Banach spaces and even more generally in bi-continuous settings. It is inspired by recent advances in peturbation theory and regularization techniques. The dual gradient descent method can be viewed as a proximal regularization scheme where the regulator exhibits unique characteristics. The scheme shows rapid convergence both locally and globally. Experimental results in computer tomography confirm that utilizing dual gradient descent can lead to superior solutions for poorly posed systems. Additionally, this work provides a comprehensive review of peturbation theory and regularization techniques in Banach spaces, including discussions of operator regularity and constraints on linear systems, and highlights the practical applications of dual gradient descent in resolving large-scale ill-posed systems in bi-continuous settings. Moreover, this work illustrates the importance of using complex-valued regulators in regulating m-set valued mappings, and further extends the theoretical results to multi-dimensional ill-posed systems of linear equations. The research demonstrates that dual gradient descent can be modified to handle multi-dimensional systems and yields comparable convergence rates. Finally, this work illustrates how dual gradient descent can be applied to solve multi-dimensional systems and demonstrates its efficiency in solving a 3D ill-posed computer tomography problem. The source code of dual gradient descent is publicly available on the GitHub platform. Its practical applications include its use in resolving large-scale systems of linear equations in bi-continuous settings, as demonstrated in the experimental results in resolving a (3D) computer tomography problem. The experimental results in this work confirm that dual gradient descent can be easily extended to handle multi-dimensional systems and outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in resolving large-scale systems of linear equations in bi-continuous settings. The expected outcomes of this research include the development of a new class of efficient algorithms for solving multi-dimensional systems of linear equations in bi-continuous settings using dual gradient descent, and their successful application in resolving a multi-dimensional computer tomography problem. A key factor determining the performance of light field-based applications is accurate depth estimation. The majority of existing methods focus on developing highly efficient algorithms that achieve high accuracy using a large amount of data. Nevertheless, conventional approaches usually fail to account for occlusion in the data, which significantly hampers their performance. In this research, we introduce a new method that addresses the issue of occlusion by training an explicit network to synthesize reference images unobstructed by objects and by doing so contributes to the development of a post-processing refinement technique. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through comprehensive comparison tests on the established LF-D dataset. The results facilitated the estimation of accurate depth values, which in turn, led to the enhancement of sharpness and accuracy, while also showing substantial improvement over state-of-the-art depth estimation techniques. Specifically, our approach surpasses the state-of-the-art methods by achieving 35.78% better accuracy on the LF-D dataset. The source code for this research has been made available to the public on the GitHub repository located at https://github.com/aminmohamadi2/LF-OCN-R. and the visual illustrations of our research results can be viewed at https://github.com/aminmohamadi2/LF-OCN-R/wiki. Selecting the optimal Access Point or Extender from a range of available options is crucial in maximizing network performance, particularly in crowded networks. This performance optimization task is typically done manually by network administrators who continuously monitor network load. To streamline this process, we propose choosing the optimal AP or Extender through automated selection consideration of signal strength, distance, and channel load, all of which can be gathered using IEEE 802.11k/v standard tools. We examine the effectiveness of using signal strength and distance metrics, and discover that they correlate with network load. Consequently, we introduce a load-sensitive choice process that combines load, distance, and load-considering association techniques to choose the best AP or Extender for each device, resulting in better performance in crowded networks. We evaluate our approach by comparing it to other methods, such as choosing the device with the best signal strength or an alternative load-considering method, and reveal that it yields a performance improvement of up to 60% in certain metrics. This performance boost implies that devices can achieve faster data transfer rates, which could lead to higher overall network load and ultimately result in better quality of service for all devices. This is particularly true when we test our approach in real-world environments, and verify that it outperforms other methods in choosing the optimal AP or Extender for each device. This case study takes place in two different scenarios, one in an office setting with two devices and another in a home network with six devices, and confirms that our approach yields a performance improvement of up to 60% in certain metrics. This performance boost implies that devices can achieve faster data transfer rates, which could lead to higher overall network load and ultimately result in better quality of service for all devices. A demonstration tool called load-choice is also made available to the public to showcase our approach and facilitate its implementation. This implementation was not possible without a network load measurement tool, which I developed in conjunction with the load-choice demonstration. The code for this measurement tool has also been made available to the public.
